stem:
A 28-year-old man on methadone 100 mg daily for opioid use disorder is found unresponsive in a Newcastle community park after combining methadone with diazepam in an attempt to potentiate sedation. He is brought to the ED 30 minutes after the witnessed event with RR 6, GCS 8, SpO2 86 percent on room air, pinpoint pupils, no track marks suggesting concurrent injection.

He responds briefly to 400 microgram IV naloxone with respiratory rate rising to 12 and GCS improving to 12 over 90 seconds. He then deteriorates again over the next 30 minutes back to RR 8 and GCS 9. Bedside glucose 5.4 mmol/L, T 36.4, BP 102/68.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 6 (improved to 12 with naloxone bolus then back to 8), GCS 8 -> 12 -> 9, SpO2 86% RA -> 96% with BVM, BP 102/68.
data_table.Examination: Pinpoint pupils, no track marks, no aspiration evidence, no head injury signs.
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 5.4, paracetamol level pending, ECG sinus normal axis QRS 86 QTc 460.

lead_in: Why has he re-sedated after initial response, and what is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Naloxone has worn off because its half-life (~60 min) is much shorter than methadone (~24 h); commence naloxone infusion at two-thirds the effective bolus dose per hour (0.4 mg/h)
Methadone causes tolerance, so additional doses of methadone should be given to maintain consciousness
Diazepam reversal with flumazenil 0.2 mg IV is the priority
Intubation under RSI rather than continued naloxone, since recurrent doses prolong ED length of stay
Activated charcoal 50 g orally to reduce further methadone absorption

subtopic_detail: Naloxone infusion for methadone overdose - pharmacokinetic mismatch

stem: A 24-year-old previously well woman is admitted to a Gosford acute mental health unit with 3 weeks of progressive anxiety, paranoid delusions, and disorganised speech. Over the past 5 days she has developed orofacial dyskinesias (intermittent lip-smacking and chewing movements), choreoathetoid limb movements, low-grade fever (37.8), and one witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure. She had previously been started on risperidone 2 mg BD 8 days ago for presumed first-episode psychosis with no improvement. She has a history of menstrual irregularity. No personal or family history of psychiatric illness. No drug use confirmed on urine toxicology screen.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8, HR 118 sinus, BP 142/88, RR 22, SpO2 98% RA.
data_table.Examination: Disorganised speech, orofacial dyskinesias, choreoathetoid limb movements, no focal weakness, no rash, mild abdominal mass on bimanual palpation.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFT normal. TSH normal. Urine toxicology negative. CT brain normal. LP CSF: lymphocytosis 36 (mostly lymphocytes), protein 0.52 g/L, glucose normal, ANTI-NMDA-receptor antibodies STRONGLY POSITIVE in CSF; serum anti-NMDA also positive. EEG generalised slowing with delta brushes.

lead_in: Which is the unifying diagnosis, and what additional investigation must be requested urgently?

options.text: First-episode schizophrenia with neuroleptic malignant syndrome from risperidone; cease risperidone and supportive care
Anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis; urgent abdominal/pelvic imaging for ovarian teratoma
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM); high-dose methylprednisolone alone
Limbic encephalitis (anti-Hu); CT chest for small-cell lung cancer
Substance-induced psychosis from undetected synthetic cannabinoid; urine ELISA for synthetic cannabinoids

subtopic_detail: Anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis psychiatric mimic + teratoma search

stem:
A 22-year-old man is brought to ED at John Hunter Hospital after using crystal methamphetamine at a nightclub 90 minutes ago. He is agitated and combative. Initial parenteral midazolam 5 mg IV has reduced agitation partially. His BP remains markedly elevated and he is now developing chest pain radiating to the left arm with diaphoresis. ECG shows ST elevation in the inferolateral leads.

Bedside echo shows preserved LV function and no regional wall motion abnormality at rest. The cardiology registrar asks for pharmacological management of his hypertension prior to angiography, recognising the agent he has used is a presynaptic monoamine releaser causing massive endogenous noradrenaline release acting at both alpha-1 and beta-1 receptors.

data_table.Examination: Agitated but redirectable after midazolam, BP 198/118, HR 142 sinus, temperature 38.1, diaphoretic, mydriatic pupils 6 mm, chest pain 7/10 retrosternal.
data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 180 ng/L (rising), ECG ST elevation II, III, aVF and V5-V6 with reciprocal change, urine drug screen positive amphetamines, ABG pH 7.32 lactate 4.1 mmol/L.

lead_in: Which agent is the single most appropriate first-line for blood pressure control in this setting?

options.text: Glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated to BP and chest pain
Metoprolol 5 mg IV
Atenolol 25 mg orally
Adrenaline 1 mg IV
Verapamil 5 mg IV

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological reversal logic in sympathomimetic ACS

stem:
A 34-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been stable on clozapine 450 mg nocte for 11 months, attending a Newcastle community mental health clinic. He smokes 20 cigarettes daily and has been advised against changing his smoking behaviour without consultation. He presents today with 4 days of intermittent sharp left-sided chest pain, mild dyspnoea on exertion (climbing one flight of stairs), and a single self-recorded resting heart rate of 122.

He denies fever, cough, sputum, syncope, or recent travel. His most recent FBC, UEC, LFT, and CK are within 7 days and normal except WCC 7.2 (with neutrophils 4.8) and CK 142 U/L. He has gained 8 kg over 11 months.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9, HR 118 sinus, BP 124/82, RR 22, SpO2 97% room air.
data_table.Examination: Heart sounds normal, no rub, mild bibasal fine crackles, no peripheral oedema, no calf tenderness, no rash.
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia 118, no ST changes. Troponin I 142 ng/L (ULN 14). NT-proBNP 380 pg/mL. CXR mild cardiomegaly. FBC: WCC 7.2 N 4.8; UEC normal; CK 142; LFT normal.

lead_in: Which clozapine-associated adverse effect is the single most likely explanation for this presentation, and what is the immediate monitoring response?

options.text: Clozapine-induced agranulocytosis; cease clozapine and admit for haematology review
Clozapine-induced myocarditis; cease clozapine, admit, urgent echocardiogram and cardiology consult
Clozapine-induced metabolic syndrome and weight gain; commence atorvastatin 40 mg daily and dietitian referral
Clozapine-induced sialorrhoea; commence hyoscine hydrobromide 0.4 mg sublingually nocte
Clozapine-induced ileus; nil orally, IV fluids, urgent abdominal X-ray

stem:
A 31-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder presents to a Gosford perinatal mental health clinic at 7 weeks gestation. Her bipolar history includes two manic episodes requiring hospitalisation 5 and 8 years ago, three depressive episodes between, and one suicide attempt by overdose 3 years ago. She has been euthymic for 18 months on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily as monotherapy.

She has now stopped valproate on her own initiative 2 weeks ago after discovering the pregnancy. She has a personal history of acne treated with isotretinoin 8 years ago (now resolved), no thyroid disease, normal renal function (Cr 65), and a strong family history of bipolar disorder in her mother. She is keen to continue the pregnancy and plans to breastfeed. She has a supportive partner.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no psychotic symptoms, MSE unremarkable, judgment intact.
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.8 mIU/L, free T4 normal. Cr 65 micromol/L. LFT normal. Beta-hCG confirms 7-week pregnancy.

lead_in: Which mood stabiliser strategy best satisfies ALL the following constraints: minimal teratogenic risk, established efficacy in bipolar maintenance, compatibility with breastfeeding, and minimum complexity of monitoring?

options.text: Restart sodium valproate at half-dose with 5 mg folate; the second trimester is past the highest teratogenicity window
Quetiapine 300-600 mg daily as monotherapy; trimester-specific dose reviews; compatible with breastfeeding
Lithium 750 mg daily; weekly levels first trimester; 12-week and 20-week fetal echo for Ebstein anomaly; cease at 6 weeks postpartum to enable breastfeeding
Carbamazepine 600 mg daily; 5 mg folate daily; vitamin K 20 mg from 36 weeks to prevent neonatal haemorrhage
Cease all mood stabilisers; weekly psychiatry review; restart only if relapse occurs

subtopic_detail: Mood stabiliser selection under multiple pregnancy/BF constraints

stem:
A 22-year-old woman with severe restricting-type anorexia nervosa over 5 years is brought to John Hunter Hospital ED by her mother. The patient is refusing admission. She weighs 38 kg (height 168 cm, BMI 13.5), heart rate 38 bpm sinus, BP 78/48 supine and 65/40 standing, T 35.2 degrees Celsius, glucose 2.8 mmol/L, K 2.6 mmol/L, P 0.42 mmol/L, Mg 0.62 mmol/L.

ECG shows sinus bradycardia with QTc 510 ms. She is alert, coherent, and capable of stating she understands she could die but does not want medical treatment because she fears weight restoration. She has no other psychiatric comorbidity and no acute psychosis. Her mother has lasting power of attorney for property only.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 38 sinus, BP 78/48 supine to 65/40 standing, T 35.2 deg C, weight 38 kg (BMI 13.5), SpO2 95%.
data_table.Examination: Cachexia, lanugo hair, dry mucous membranes, peripheral cyanosis, alert and oriented, MSE no thought disorder, insight present for medical consequences but absent for need for treatment.
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 2.8 mmol/L, K 2.6 mmol/L, P 0.42 mmol/L (low), Mg 0.62 mmol/L (low), ECG sinus brady 38 with QTc 510 ms. Cr 75, urea 4.

lead_in: Which combination of MARSIPAN-AU admission criteria and NSW Mental Health Act 2007 framework most appropriately governs her treatment, given that she is refusing care?

options.text: Discharge against advice with daily outpatient follow-up; her capacity is intact so no involuntary admission is possible

Admit to a medical ward under NSW MHA 2007 Schedule 1 (involuntary mental health assessment) with refeeding under specialist eating-disorder protocol; commence oral phosphate, low-dose IV thiamine 300 mg BD, refeed at 5-10 kcal/kg/day initial rate; daily P/Mg/K; cardiac monitoring for QTc and bradycardia
Admit voluntarily and commence standard adult enteral nutrition at 30 kcal/kg/day via nasogastric tube to rapidly restore weight
Apply for guardianship through the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT) for medical treatment authority; defer treatment until order is granted
Sedate with IM midazolam 5 mg, intubate for airway protection, commence IV TPN 25 kcal/kg/day with continuous insulin infusion to manage hyperglycaemia

subtopic_detail: MARSIPAN-AU admission threshold + NSW MHA 2007 framework

stem:
A 58-year-old man with bipolar I disorder on lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte for 12 years presents to Gosford ED with 5 days of nausea, coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech and increasing confusion. He started ramipril 5 mg 3 weeks ago for new hypertension. Three weeks ago he also started ibuprofen 400 mg TDS for chronic shoulder pain. He has had no fluid losses, no fever, no diuretics.

His last documented serum lithium 6 months ago was 0.7 mmol/L. Today: lithium 2.4 mmol/L, creatinine 138 micromol/L (baseline 84), Na 142, K 4.2, TSH normal, glucose 5.8. ECG sinus rhythm with U waves and prolonged QT.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 102 sinus, BP 142/88, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6).
data_table.Examination: Coarse upper-limb tremor at rest, hyperreflexia 3+, ataxic gait, dysarthria, dysmetria, no focal weakness, confusion to recent events.
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 2.4 mmol/L (therapeutic 0.6-1.0), Cr 138 (baseline 84), Na 142, K 4.2, glucose 5.8. ECG sinus 102 with prolonged QT, U waves. TSH normal.

lead_in: Which is the single best explanation for the cerebellar and basal ganglia signs described, and which clinical scenario most predictably reproduces this mechanism?

options.text: Lithium interferes with neuronal sodium-potassium ATPase and Purkinje-cell function in cerebellum; recurs predictably when CYP450 inhibitors are added to the regimen

Lithium accumulates in neurons via secondary active transport substituting for sodium; clearance falls when GFR drops or proximal tubule sodium reabsorption increases (NSAID, ACEI, dehydration, low salt intake)
Lithium is hepatically metabolised by CYP3A4 and accumulates when CYP3A4 inhibitors are added; clarithromycin and grapefruit juice are the classic triggers
Lithium chelates calcium and reduces parathyroid hormone production; chronic toxicity produces hypocalcaemic tetany and Trousseau sign
Lithium directly inhibits muscarinic receptors causing central anticholinergic toxicity; trigger is co-administration with other antimuscarinic agents

subtopic_detail: Lithium toxicity mechanism + drug interaction predictability

stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 62-year-old woman in clinic. She has been on lithium 750 mg nocte for bipolar I disorder for 14 years and remains euthymic. Her last lithium level 4 months ago was 0.7 mmol/L. Her eGFR has declined gradually from 78 to 62 mL/min/1.73m^2 over 2 years. She is asymptomatic and her urine albumin to creatinine ratio is 2.1 mg/mmol. There is no NSAID use and her blood pressure is well controlled on perindopril 5 mg daily.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic affect; no tremor; no oedema; no goitre; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Na 139, K 4.3, Cr 92, eGFR 62, TSH 3.8, fT4 14, corrected calcium 2.36, lithium 0.7 (target 0.6 to 0.8), HbA1c 5.4%
data_table.Medications: Lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte, perindopril 5 mg mane

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue lithium; recheck lithium level, U&E, TSH and calcium every 3 to 6 months with nephrology referral
Cease lithium and switch to sodium valproate; arrange psychiatry review within 2 weeks for cross-titration
Reduce lithium to 375 mg nocte; recheck lithium level, U&E and TSH at 7 days then again at 4 weeks
Add candesartan 8 mg daily for renoprotection; recheck eGFR, electrolytes and lithium level in 4 weeks
Arrange an urgent renal tract ultrasound and refer to nephrology for renal biopsy within the next 14 days

subtopic_detail: Lithium-induced hypothyroidism in early pregnancy planning
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, stable on lithium 900 mg nocte for 5 years. She and her partner are planning pregnancy in 6 months. She has gained 3 kg, feels cold, and reports new constipation over 8 weeks. Her last manic episode required ICU admission and her psychiatrist regards her as high relapse risk. She is using condoms reliably. The pre-pregnancy bloods are back.

data_table.Examination: Mildly dry skin; slow ankle reflex relaxation; no goitre; affect euthymic; no tremor
data_table.Investigations: TSH 8.4, fT4 11 (low-normal), TPO antibody positive, lithium 0.8, Cr 76, eGFR 92, beta-hCG negative
data_table.Medications: Lithium carbonate 900 mg nocte; folic acid 500 micrograms daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Cease lithium immediately and substitute quetiapine 300 mg nocte; refer to obstetric psychiatry for monitoring
Continue lithium at current dose and commence levothyroxine 50 micrograms daily; recheck TSH and fT4 in 6 weeks
Continue lithium and start carbimazole 5 mg daily; recheck thyroid function and lithium level in 4 weeks
Reduce lithium to 600 mg nocte and start levothyroxine 25 micrograms daily; recheck TSH and lithium in 2 weeks
Continue lithium, withhold levothyroxine and recheck TSH in 12 weeks before any decision on thyroid replacement

stem: You are the early psychosis registrar reviewing a 24-year-old man who started olanzapine 10 mg nocte 3 months ago after a first episode of schizophrenia. He reports a 4 kg weight gain and increased appetite. He smokes 10 cigarettes daily, drinks no alcohol, and has a strong family history of type 2 diabetes. He is otherwise asymptomatic, attending TAFE, and adherent to treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78, HR 78, RR 14, SpO2 99% RA, T 36.7; waist 96 cm, BMI 27
data_table.Examination: Settled affect; no EPS; no tremor; no acanthosis nigricans
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 5.5, HbA1c 5.8%, total cholesterol 5.2, LDL 3.4, HDL 1.0, triglycerides 2.0, ALT 32, prolactin 280 (normal)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management strategy?

options.text: Continue olanzapine; arrange lifestyle counselling and recheck weight, fasting glucose and lipids at 6 months
Switch to aripiprazole 10 mg daily over 4 weeks; recheck weight, fasting glucose and lipids in 3 months
Continue olanzapine with lifestyle intervention; arrange 3-monthly weight, BP, fasting glucose and lipids in year 1
Continue olanzapine; add metformin 500 mg twice daily and recheck weight, HbA1c and fasting lipids in 3 months
Stop olanzapine; switch to risperidone 2 mg twice daily and commence atorvastatin 20 mg nocte for CV risk

stem: You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman with schizophrenia, stable on risperidone 4 mg daily for 18 months. She reports 4 months of amenorrhoea, breast tenderness and recent galactorrhoea. She is not pregnant. She is otherwise mentally well and has previously failed olanzapine due to weight gain. Her prolactin is 1850 mIU/L (normal less than 500 in non-pregnant adult).

data_table.Examination: Galactorrhoea bilateral on expression; no visual field defect; no acromegalic features
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 1850, beta-hCG negative, TSH 1.8, fT4 14, oestradiol low, LH and FSH low-normal; MRI pituitary normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue risperidone and commence cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly; recheck prolactin in 6 weeks
Reduce risperidone to 2 mg daily; arrange endocrinology review and recheck prolactin within 4 weeks
Continue risperidone at current dose; reassure that mild prolactin rise is expected and recheck symptoms in 6 months
Switch risperidone to aripiprazole 10 mg daily over 4 weeks; recheck prolactin and review symptoms at 6 weeks
Cease risperidone abruptly; commence quetiapine 100 mg twice daily and refer to gynaecology for amenorrhoea workup

stem: You are the adult psychiatry registrar reviewing a 26-year-old man with newly diagnosed ADHD-combined type confirmed on DIVA-5 interview and corroborated by partner and parents. Childhood symptoms documented in school reports. He has no current substance use disorder, no cardiac history, no family history of sudden cardiac death and is otherwise well. He drives a car as part of his work delivering parcels. His ECG and BP are normal.

data_table.Examination: Distractible during interview; otherwise normal; ECG sinus rhythm QTc 410 ms
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative; TSH normal; FBC, U&E and LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological choice and the most important counselling point about driving?

options.text: Commence atomoxetine 40 mg daily; advise that he must surrender his licence to Vicroads while on stimulant medication
Commence guanfacine extended release 1 mg daily; advise that driving is contraindicated for the first 6 weeks of treatment
Commence bupropion 150 mg daily; advise that ADHD without comorbid depression rarely requires pharmacotherapy
Commence dexamfetamine 5 mg twice daily; counsel that he must inform police about stimulant use at every interaction
Commence lisdexamfetamine 30 mg morning; counsel that untreated ADHD increases crash risk and treated driving is generally safe

subtopic_detail: Nicotine withdrawal in a hospital inpatient
stem: You admit a 58-year-old man with a fractured tibia for theatre tomorrow. He smokes 25 cigarettes daily, last smoked four hours ago, and is now restless, irritable and demanding to leave the ward.

data_table.Observations: BP 146/88, HR 96, afebrile, pain 4/10 on regular analgesia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Apply a 21 mg nicotine patch now, with lozenges for breakthrough craving
Prescribe diazepam 5 mg orally as required for agitation and review tomorrow
Start varenicline 0.5 mg daily and plan a quit date postoperatively
Allow supervised leave from the ward to smoke before theatre
Defer any nicotine treatment until after his operation tomorrow

stem: You are the emergency medicine registrar called to a 32-year-old man in the resus bay who arrived via police. He is shouting, swinging at staff and security, and refusing oral medication. There is no obtainable history beyond that he was found wandering on a freeway. Five staff and two security officers have established physical containment in lateral recumbent position. There is no IV access. His airway is patent.

data_table.Vital signs: BP estimated 150/90 by manual, HR 132, RR 28, SpO2 unmeasured, T not yet measured; finger-prick glucose 6.8
data_table.Examination: Sweating, dilated pupils, dry mucosa, no obvious trauma, no track marks visible
data_table.Investigations: ECG not yet feasible; capillary glucose 6.8; venous gas pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first parenteral medication?

options.text: Midazolam 10 mg intramuscular into deltoid; reassess at 15 minutes and repeat 5 mg if not adequately settled
Droperidol 10 mg intramuscular into deltoid; reassess at 15 minutes and repeat once if not adequately settled
Haloperidol 5 mg with lorazepam 2 mg intramuscular into deltoid; reassess at 30 minutes for response
Olanzapine 10 mg intramuscular into deltoid; await onset over 20 minutes before considering further sedation
Ketamine 4 mg/kg intramuscular into deltoid as immediate dissociative sedation pending ICU transfer for intubation

stem: You are the emergency medicine consultant overseeing the resuscitation of a 26-year-old man with suspected methamphetamine intoxication. He has received droperidol 10 mg IM 25 minutes ago and a repeat droperidol 10 mg IM 10 minutes ago. He continues to thrash against restraints despite a brief period of partial settling. His core temperature is now 39.1, HR 168 sinus on monitor, BP 168/104, and he has bitten his lip with blood in airway. There is one functional IV line. The team is preparing to intubate.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.1, HR 168 sinus, BP 168/104, RR 36, SpO2 92% on 15 L NRB; capillary glucose 8.2
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, rigid, clenched jaw, lip laceration with airway blood; pupils 6 mm reactive
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.18, lactate 8.2, K 5.8, Na 142; CK 4200; troponin pending; ECG sinus tachycardia, QTc 480
data_table.Medications: Droperidol 10 mg IM x2 in last 25 minutes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Ketamine 4 mg/kg intramuscular as immediate sedation; defer intubation until obtainable cooperation for nasal airway placement
Repeat droperidol 10 mg IM and add midazolam 5 mg IV; reassess in 10 minutes before considering airway intervention
Rapid sequence intubation with ketamine 1.5 mg/kg IV and rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg IV; commence active cooling with cold IV fluids
Dantrolene 1 mg/kg IV with active surface cooling; transfer to ICU and defer airway intervention
Suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg IV alone with bag mask ventilation; insert nasogastric tube for activated charcoal administration

stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman admitted under medicine for dehydration and reduced oral intake over 5 days. She has known schizophrenia previously stable on aripiprazole. She is mute, holds bizarre postures for minutes at a time, and appears to be staring at the wall. Bush-Francis catatonia rating scale is 14. CT brain unremarkable. EEG, infection screen and lithium not contributory. Her aripiprazole was stopped on admission by the medical team.

data_table.Examination: Mute, waxy flexibility, posturing arms above head 60 seconds, no tremor, no rigidity, no fever
data_table.Investigations: CK 320 (mildly elevated), Na 142, K 4.0, WCC 8.4, CRP 6, TSH normal, CT brain normal, lumbar puncture deferred
data_table.Medications: Aripiprazole ceased on admission; IV maintenance fluids

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Restart aripiprazole 10 mg orally daily; continue intravenous maintenance fluids and reassess catatonia at 48 hours
Administer haloperidol 5 mg intramuscularly with promethazine 25 mg intramuscularly and reassess in 30 minutes
Refer urgently for electroconvulsive therapy without prior pharmacological challenge; consent through guardianship board
Administer lorazepam 2 mg intravenously and reassess Bush-Francis score within 10 to 15 minutes for response
Administer amantadine 100 mg orally twice daily; arrange MRI brain with contrast over the next 48 hours

stem: You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 22-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder. She has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 3 years. She has a new male partner and reports inconsistent condom use. She does not currently want to become pregnant but is open to pregnancy in 2 to 3 years. She has not been counselled about valproate and pregnancy. Her TGA-listed indication and the AU pregnancy prevention requirements apply.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no tremor, no peripheral oedema, normal gait
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, LFTs normal, valproate 480 micromol/L (target 350 to 700), beta-hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue valproate; arrange annual ultrasound screening for ovarian morphology and reassess teratogenic counselling in 12 months
Switch valproate to lamotrigine 200 mg daily; commence folic acid 5 mg daily and continue current condom-only contraception
Continue valproate; commence high-dose folic acid 5 mg daily and reassure that contraception is not yet necessary
Cease valproate abruptly; bridge with quetiapine 300 mg nocte and arrange psychiatry review within 2 weeks for stability
Continue valproate; arrange counselling on teratogenic risk and ensure highly effective contraception is in place

stem: You are the community mental health team registrar reviewing a 26-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder. She has had 4 self-harm episodes by superficial cutting in the last 6 weeks and 1 emergency presentation with paracetamol ingestion of 8 g 3 weeks ago, managed conservatively. She is currently on no psychotropic medication and is willing to engage in psychological therapy. She has chronic feelings of emptiness, fear of abandonment and intense unstable relationships. There are no psychotic features.

data_table.Examination: Multiple superficial healing forearm lacerations; mood reactive; no psychosis; no acute suicidality at interview
data_table.Investigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs (post-paracetamol) normal; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line management strategy?

options.text: Refer for dialectical behaviour therapy with weekly individual and weekly skills group for at least 12 months
Commence quetiapine 100 mg nocte; arrange GP review in 4 weeks; defer psychological therapy until mood is more stable
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy of 12 sessions focused on cognitive restructuring for self-harm thoughts
Admit for inpatient stabilisation under the Mental Health Act; arrange psychiatric review for medication initiation
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily; refer to GP-led mental health treatment plan for 10 sessions of supportive counselling

stem: You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman who took her dosette tray of amitriptyline 50 mg tablets approximately 90 minutes ago after a relationship breakup. She estimates 28 tablets ingested. On arrival she is drowsy but rousable, with dry mucous membranes and an ECG showing sinus tachycardia. She has just had one self-terminating generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 45 seconds. The ECG is in front of you.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 92/58, HR 132, RR 18, SpO2 96% on 6 L Hudson mask, T 37.2, GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5)
data_table.Examination: Dry mucosa, dilated pupils, hyperreflexia, no focal deficit, no airway compromise after seizure
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia HR 132, QRS 140 ms, terminal R wave aVR 5 mm; pH 7.28, lactate 3.4, K 3.6, paracetamol negative
data_table.Medications: Amitriptyline 50 mg nocte usually; no other regular medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer flumazenil 200 micrograms IV; commence intravenous normal saline 1 L over 30 minutes and recheck ECG
Administer sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol IV bolus and prepare an infusion; intubate if GCS drops or seizures recur
Administer activated charcoal 50 g orally; commence intravenous diazepam 5 mg for sedation and seizure prophylaxis
Administer magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 10 minutes; commence amiodarone 300 mg infusion for arrhythmia prophylaxis
Administer intravenous lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg over 1 minute; commence noradrenaline infusion for hypotension control

stem: You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 28-year-old teacher with 4 weeks of right leg weakness preventing her from walking unassisted. There is no antecedent trauma. She is currently on workers' compensation for unrelated stress leave. Examination shows Hoover sign positive on the right leg, give-way weakness throughout the right leg with normal tone and reflexes, and a non-anatomical sensory loss. MRI brain and spine are normal. Nerve conduction studies are normal.

data_table.Examination: Right leg 2/5 power on direct testing with give-way pattern; Hoover sign positive; sensory loss to fingertip threshold non-anatomical; reflexes 2+; toes downgoing
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain and spine normal; NCS and EMG normal; B12, TSH, glucose normal

lead_in: Which statement most accurately describes the diagnostic framework?

options.text: Defer diagnosis; arrange repeat MRI with contrast and lumbar puncture in 4 weeks to exclude inflammatory disease conclusively
Diagnose malingering based on the workers' compensation context and refer to occupational physician for capacity assessment
Diagnose factitious disorder imposed on self based on absence of physical findings and presence of psychosocial stressor
Diagnose functional neurological disorder based on positive Hoover sign and rule-in clinical features; explain the diagnosis collaboratively
Diagnose generalised anxiety disorder based on the work-related stress; commence sertraline 50 mg daily and refer for CBT

subtopic_detail: Refeeding syndrome prevention in severe anorexia
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 19-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa restricting subtype. BMI is 13.4, she has been eating less than 500 kcal per day for 8 weeks and her phosphate on admission is 0.65 mmol/L. She has no oedema. Her ECG shows sinus bradycardia at 38 with QTc 470 ms. She is awake and oriented. The eating disorder service has requested admission for refeeding under their protocol.

data_table.Examination: Cachectic, lanugo, cool peripheries, no peripheral oedema, mild orthostatic drop
data_table.Investigations: Na 140, K 3.1, phosphate 0.65 (low), Mg 0.62 (low), Cr 64, glucose 3.4, Hb 102, WCC 3.2, LFTs ALT 78, ALP 92, INR 1.1, ECG QTc 470, HR 38

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial refeeding strategy?

options.text: Commence enteral feed at 30 kcal/kg per day with daily electrolyte monitoring; replace phosphate and magnesium intravenously
Defer feeding for 24 hours; correct electrolytes first then start enteral feed at 20 kcal/kg per day with weekly electrolytes
Commence parenteral nutrition at 25 kcal/kg per day; replace electrolytes intravenously and start propranolol for bradycardia
Commence oral diet ad libitum with appetite-led portions; check phosphate and magnesium twice weekly during refeeding admission
Commence oral feed at 5 to 10 kcal/kg per day with cardiac monitoring; replace phosphate, magnesium and potassium and give thiamine 200 mg IV daily for 3 days

stem: You are the community mental health registrar reviewing a 24-year-old woman with a 4-year history of intense unstable relationships, recurrent self-harm by superficial cutting, chronic feelings of emptiness, and impulsive spending. She has had 3 brief inpatient admissions for safety after threats of self-harm. She is not currently suicidal. There is no active substance use disorder, no eating disorder, and her PHQ-9 today is 7 (mild). She wants to feel more stable in herself.

data_table.Examination: Healed superficial linear scars on forearms; reactive affect; no current SI; no thought disorder; no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 7, GAD-7 9, ASRS negative, AUDIT 3; FBC, U&E, TSH normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate evidence-based first-line intervention?

options.text: Refer for dialectical behaviour therapy; arrange care coordination with crisis plan and skills coaching access
Commence olanzapine 5 mg nocte and arrange psychiatry review in 4 weeks for response and side effects
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily; review at 4 weeks for response and adverse effects with structured measurement
Arrange weekly individual supportive psychotherapy alone; review every 12 weeks with non-structured care coordination
Admit for short-term inpatient psychiatric care; commence quetiapine 50 mg nocte during stabilisation phase

stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 32-year-old man who was a passenger in a fatal car accident 6 months ago. He has flashbacks 3 times daily, sleep disturbance with nightmares 4 nights per week, avoids driving on motorways, and is hypervigilant. He drinks 2 standard drinks per week, no other substance use. He has no past psychiatric history. He is keen to engage in treatment and prefers psychological therapy over medication. PHQ-9 today is 14 (moderate).

data_table.Examination: Anxious but cooperative; intrusive thoughts of the accident on direct questioning; intact thought form; no psychosis; no SI
data_table.Investigations: PCL-5 score 52; PHQ-9 14; AUDIT 3; thyroid and CMP normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily titrated to 100 mg at 4 weeks; review response at 6 weeks
Refer for trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy; review response after 8 to 12 sessions
Commence prazosin 1 mg nocte titrated for nightmares; review and add sertraline at 4 weeks if no response
Recommend supportive counselling and watchful waiting for 3 months before commencing any active intervention
Commence quetiapine 50 mg nocte for sleep and anxiety; review response at 4 weeks for symptom control

subtopic_detail: Adult ASD recognition in women with masking
stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman with a 12-year history of recurrent burnout from work and social demands. She describes feeling like she is acting in social situations and reports intense sensory sensitivity to fluorescent lights and clothing tags. She has narrow restricted interests in 19th century botany. She has a history of anorexia nervosa and a previous diagnosis of social anxiety. Her cousin has autism. She has come because she suspects she might be autistic.

data_table.Examination: Eye contact intermittent; affect appropriate; no thought disorder; no psychotic features; settled mood
data_table.Investigations: AQ-50 score 38, RAADS-R score 168, no hearing or vision deficit; previous PHQ-9 8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure that adult diagnosis of autism is uncommon in women; address presenting anxiety with CBT and lifestyle measures
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily for social anxiety; review in 4 weeks for response and tolerability
Refer for formal multidisciplinary autism assessment using ADOS-2 and developmental history with collateral
Refer for borderline personality disorder assessment with DBT consideration; defer autism workup pending personality diagnosis
Recommend reading on social skills training and self-directed online ASD modules; review at 6 months

stem: You are the inpatient psychiatry registrar reviewing a 27-year-old man on admission. Over the past 8 weeks he has been hearing third-person voices commenting on his actions and believing the government is monitoring him through his phone. For the last 3 weeks of that period he has been elated, sleeping 2 hours per night, hyperactive and grandiose, spending $20,000 on cryptocurrency. He has a prior depressive episode 18 months ago. He denies substance use, urine drug screen negative.

data_table.Examination: Pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiose delusions, third-person auditory hallucinations; thought broadcasting; no insight
data_table.Investigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs, TSH normal; urine drug screen negative; CT head normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychosis; start olanzapine 10 mg nocte and lithium 750 mg nocte with monitoring
Schizophreniform disorder; commence risperidone 2 mg twice daily and refer to early psychosis intervention service
Substance-induced psychosis; observe over 7 days off all substances and reassess for diagnostic clarification
Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type; commence olanzapine 10 mg nocte plus mood stabiliser (lithium) with ongoing monitoring
Brief psychotic disorder; commence aripiprazole 10 mg daily; review for resolution over 1 month before further treatment

stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman admitted with left-sided weakness for 3 days. The neurologist has ruled out stroke (MRI, CTA and CSF normal) and a video EEG of an episode shows preserved consciousness with normal background. She demonstrates Hoover sign with weakness ablating on contralateral hip extension. She works as a teacher and is not facing legal proceedings or insurance claims. She is distressed by her symptoms and wants to return to work.

data_table.Examination: Left hemiparesis 3/5 globally; positive Hoover sign; normal reflexes and tone; intact sensation to pinprick; tremor entrainment positive
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain and CTA normal; CSF normal; video EEG normal background during episode; FBC, U&E, TFT normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate management?

options.text: Malingering; document discrepancy, withdraw analgesia and refer to occupational health for fitness for duty
Factitious disorder; transfer to psychiatry under involuntary section for ongoing observation and confrontation with team
Somatic symptom disorder; commence sertraline 50 mg daily and refer for CBT for somatic symptoms over 12 weeks
Stroke mimic with conversion overlay; arrange thrombectomy review and add aspirin 100 mg daily for secondary prevention
Functional neurological disorder; explain diagnosis using positive signs and refer to physiotherapy with FND-specific approach

stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 19-year-old woman with severe anorexia nervosa (BMI 13.4, weight 36 kg, recent 5 kg loss over 4 weeks) to a general medical ward. She has been eating less than 500 kcal per day for 2 months and reports occasional dizzy spells. She is alert, hydrated and apyrexial. Bloods on arrival show low normal electrolytes and the dietitian has commenced a structured refeeding plan starting at 20 kcal/kg/day.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.2, HR 48 sinus, BP 88/52, RR 14, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: Cachectic; lanugo hair; dry skin; reduced subcutaneous fat; alert, no focal deficits
data_table.Investigations: Na 137, K 3.4, urea 4.2, Cr 76, phosphate 0.74, magnesium 0.68, glucose 4.0, ALT 22, ECG QTc 470 ms

lead_in: Which prophylactic regimen is most appropriate before commencing the refeeding plan?

options.text: Oral thiamine 300 mg daily, oral phosphate 500 mg three times daily, and daily phosphate, magnesium and potassium monitoring for 7 days
Intravenous insulin 0.05 unit/kg/hour to maintain glucose between 4 and 6 mmol/L during refeeding; routine vitamin replacement
Rapid escalation to 40 kcal/kg/day from day 2 with weekly biochemistry monitoring; restrict thiamine to symptomatic patients
Withhold nutrition for 48 hours; correct electrolytes intravenously first before any oral intake; defer thiamine
Parenteral nutrition only for 5 days; resume enteral feeding at 30 kcal/kg/day once electrolytes have normalised

stem: You are the emergency medicine registrar managing a 26-year-old woman 90 minutes after deliberate ingestion of 60 amitriptyline 50 mg tablets (3 g total). She is drowsy with GCS 9 (E2V3M4). The team has secured the airway with a nasopharyngeal adjunct and applied oxygen. Vitals and bloods are back. A first 12-lead ECG shows broad complexes with QRS 140 ms and a tall terminal R wave in aVR.

data_table.Vital signs: GCS 9, BP 88/52, HR 128 sinus, RR 22, SpO2 96% on 6 L mask, T 36.4
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, mydriasis 6 mm reactive, dry skin, urinary retention; absent bowel sounds; lateral chest clear
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.30, lactate 3.0, K 3.6; ECG QRS 140 ms, terminal R in aVR 4 mm, QTc 510 ms; paracetamol negative

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous lipid emulsion 20 percent 1.5 mL/kg bolus over 1 minute; defer sodium bicarbonate until ECG worsens
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus and prepare for intubation; recheck ECG and pH 5 minutes after bolus
Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg every minute to a maximum of 1 mg; arrange psychiatric review for risk assessment
Synchronised DC cardioversion at 100 J for the broad-complex tachycardia; followed by lidocaine infusion 1 mg/kg loading
Activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube; defer airway intervention and observe for 4 hours before further escalation

stem: You are the psychiatry registrar admitting a 28-year-old man with schizophrenia who has failed adequate trials of risperidone and olanzapine at therapeutic doses over the last 18 months. He has ongoing positive symptoms and severe functional impairment. He has been counselled regarding clozapine therapy and has consented. He has no cardiac history, no fever, no neutropenia, and pre-clozapine baseline bloods including FBC, ECG, lipids and HbA1c are normal. He is registered on the clozapine patient monitoring system.

data_table.Examination: Settled, no extrapyramidal features; no abnormal cardiac findings
data_table.Investigations: FBC: WCC 6.8, neutrophils 4.2; ECG: normal sinus, QTc 410 ms; troponin pending baseline; HbA1c 5.2; lipids normal
data_table.Medications: Olanzapine 20 mg daily (to taper); lorazepam 1 mg PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate clozapine initiation regimen?

options.text: Start at 200 mg twice daily and continue full dose without titration; monitor only WCC and neutrophils for safety
Defer clozapine and switch to aripiprazole 30 mg as a fourth antipsychotic trial; reserve clozapine for failure of aripiprazole
Start at 100 mg twice daily and continue without dose titration unless side effects occur; monthly FBC monitoring is sufficient
Start at 25 mg twice daily with monthly FBC monitoring throughout the first 18 weeks regardless of dose changes
Start at 12.5 mg in the evening on day 1; titrate by 25 to 50 mg per day to a target of 300 to 450 mg by 3 to 4 weeks with weekly FBC

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 42-year-old man with schizophrenia who has been stable on olanzapine 15 mg nocte for 18 months. His last metabolic review was 9 months ago. He has gained 8 kg over the past year and reports increased thirst and polyuria. His mother has type 2 diabetes. He smokes 10 cigarettes daily and walks for 20 minutes most days. He drinks 2 standard drinks twice weekly. His latest set of bloods is back.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/88, HR 84, RR 16, SpO2 99% RA, T 36.6; BMI 33 (up from 29)
data_table.Examination: Central adiposity; no acanthosis nigricans; no thyroid mass
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 7.4 percent, fasting glucose 8.6 mmol/L; total cholesterol 5.8, LDL 3.6, HDL 0.9, triglycerides 3.2; ALT 48; eGFR 92; TSH 1.8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Continue current antipsychotic and lifestyle changes alone; defer diabetes pharmacotherapy until HbA1c above 8 percent at next review
Stop olanzapine abruptly and substitute haloperidol 5 mg daily as a lower-metabolic-risk first-generation antipsychotic option
Continue olanzapine unchanged and add metformin 500 mg twice daily for newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes; lifestyle measures and statin discussion
Switch olanzapine to clozapine to address treatment resistance and metabolic syndrome together as a single intervention
Cease olanzapine and offer cognitive behavioural therapy for schizophrenia as monotherapy until metabolic parameters normalise

stem: You are the consult psychiatry registrar called to ED for a 64-year-old woman brought in by her family because of 5 days of progressive immobility, mutism and refusal of food and fluid. She has a history of bipolar I disorder controlled on lithium and valproate. She was discharged 2 weeks ago after a depressive episode. On examination she stares fixedly, holds postures imposed by the examiner, and does not respond verbally. There is no fever, no rigidity, no rash and no recent medication change. Her observations are otherwise normal.

data_table.Examination: Mutism; immobility; posturing (maintains examiner-placed arm position 90 seconds); waxy flexibility; staring; no rigidity, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 280, FBC normal, electrolytes normal, lithium 0.7, valproate 480, BSL 5.8, urine bHCG negative; ECG normal sinus
data_table.Medications: Lithium 750 mg nocte; sodium valproate 1000 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg as a first-line antipsychotic to treat presumed psychotic stupor and observe for response
Administer IV lorazepam 2 mg as a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge; observe response over 30 to 60 minutes for partial reversal
Discontinue lithium and valproate and observe over 48 hours for clinical improvement before any further pharmacological intervention
Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy as first-line therapy without a prior lorazepam trial or other diagnostic intervention attempt
Commence subcutaneous heparin and intravenous fluids only; defer catatonia-specific intervention until psychiatric consultant review tomorrow

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy in psychiatric patient
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 38-year-old man with paranoid schizophrenia stable on aripiprazole 15 mg daily for 3 years. He smokes 25 cigarettes daily, smokes within 15 minutes of waking, and has tried cold turkey 4 times unsuccessfully. He is motivated to quit and asks for the best option. He has no history of depression, no recent suicidality, no cardiovascular disease, no seizure history. His current mental state is stable. He has tried 8 weeks of nicotine patches alone last year with relapse at week 4.

data_table.Examination: Stable mental state, no thought disorder; nicotine staining on fingers
data_table.Investigations: FBC, LFT, UEC normal; ECG normal sinus rhythm; PHQ-9 score 4

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Repeat nicotine patch monotherapy at higher dose (21 mg per 24 hours) for 12 weeks without combination or alternative therapy
Avoid varenicline due to historical black box warnings and use bupropion 150 mg twice daily as the safer first-line agent in schizophrenia
Commence varenicline 0.5 mg daily titrated up to 1 mg twice daily over 7 days; set quit date for 8 days; review at 4 weeks for mood and tolerance
Refer to behavioural counselling only without pharmacotherapy given his stable psychiatric illness and previous medication trials
Prescribe nortriptyline 75 mg nocte for cessation as a tricyclic with proven cessation efficacy and antidepressant effect

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 34-year-old former paramedic with 8 months of intrusive memories of a multi-fatality road traffic crash, nightmares 3 to 4 nights per week, avoidance of driving on highways, hyperarousal, sleep onset insomnia and irritability. He drinks 6 standard drinks 3 nights per week to sleep. He scores 56 on the PCL-5. He has no current suicidal ideation and has not commenced any treatment. There is no active psychosis. He is willing to engage in therapy or medication.

data_table.Examination: Hypervigilant; mildly tremulous; PHQ-9 score 14
data_table.Investigations: PCL-5 score 56; LFTs mildly raised (GGT 92); FBC and UEC normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Recommend cannabidiol oil under specialist prescribing for sleep and intrusive symptoms; defer formal trauma-focused therapy referral
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily titrated to 200 mg over 8 weeks as first-line monotherapy; defer psychological therapy until response
Prescribe oral benzodiazepine (diazepam 5 mg three times daily) for hyperarousal and insomnia; consider therapy at 3-month review
Commence quetiapine 25 mg nocte for sleep and arousal; review at 4 weeks to consider trauma-focused therapy referral and engagement
Refer for trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy or EMDR; address harmful alcohol use in parallel with support

stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 19-year-old woman with severe anorexia nervosa for medical stabilisation. She has lost 18 kg over 8 months. BMI is 13.4. She has minimal oral intake for 3 weeks. The eating disorders team plans to commence nutritional rehabilitation. Her admission bloods are back. Her ECG shows sinus bradycardia with QTc 478 ms. She has no purging behaviour. She is on no medications. She accepts admission and refeeding under supervision.

data_table.Examination: Cachectic; lanugo; cold peripheries; capillary refill 3 s; muscle wasting; alert oriented; no proximal myopathy yet
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.0, phosphate 0.62, magnesium 0.65, sodium 134, glucose 3.6, albumin 32, LFT mildly raised, FBC: Hb 102 microcytic; ECG sinus bradycardia, QTc 478, no U waves

lead_in: What is the most appropriate refeeding plan?

options.text: Commence enteral feeds at 1500 to 2000 kcal/day from day 1 to rapidly correct undernutrition; defer electrolyte correction until refeeding established
Refuse admission for refeeding because BMI 13 is unsafe outside intensive care; arrange community day-program review next week
Withhold feeds entirely for the first 48 hours and rehydrate with 4 L per day of dextrose 5 percent in saline to correct dehydration first
Replace phosphate, potassium, magnesium and start thiamine; commence feeds at 10 kcal/kg/day on day 1 with daily electrolyte monitoring and slow titration
Commence total parenteral nutrition at full caloric requirement immediately and defer oral or enteral nutrition for 7 days

stem: You are the GP shared-care registrar reviewing a 26-year-old man with first-episode schizophrenia who started olanzapine 10 mg nocte at discharge from inpatient care 12 weeks ago. His mental state has stabilised and he attends the appointment with his community mental health nurse. He reports increased appetite, has gained 5 kg since discharge and notices a thicker waist. He has no chest pain, no family history of premature cardiovascular disease and is a never smoker. He drinks two standard drinks per week.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78, HR 78, weight 84 kg (was 79 at discharge), waist 102 cm, BMI 27
data_table.Examination: Mental state stable; no extrapyramidal signs; no acanthosis nigricans; cardiovascular examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: No bloods since discharge; ECG at discharge QTc 412 ms; HbA1c at discharge 5.4 percent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation panel today?

options.text: Fasting glucose only with deferral of lipid profile until the 12-month annual review according to the standard antipsychotic monitoring schedule recommended for ongoing therapy
Serum olanzapine concentration as the priority biochemistry test today to assess therapeutic blood drug level guidance for any further olanzapine dose adjustment
Echocardiogram and 24-hour ambulatory ECG monitoring as the first-line cardiac screening for any patient stable on antipsychotic therapy at the 12-week review milestone
Fasting lipid profile, fasting glucose or HbA1c, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests and prolactin to complete the 12-week metabolic monitoring panel today
Sleep-deprived electroencephalogram and brain magnetic resonance imaging as the standard structural and electrophysiological review at three months of antipsychotic therapy

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 42-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder who has been stable on lithium carbonate 1000 mg nocte for the past five years with euthymia and full functional recovery. She attends every six months for routine review. She has no symptoms of lithium toxicity, no tremor and no polyuria. She uses ibuprofen occasionally for menstrual pain but has not taken any over the past two weeks. She has no acute illness or change in fluid status today and is keen to complete her routine 12-monthly biochemistry panel.

data_table.Examination: No fine tremor; no goitre; cognition intact; cardiovascular and neurological examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Last six months: lithium 0.78 mmol/L, creatinine 75, TSH 2.1, calcium 2.42; today's bloods not yet drawn
data_table.Medications: Lithium carbonate 1000 mg nocte; quetiapine 50 mg nocte for sleep; combined contraceptive pill

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation panel today?

options.text: Lithium concentration, urea, electrolytes and creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate, thyroid function, calcium and weight as the comprehensive annual monitoring
Lithium concentration alone given that recent thyroid and renal function were normal at six months and she remains clinically euthymic without tremor or polyuria
Lithium concentration plus full blood count and liver function tests as the annual review panel reflecting standard antipsychotic monitoring transposed onto her current bipolar therapy
Echocardiogram and 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure as a cardiovascular screen reflecting concern about long-term lithium-related cardiovascular toxicity in stable euthymic patients
Defer all blood tests until next clinically indicated review or annual review the following year because she has been entirely stable on her current dose for the past five years

stem: A 34-year-old woman asks for bupropion to stop smoking after reading about it. She smokes 20 cigarettes daily. She has bulimia nervosa in partial remission and drinks heavily on weekends.

data_table.Background: Bulimia nervosa, purging fortnightly; 12 standard drinks most weekends

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her request?

options.text: Avoid bupropion and offer a nicotine patch with short-acting lozenges
Prescribe bupropion 150 mg daily, increasing to twice daily after three days
Prescribe bupropion once her weekend drinking has settled for four weeks
Prescribe nortriptyline 25 mg nightly, titrated to 75 mg over a fortnight
Defer all cessation treatment until her eating disorder is fully treated

stem:
You are the GP reviewing a 28-year-old woman who self-refers requesting assessment for adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. She describes lifelong difficulty sustaining attention, procrastinating on tasks, losing her keys regularly and missing deadlines at her marketing job. She recalls being told she daydreamed in primary school but never received formal assessment. She is otherwise well, with no past psychiatric history.

She does not use illicit substances. She has read about adult ADHD online and asks what the next step in formal diagnosis would be from primary care today.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: euthymic; thought form linear; no psychotic features; cognition grossly intact
data_table.Investigations: Recent FBC, UEC, TFT, B12 normal; ECG sinus rhythm with QTc 405 ms; not pregnant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe a trial of methylphenidate immediate release 10 mg twice daily for two weeks as a diagnostic trial to confirm adult ADHD by symptomatic response
Order overnight polysomnography and brain magnetic resonance imaging as the standard initial workup investigations for any presentation of adult attentional concerns
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily empirically as initial pharmacotherapy because anxiety is more likely than ADHD in adult women presenting with attentional symptoms
Reassure her that adult-onset ADHD is not a recognised diagnostic entity and recommend cognitive behavioural therapy for non-specific attention concerns from primary care
Refer to a psychiatrist or paediatrician authorised to assess and prescribe for adult ADHD with collateral history from childhood and adult symptom rating scales

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 35-year-old woman who was the driver in a serious motor vehicle accident eight months ago. She describes intrusive flashbacks, hypervigilance, avoiding driving, nightmares disrupting sleep four nights a week, and irritability with her partner. Symptoms have not improved spontaneously and now meet DSM-5 criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder. She has no history of depression, no current suicidal ideation, no substance misuse and is keen to engage in evidence-based therapy. She is wary of medication and asks what will help her most.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: anxious affect, no psychotic features; cognition intact; insight retained
data_table.Investigations: Recent FBC, UEC, TFT all normal; PTSD Checklist score 56 of 80

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily titrated to 200 mg as the first-line pharmacological treatment in preference to trauma-focused psychological therapies for this presentation
Refer for trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing therapy as the evidence-based first-line treatment in PTSD
Prescribe prazosin 1 mg nocte and a long-acting benzodiazepine for sleep restoration and to suppress traumatic re-experiencing symptoms before any psychological therapy starts
Provide supportive counselling alone through generalist primary care without referral to specific evidence-based trauma-focused psychological therapy in the first six months
Refer for inpatient psychiatric admission to a tertiary trauma service for intensive group-based therapy because symptoms have persisted for eight months without intervention

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 26-year-old woman with established borderline personality disorder confirmed by community mental health team assessment two years ago. She has a five-year history of recurrent superficial wrist cutting in response to perceived rejection, two prior low-lethality paracetamol overdoses in the past three years, and unstable interpersonal relationships. She has previously had supportive counselling without sustained benefit. She is not currently suicidal and is engaged in care. She asks what intervention would most reduce her self-harm and admissions over time.

data_table.Examination: Old linear scars on bilateral forearms; mental state: euthymic, no acute risk; cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Recent FBC, UEC, LFTs, urine drug screen all normal; no current pregnancy
data_table.Medications: Quetiapine 50 mg nocte for sleep; nil other

lead_in: What is the most appropriate evidence-based recommendation?

options.text: Commence high-dose fluoxetine 60 mg daily as first-line pharmacotherapy for the core features of borderline personality disorder with quarterly review and dose titration
Refer for inpatient psychiatric admission whenever she presents with self-harm to interrupt the behaviour and provide containment until stable for outpatient discharge
Recommend electroconvulsive therapy as the next escalation in management given previous failure of supportive counselling and ongoing high-risk behaviours over years
Refer for a structured dialectical behaviour therapy program combining weekly individual therapy with group skills training over 12 months as the recommended intervention
Continue supportive counselling alone in primary care without escalation to specialist evidence-based psychotherapy because she has stabilised on her current management plan

subtopic_detail: ECT indication for severe melancholic depression
stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 68-year-old woman admitted under medicine for severe weight loss, dehydration and refusal of oral intake. She has severe melancholic depression with psychomotor retardation, nihilistic delusions that her bowels have rotted, and has lost 12 kg over three months. She has failed adequate trials of sertraline and venlafaxine. She is malnourished and her oral intake risks aspiration. She retains capacity and understands her situation. Her family ask about electroconvulsive therapy as the next treatment step.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.4, BP 102/65, HR 68, RR 14, SpO2 98 percent RA, weight 48 kg, BMI 17
data_table.Examination: Psychomotor retardation; flat affect; nihilistic delusions of rotted bowels; cognition intact on testing; passive suicidal ideation without plan
data_table.Investigations: Na 134, K 3.4, creatinine 75, albumin 28, TSH 1.4; ECG sinus bradycardia, QTc 420 ms; MRI brain age-appropriate
data_table.Medications: Venlafaxine 225 mg daily (current); sertraline 200 mg failed trial 4 months ago; mirtazapine 15 mg nocte added 2 weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discuss electroconvulsive therapy as first-line treatment given severe melancholic depression with psychotic features, nutritional failure and inadequate response to two antidepressants
Add lithium carbonate 500 mg nocte as augmentation strategy with monthly drug-level monitoring before any consideration of physical brain stimulation treatment options today
Trial transcranial magnetic stimulation as first-line physical therapy option because it avoids general anaesthesia and carries fewer cognitive risks than electroconvulsive treatment
Recommend further talking therapy with twice-weekly cognitive behavioural therapy as evidence-based first-line treatment for any severity of unipolar depression in older adults today
Continue current antidepressant regimen for at least eight further weeks before considering any escalation to electroconvulsive treatment to ensure full pharmacological response

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective disorder versus bipolar with psychosis
stem: You are the inpatient psychiatry registrar admitting a 30-year-old man for his third presentation with persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations and disorganised speech. Collateral history from his community case manager confirms that during his last 12-month inter-episode period he continued to experience daily auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions despite no concurrent mood symptoms. He has had two prior manic episodes meeting DSM-5 criteria. His current presentation includes elevated mood, decreased sleep need, racing thoughts and grandiose delusions. He uses no substances.

data_table.Examination: Pressured speech; flight of ideas; persecutory and grandiose delusions; auditory hallucinations; insight absent
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, B12, syphilis serology, urine drug screen all normal or negative; CT brain unremarkable
data_table.Medications: Nil currently (recently stopped olanzapine 20 mg, last dose 4 weeks ago by patient choice)

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features given his clear manic episodes with mood-congruent grandiose delusions and prior history of mania meeting full DSM-5 criteria
Schizophrenia with secondary mood symptoms because his three psychotic presentations meet the duration criterion for primary schizophrenia spectrum diagnosis under DSM-5-TR criteria
Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type given persistent psychotic symptoms for over two weeks without major mood symptoms in addition to recurrent mood episodes
Substance-induced psychotic disorder despite negative routine drug screen because synthetic cannabinoids and novel psychoactive substances are not detected on standard panels today
Delusional disorder grandiose type given the prominence of grandiose delusions, absent disorganisation and largely preserved functioning between acute presentation episodes today

stem: You are the community mental health team registrar reviewing a 52-year-old man with a four-year history of an unshakeable belief that his neighbour is broadcasting his thoughts via a device hidden in the shared garden fence. He has filed three complaints with police about this. Outside of this belief his thinking, speech, behaviour and self-care are intact. He continues to work as an accountant, maintains friendships and shows no hallucinations, no disorganisation, no negative symptoms. There is no mood disturbance, no substance use and no medical cause identified on workup.

data_table.Examination: Single fixed persecutory delusion about neighbour; speech, behaviour and self-care intact; no hallucinations or disorganisation; affect appropriate
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TFT, B12, syphilis serology, HIV serology all normal; urine drug screen negative; MRI brain normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Schizophrenia paranoid subtype given the four-year duration with persistent persecutory delusions about being targeted by his neighbour through a covert technological device
Brief psychotic disorder given an acute persecutory delusion arising in middle age in the context of perceived intrusive behaviour by a neighbouring household disturbing his routine
Schizophreniform disorder given the persistent persecutory delusions and a clinical presentation that meets criteria for schizophrenia but for a duration of less than six months
Obsessive compulsive disorder with poor insight given the recurrent intrusive thought about the neighbour disturbing his sense of safety and his repeated checking complaints today
Delusional disorder persecutory type given an isolated non-bizarre persecutory delusion present for over one month with preserved function and absence of other psychotic symptoms

stem:
You are the ED registrar assessing a 24-year-old man brought by police after threatening his housemates with a knife in response to a belief that they were poisoning his food. He has been using methamphetamine intravenously for the past three years with daily use over the past month. His housemates report he has had similar paranoid beliefs during binges in the past, but these have always resolved within a week of stopping use.

He has had no episodes when abstinent in his three years of use. He has no family history of psychotic illness. Workup including drug screen is positive only for amphetamines.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, BP 154/96, HR 118, RR 22, SpO2 99 percent RA, pupils 6 mm reactive
data_table.Examination: Agitated; persecutory delusions; auditory hallucinations; no formal thought disorder; insight absent; mild tremor
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen amphetamines positive; FBC, UEC, CRP unremarkable; CT brain normal; ECG sinus tachycardia QTc 430 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic framing and management plan?

options.text: Diagnose first-episode schizophrenia and commence aripiprazole 10 mg daily today with referral to early psychosis intervention team for sustained outpatient treatment
Treat as methamphetamine-induced psychotic disorder with short-term antipsychotic and benzodiazepine, observe over 7 to 14 days of abstinence and reassess for primary psychotic disorder
Discharge with brief intervention only about substance use because symptoms are wholly attributable to acute intoxication and will resolve spontaneously without psychiatric treatment
Commence clozapine 12.5 mg as initial pharmacotherapy because methamphetamine psychosis has highest evidence for clozapine response in this clinical and demographic context
Refer immediately for community drug and alcohol detoxification at a residential service without inpatient psychiatric admission, antipsychotic prescription or short-term observation period

stem:
You are the ED registrar assessing an 18-year-old man brought by family with three weeks of progressive persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations and disorganised speech. He has used high-potency cannabis daily for the past 14 months, escalating to multiple uses per day in the past three months. He has no past psychiatric history. His parents have no history of psychotic illness.

He has not used other substances. He is medically well and his workup including basic biochemistry, drug screen, MRI brain and EEG is unremarkable apart from cannabinoid positive urine.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, BP 124/78, HR 88, RR 16, SpO2 99 percent RA
data_table.Examination: Persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations; tangential speech; affect blunted; insight absent; mental status otherwise unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Urine THC positive, all other drugs negative; FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, B12, syphilis serology, HIV all normal; CT brain and EEG normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Discharge with brief substance counselling and outpatient mental health team follow up in two weeks because symptoms will resolve spontaneously once active cannabis use ceases
Commence clozapine 12.5 mg daily today as first-line antipsychotic for cannabis-induced psychotic disorder in adolescents and arrange weekly community FBC monitoring
Manage with high-dose benzodiazepines and supportive care only without antipsychotic medication to allow the cannabis-induced psychosis to remit completely with abstinence and sleep
Admit voluntarily or under the Mental Health Act, commence olanzapine 10 mg, support cessation of cannabis use and reassess for primary psychotic illness after 4 weeks of abstinence
Refer for residential drug rehabilitation as the next step and defer antipsychotic prescription until completion of a four-week inpatient cannabis abstinence and behavioural therapy program

subtopic_detail: Valproate use in women of childbearing potential
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder who has recently been started on sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily by an inpatient team after failure of lithium for a manic episode. She is sexually active in a stable relationship with a male partner, using condoms inconsistently. She is not planning pregnancy in the next two years but is undecided about future pregnancy.

She has no past obstetric history. She has read online about birth defects with the medication and is concerned about the choice of mood stabiliser at her age and stage today.

data_table.Examination: Mental state euthymic on current treatment; cognition intact; no extrapyramidal signs
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, beta-hCG negative, TSH 1.6, valproate trough 480 micromol/L (target 350 to 700)
data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily; condoms used inconsistently

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch to an alternative mood stabiliser such as lamotrigine or quetiapine after psychiatric review and arrange long-acting reversible contraception before further valproate prescribing
Continue valproate at current dose and counsel about taking high-dose folate 5 mg daily as the most effective single intervention to mitigate neural tube defect risk in pregnancy
Continue valproate and add depot medroxyprogesterone every 12 weeks as the appropriate Pregnancy Prevention Program requirement to allow ongoing safe valproate prescribing in this patient
Reduce valproate to 250 mg twice daily and recommend tubal ligation as the only acceptable contraception meeting valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program requirements in childbearing-age women
Continue valproate at the same dose and review at the next inpatient admission without discussing teratogenicity or contraception because she has stabilised mentally on the current regimen

stem: You are the ED registrar receiving a 27-year-old woman brought by ambulance two hours after a witnessed deliberate overdose of approximately 50 amitriptyline 25 mg tablets. She is drowsy with reduced GCS and has had one tonic-clonic seizure on the way to hospital terminated with midazolam IV. On arrival she is hypotensive and tachycardic. ECG demonstrates a sinus tachycardia with a wide QRS complex. Her airway has just been secured by the senior anaesthetist on arrival to the resuscitation area, and bloods have been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 85/50, HR 140, RR 18 (intubated and ventilated), SpO2 99 percent FiO2 1.0, T 36.4
data_table.Examination: GCS 7 (E1 V2 M4) prior to intubation; pupils 6 mm reactive; chest clear; warm peripheries
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia QRS 160 ms, terminal R wave above 3 mm in aVR; ABG pH 7.28, HCO3 18, lactate 4.2; potassium 3.6, sodium 138; paracetamol level negative
data_table.Medications: Amitriptyline 25 mg tablets at home for chronic pain; sertraline 100 mg daily for depression

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous lipid emulsion 20 percent at 1.5 mL/kg bolus followed by 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion as the first-line antidote for tricyclic antidepressant cardiotoxicity in this case
Administer intravenous physostigmine 1 mg slow bolus as the targeted reversal agent for tricyclic antidepressant anticholinergic and cardiotoxic effects in this presentation
Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4 percent 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus and titrate further boluses to narrow QRS toward 100 ms and target serum pH 7.45 to 7.55
Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 10 minutes as the first-line antiarrhythmic for QRS prolongation in this tricyclic antidepressant overdose presentation today
Commence intravenous amiodarone 300 mg loading followed by infusion as the first-line antiarrhythmic to treat the wide QRS complex in this tricyclic antidepressant overdose presentation

stem:
You are the neurology liaison registrar assessing a 32-year-old primary school teacher with three weeks of right leg weakness that came on the day after a difficult workplace incident. Neurological examination demonstrates a positive Hoover sign with right hip extension restored when contralateral hip flexion is tested, give-way weakness on confrontation, and intact reflexes with downgoing plantars. MRI of brain and spine is normal.

She has resigned from work and applied for income protection insurance, but appears genuinely distressed and engaged in clinic. She has no history of feigning illness for gain.

data_table.Examination: Right leg power 2/5 on confrontation testing but normal Hoover sign; reflexes 2+ symmetric; plantars downgoing; sensory exam non-dermatomal patchy; gait dragging right leg with normal balance
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain and whole spine normal; nerve conduction studies normal; FBC, UEC, B12, vitamin D, TSH all normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Malingering with intentional production of weakness given the income protection insurance claim and the timing immediately following a workplace incident known to her family
Factitious disorder imposed on self because she has presented for assessment without an obvious external gain motivating the deliberate production of right-sided lower limb weakness today
Acute psychogenic stroke variant with right hemiparesis given the temporal relationship to the workplace stressor and a lack of structural imaging abnormality on initial brain scan today
Somatic symptom disorder predominant with pain because chronic right leg discomfort accompanies the weakness despite normal investigation and imaging of brain spine and electrophysiology
Functional neurological disorder with motor weakness given positive Hoover sign and inconsistent give-way weakness in the setting of a recent psychosocial stressor and otherwise normal workup

stem:
You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 38-year-old man admitted under medicine with a five-day history of progressive immobility, refusal of food and fluids, and now mutism. He has a history of bipolar disorder. Examination reveals waxy flexibility with maintained postures held for over a minute and rigidity with passive movement. He appears awake with eye contact but does not speak or respond to commands.

There is no fever, no autonomic instability and no neurological deficit. Bedside workup is unremarkable to date and his vital signs are stable on arrival to the consult.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, BP 124/78, HR 78, RR 16, SpO2 98 percent RA
data_table.Examination: Mutism; waxy flexibility maintaining imposed postures over 60 seconds; rigidity; eye contact preserved; no fever; no rigidity differential with cogwheeling
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TFT, calcium, CRP all normal; CK 280; CT brain unremarkable; ECG sinus rhythm QTc 410 ms
data_table.Medications: Lithium 750 mg nocte (last serum level 0.8 four weeks ago); quetiapine 200 mg nocte

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic and therapeutic next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous haloperidol 5 mg as the first-line antipsychotic to address the underlying primary psychotic phenomenon causing the immobility and mutism in this presentation
Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg intravenous challenge with reassessment of catatonia signs at 5 to 10 minutes; significant improvement supports diagnosis and guides ongoing lorazepam therapy

Refer for electroconvulsive therapy this week as first-line treatment without prior pharmacological trial because catatonia mortality demands the fastest available physical brain stimulation intervention
Increase lithium dose to 1000 mg nocte as treatment for the suspected bipolar depressive episode driving catatonic immobility while awaiting next morning trough lithium serum level
Order overnight polysomnography and brain MRI as the initial workup before any pharmacological intervention is attempted in this catatonic presentation with new-onset mutism today

stem: You are the emergency psychiatry registrar called to assess a 35-year-old man brought by police with acute agitation, paranoia and verbal threats to staff. Verbal de-escalation has been attempted for 15 minutes without effect, including offer of food, quiet space and reduced stimulation. He continues to pace, shout and threaten violence. Background is unclear and history is limited; no medical history is known and no medications can be confirmed. He has no current intravenous access. The senior nurse asks for your immediate medication plan to enable safe assessment of the patient.
