data_table.Vital signs: Estimated HR 110, RR 22 from across the room; full vital signs not yet obtainable due to agitation and refusal to engage
data_table.Examination: Pacing; raised voice; persecutory threats; clenched fists; no obvious head injury; no obvious intoxication odour but limited assessment possible
data_table.Investigations: None possible currently; bedside glucose not yet measured; no IV access; ECG not feasible
data_table.Medications: Unknown background medications; reported history of methamphetamine use by police but uncorroborated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line rapid tranquillisation plan?

options.text: Intravenous diazepam 10 mg slowly through a freshly inserted line after restraint while monitoring for respiratory depression and arrhythmia on continuous cardiac telemetry today
Intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg combined with intramuscular midazolam 10 mg co-administered together as a single first-line agent without IV access or telemetry
Intramuscular ketamine 5 mg per kilogram body weight as the first-line agent for rapid sedation given the unknown medical history and rapid onset of dissociation usually within minutes
Intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg as a single agent first-line with reassessment of agitation and vital signs at 30 minutes before any further sedative medication is considered
Continue verbal de-escalation for a further 30 minutes without any pharmacological tranquillisation because medication carries inherent cardiovascular and respiratory risks in unmonitored patients

subtopic_detail: Metabolic monitoring and intervention on olanzapine
stem: You are the community psychiatry registrar reviewing a 38-year-old man with schizophrenia who has been stable on olanzapine 15 mg nocte for 2 years following several relapses on lower doses. A switch to aripiprazole 8 months ago caused an acute relapse requiring admission. His family report substantial weight gain over the past 18 months. He acknowledges a sedentary lifestyle and increased calorie intake but reports stable mood with no psychotic symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/86, HR 78, weight 95 kg (was 78 kg at olanzapine start), BMI 31
data_table.Examination: Central adiposity; no extrapyramidal signs; mental state stable
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.4 mmol/L, HbA1c 6.0 percent, total cholesterol 5.8, LDL 3.6, HDL 0.9, triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L; UEC and LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Refer for a structured lifestyle program alone and repeat fasting glucose and lipids in 6 months
Commence metformin 500 mg twice daily with structured lifestyle changes while continuing olanzapine
Switch olanzapine to aripiprazole and provide lifestyle counselling at the same psychiatric review
Reduce olanzapine to 7.5 mg nocte and add a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist
Refer for bariatric surgical assessment as the next stage of weight management

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD diagnostic pathway with comorbid substance use
stem: A 28-year-old man presents to your GP clinic asking for assessment of adult ADHD. He has been struggling with chronic disorganisation and missed deadlines and was recently dismissed from a third role in 5 years for performance issues. He uses cannabis daily to 'calm down' and has been using since age 17. Mood is mildly low secondary to job loss but not pervasively depressed. He brings online ASRS-v1.1 self-screening results scoring 5/6 in Part A. He has not been previously assessed and brings no childhood records.

data_table.Examination: Restless, fidgety, tangential at times but conversation coherent; no psychomotor retardation; no thought disorder
data_table.Investigations: Nil to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange childhood collateral and refer to a psychiatrist for structured ADHD assessment alongside cannabis cessation support
Commence a 4-week trial of methylphenidate immediate-release and review response as diagnostic confirmation
Order an electroencephalogram and a structural brain MRI before any further specialist referral today
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily as the first-line treatment of adult attentional symptoms in this patient
Refer for neuropsychological testing as the single gold-standard diagnostic before any further action today

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation and CYP1A2 interaction with clozapine
stem:
You are the psychiatric registrar in a community mental health clinic reviewing a 52-year-old man with schizophrenia who has been stable on clozapine 450 mg daily for 6 years. He smokes 25 cigarettes daily and now wants to quit after a recent CT chest showed early emphysematous changes. His daughter is having a baby and he wants to be smoke-free.

He has no current depression and no cardiovascular disease. His last clozapine level 4 weeks ago was 540 ng/mL (target 350-600). He plans to stop completely within 2 weeks.

data_table.Examination: Mental state stable; mild bilateral basal crackles
data_table.Investigations: Clozapine level 540 ng/mL (4 weeks ago); FBC WCC 6.2 with neutrophils 3.4; LFTs normal; ECG sinus rhythm with QTc 430 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence varenicline 0.5 mg titration as monotherapy and maintain the current clozapine dose throughout the cessation period
Commence nicotine replacement therapy at full dose and maintain the current clozapine dose throughout the cessation period
Commence varenicline 0.5 mg titration and reduce clozapine dose with serial clozapine-level monitoring during cessation
Defer cessation pharmacotherapy and recommend behavioural therapy alone with monthly review until he stops independently
Switch clozapine to olanzapine before commencing any cessation pharmacotherapy to avoid medication interactions today

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose with sodium-channel blockade
stem: A 24-year-old woman is brought to your emergency department by ambulance after being found unconscious by her flatmate next to an empty box of amitriptyline tablets prescribed for chronic neuropathic pain. Time of ingestion is unknown but the flatmate last saw her 6 hours ago. She is intubated by anaesthetics for airway protection. You are leading her resuscitation in resus.

data_table.Vital signs: GCS 7 prior to intubation; BP 88/52; HR 132; T 36.8; SpO2 99 percent on FiO2 50 percent post-intubation
data_table.Examination: Dilated pupils; warm dry skin; absent bowel sounds
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia 132, QRS 140 ms, terminal R wave aVR 5 mm, QTc 480 ms; VBG pH 7.28, lactate 3.4, bicarbonate 18; paracetamol and alcohol levels pending

lead_in: After the airway is secured, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous physostigmine 0.5 mg over 5 minutes to reverse anticholinergic toxicity
Administer intravenous lipid emulsion 20 percent 1.5 mL/kg bolus followed by infusion now
Administer intravenous flumazenil 200 micrograms repeated to a total of 1 mg to reverse coma
Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg bolus and recheck QRS width after each dose
Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 10 minutes to shorten the QTc interval

stem: A 32-year-old man with no past psychiatric history is admitted from the emergency department to your inpatient psychiatry unit with progressive social withdrawal, mutism, and immobility for 5 days. His wife reports he stopped eating and drinking 2 days ago. On examination he sits motionless, will not respond to questions, and his arm remains in the position you place it. He postures with an awkward arm held against gravity. Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale scores 17. He is intermittently staring and grimacing.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8, BP 102/68, HR 92, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent RA, weight 72 kg
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, waxy flexibility, posturing, grimacing; no rigidity, no tremor, mild fever only
data_table.Investigations: Na 140, K 4.0, creatinine 78, CK 410, FBC normal, urinary toxicology negative, TFTs normal, CT brain non-contrast normal
data_table.Medications: Nil regular; trial of risperidone 2 mg given 24 hours ago in ED

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous lorazepam 1-2 mg as a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge with response assessed at 15 minutes
Withhold all antipsychotics and arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy within the next 12 hours
Continue risperidone and add olanzapine 10 mg to consolidate antipsychotic coverage during catatonia
Administer intravenous haloperidol 5 mg with promethazine 25 mg as rapid sedation per the unit protocol
Administer intravenous dantrolene 1 mg/kg for presumed neuroleptic malignant syndrome from the risperidone dose

subtopic_detail: Autoimmune encephalitis presenting as first-episode psychosis
stem:
A 22-year-old previously well woman is admitted to your inpatient psychiatric unit with new-onset psychosis, prominent paranoid delusions, agitation, and disorganised speech progressing over 10 days. Family report she became uncharacteristically forgetful 3 weeks ago. On day 3 of admission she develops orofacial dyskinesias, intermittent rigidity, autonomic lability (BP 175/100 then 90/55 within 30 minutes), low-grade fever 38.2, and one witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure.

She was started on olanzapine 10 mg on admission. Her family deny any drug or alcohol use, and there is no personal or family history of psychiatric illness.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.2, BP swinging 175/100 to 90/55, HR 60 to 130, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent RA
data_table.Examination: Orofacial dyskinesias, intermittent rigidity, fluctuating consciousness, brisk reflexes globally
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFT normal; CK 1100; urine toxicology negative; CT brain non-contrast normal; ECG normal; pregnancy test negative; troponin normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease olanzapine and commence haloperidol with scheduled lorazepam to manage agitation, posturing and autonomic features today
Transfer to intensive care and treat presumptively for neuroleptic malignant syndrome with dantrolene and supportive measures
Continue olanzapine, add propranolol for autonomic symptoms and a midazolam infusion to manage seizures during stabilisation
Cease olanzapine and arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy for presumed antipsychotic-resistant first-episode psychosis
Cease olanzapine, arrange urgent CSF autoantibody testing, commence intravenous methylprednisolone and immunoglobulin, and organise pelvic imaging

subtopic_detail: First-line stimulant choice and monitoring in newly diagnosed adult ADHD
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar in a community clinic with a 28-year-old man newly diagnosed with adult ADHD after a structured DSM-5 interview confirming inattentive and hyperactive symptoms since childhood and current significant occupational impairment. He has no cardiovascular disease, normal ECG, and a recent BP of 124/78. He has no history of psychosis or substance dependence and drinks 6 standard drinks weekly. He prefers a once-daily regimen due to work demands.

data_table.Examination: Mental state stable, no thought disorder, mood euthymic
data_table.Investigations: ECG normal sinus rhythm; UEC, FBC, TFTs normal; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy choice?

options.text: Atomoxetine 40 mg daily titrated weekly to 80 mg as the preferred first-line non-stimulant in adult care
Modafinil 200 mg daily morning to address inattention with low cardiovascular risk profile features
Bupropion sustained release 150 mg daily titrated to 300 mg over two weeks as evidence-based first-line option
Immediate release dexamfetamine 5 mg three times daily with afternoon dose adjusted to avoid insomnia
Lisdexamfetamine 30 mg daily morning with cardiovascular monitoring and titration over the following weeks

subtopic_detail: Acute management of self-harm in established borderline personality disorder
stem: You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar assessing a 26-year-old woman in ED 4 hours after superficial forearm cutting in response to a relationship breakup. She has a documented diagnosis of BPD and is engaged in a 12-month DBT program with weekly individual and skills group sessions. Wounds are sutured and she is medically stable. She is calm now, denies suicidal ideation, and wants to return home with her flatmate.

data_table.Examination: Two superficial parallel cuts to left forearm, sutured; no other injury
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, urine drug screen normal; not intoxicated
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 100 mg daily; quetiapine 25 mg nocte for anxiety

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition and follow-up plan?

options.text: Discharge with crisis plan, her DBT therapist phone contact, and clinic review in 48 hours
Discharge with no follow-up given resolution of immediate distress and continuation of existing therapy
Admit voluntarily for short-stay inpatient unit psychotherapy reinforcement and consolidation of skills
Admit involuntarily under the Mental Health Act for risk assessment and inpatient observation for 72 hours
Add olanzapine 5 mg nocte for mood stabilisation following the self-harm and discharge home after observation

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy in stable schizophrenia
stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 42-year-old man with stable schizophrenia on aripiprazole 15 mg daily for 4 years. He smokes 25 cigarettes daily and wants to quit. He has tried nicotine replacement patches without success twice. He has no depression, anxiety, or active substance use. He has a normal ECG, BP, lipids, and HbA1c. He is keen to discuss varenicline after seeing television advertising.

data_table.Examination: Mental state stable; no thought disorder; no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, HbA1c, lipids, TSH normal
data_table.Medications: Aripiprazole 15 mg daily; no other regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase aripiprazole to 20 mg daily to reduce reward salience associated with nicotine craving
Avoid varenicline because of an absolute contraindication to its use in any patient with a primary psychotic illness
Start varenicline 0.5 mg daily titrated over the standard 12 week course with mood monitoring at each review
Start bupropion sustained release 150 mg daily titrated to 300 mg over the first week of treatment
Refer for an inpatient detoxification program as the only safe approach in patients with schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Lorazepam challenge dose and route in suspected catatonia after recent antipsychotic exposure
stem: You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 38-year-old woman on the medical ward who has become mute, immobile, and waxy on examination over the last 36 hours. She was admitted 5 days ago with sepsis from cellulitis and received haloperidol 5 mg twice daily for delirium for 3 days, ceased 24 hours ago. She has a long history of bipolar disorder. Her sepsis is resolving. She is afebrile, normotensive, and her CK is mildly elevated at 380.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 86, BP 116/72, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, posturing left arm, waxy flexibility, no rigidity, no tremor, eyes open
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, calcium, magnesium normal; CK 380; CRP 22 falling; urine drug screen negative; MRI brain unremarkable; EEG no electrographic seizure
data_table.Medications: Ceftriaxone day 5 of 7; lithium 800 mg nocte; haloperidol ceased 24 hours ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic and therapeutic next step?

options.text: Commence bromocriptine 2.5 mg orally three times daily as first-line dopaminergic treatment for catatonia
Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy tomorrow as first-line treatment before any pharmacological trial
Start dantrolene infusion at 2.5 mg/kg over 30 minutes to address suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Administer lorazepam 1 mg IV as a single challenge dose and reassess catatonic features within 10 minutes
Re-initiate haloperidol 2.5 mg twice daily as low dose maintenance to treat suspected residual delirium tonight

subtopic_detail: Discrimination of cannabis-induced psychosis from first episode schizophrenia
stem: You are the early psychosis service registrar assessing a 21-year-old man brought in by his family with 3 weeks of persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations, and disorganised speech. He has been using high-potency cannabis daily for the past 6 months, increasing in the month before symptom onset. He has no prior psychiatric history but maternal half-brother has schizophrenia. He last used cannabis 9 days ago and remains symptomatic with positive symptoms unchanged after 1 week of olanzapine 10 mg nocte.

data_table.Examination: Disorganised speech, persecutory delusions, second-person auditory hallucinations, blunted affect
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain unremarkable; FBC, UEC, LFTs, TFTs, syphilis serology, HIV negative; urine drug screen positive for THC on admission, negative on day 9

lead_in: Which clinical feature most strongly supports an evolving primary psychotic disorder rather than substance-induced psychosis at this point?

options.text: Persistence of positive symptoms beyond a month after cessation of cannabis use most strongly favours a primary psychotic disorder
Presence of negative symptoms during the first month of illness rules out substance-induced psychosis entirely
Negative urine drug screen at presentation is required before a primary psychotic disorder can be diagnosed
Onset of positive symptoms during heavy cannabis use is itself sufficient to diagnose substance-induced psychosis
Positive family history of psychotic illness in a maternal half-brother is sufficient to confirm a primary psychotic disorder

subtopic_detail: Choice of first-line trauma focused therapy in adult PTSD with single index event
stem: You are the community psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman with 4 months of intrusive memories, avoidance, hyperarousal, and nightmares after a single motor vehicle crash. She is mid-grade depressed but not suicidal. She is reluctant to take medication and is asking about psychological treatment options. She has access to both a clinical psychologist with EMDR training and a clinical psychologist with TF-CBT training within the same service.

data_table.Examination: Mental state alert, mood low-mid, no psychosis, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Nil indicated; PCL-5 score 52, PHQ-9 score 13

lead_in: Which statement is the most accurate first-line recommendation under AU guidance?

options.text: Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing has clearly superior outcomes to trauma-focused CBT in adult PTSD
Generic supportive counselling has equivalent efficacy to trauma-focused therapy and is preferred in mild PTSD
Trauma-focused CBT and EMDR have comparable first-line evidence in adult PTSD and choice is guided by patient preference and clinician training
Sertraline is the recommended first-line treatment for adult PTSD before any trauma-focused psychological therapy is offered
Critical incident debriefing within a single session is the recommended first step in management of all adult PTSD

subtopic_detail: Choosing between varenicline and combination NRT for adult smoker seeking quit attempt
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 52-year-old man who smokes 25 cigarettes daily and wants to quit before an elective knee replacement in eight weeks. He has had three prior failed quit attempts using nicotine patches alone. He has stable mood with no history of suicidal ideation, no seizures, no untreated cardiovascular disease, and no contraindication to varenicline. He prefers oral medication and is willing to set a quit date in two weeks.

data_table.Mental state: Euthymic, no suicidal ideation, no recent depressive episode
data_table.Past history: Hypertension on amlodipine; no seizure disorder; no liver disease; eGFR over 60 mL/min/1.73m2
data_table.Smoking: 25 per day for 30 years; Fagerstrom score 7

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Varenicline 0.5 mg daily titrated up to 1 mg twice daily starting one week before quit date
Repeat nicotine patch monotherapy for another six week course as the proven single agent strategy
Bupropion 150 mg daily for three days then 150 mg twice daily for nine weeks from the quit date
E-cigarette as the primary cessation strategy given preference for oral nicotine substitution device
Brief advice and motivational counselling only without any pharmacotherapy this consultation

subtopic_detail: Choice of SSRI when starting antidepressant treatment in a breastfeeding mother
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 32-year-old woman at 10 weeks postpartum with moderate depressive symptoms confirmed by EPDS of 18 and clinical interview. She is exclusively breastfeeding her well 10-week-old son. She has not had antidepressant treatment previously. There is no suicidal ideation, no psychotic features, and no manic history. She wishes to start an antidepressant and continue breastfeeding.

data_table.Mental state: Tearful, low mood for six weeks, sleep disturbance beyond infant feeds, anhedonia, no suicidal ideation, no psychotic features
data_table.Past history: Nil regular medication; no thyroid disease; TSH 1.8 mIU/L
data_table.Infant: Term, well, gaining weight on the 25th centile

lead_in: Which antidepressant has the most supportive safety data in this setting?

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily orally with infant monitoring during initiation and dose titration
Citalopram 20 mg daily orally with weekly infant clinical review during the first two weeks
Mirtazapine 15 mg nightly orally with infant weight and sedation review during the first two weeks
Sertraline 50 mg daily orally with infant clinical review for sedation and feeding during initiation
Venlafaxine 75 mg daily orally with blood pressure and infant review during the first two weeks

subtopic_detail: Initial inpatient feeding plan for severe anorexia nervosa with refeeding risk markers
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 19-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa to an adolescent ward. She has BMI 13.6, has eaten less than 500 kcal daily for four weeks, and has lost 12 kg in three months. Bloods show phosphate 0.65 mmol/L, magnesium 0.7 mmol/L, and potassium 3.2 mmol/L. She is normotensive supine but with HR 38 supine. She has no severe organ failure and is consenting to treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: T 35.8, HR 38 supine, RR 14, BP 92/56 supine, BMI 13.6
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, peripheral oedema +, lanugo, no organomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Na 138, K 3.2, Mg 0.7, PO4 0.65, glucose 3.6 mmol/L; LFTs ALT 84; ECG QTc 470 ms
data_table.Mental state: Engaged, cognitively intact, no suicidal ideation, agrees to treatment

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial feeding plan?

options.text: Commence oral feeds at 5 kcal/kg/day with thiamine and replace electrolytes before any oral intake
Commence oral feeds at 20 kcal/kg/day with thiamine 300 mg IV and daily phosphate magnesium potassium
Commence oral feeds at 40 kcal/kg/day with weekly bloods and no parenteral thiamine prescribed
Commence total parenteral nutrition through central venous access with daily electrolyte review
Commence nasogastric continuous feeds at 60 mL/hour without electrolyte preloading or thiamine

subtopic_detail: Initial mental health assessment of an Aboriginal man presenting with low mood in regional GP
stem: You are the rural GP reviewing a 45-year-old Aboriginal man presenting with three months of low mood, broken sleep, and reduced engagement with family. He attends with his sister who provides collateral. He recently lost his mother and has begun attending Sorry Business in his community. He has no suicidal ideation, no psychotic features, and no alcohol or drug use. He is reluctant to see a mainstream mental health service.

data_table.Mental state: Withdrawn, congruent affect, no suicidal ideation, no perceptual abnormality
data_table.Past history: Nil regular medication; chronic lower back pain; no prior mental health treatment
data_table.Social: Lives with extended family; cultural and community connections important

lead_in: What is the most culturally appropriate first step?

options.text: Refer urgently to a mainstream community psychiatric team for inpatient assessment as a priority
Start oral sertraline 50 mg daily as monotherapy without further mental health team involvement now
Document the consultation and review in six weeks without offering any therapeutic plan today
Discharge with online self-help resources and a fact sheet about depression in adult patients now
Offer co-ordinated care with the local Aboriginal community-controlled health service and SEWB worker

subtopic_detail: Pre-treatment cardiovascular screening before adult stimulant initiation in newly diagnosed ADHD
stem: You are the psychiatrist starting methylphenidate for a 34-year-old man with newly diagnosed adult ADHD after a comprehensive assessment. He has no syncope, no chest pain, and no exertional symptoms. His father had a sudden cardiac death at 42 years from a documented arrhythmia. The patient has not had cardiology assessment previously. He is otherwise well, not on any other medication, and has no substance use.

data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular examination unremarkable, no murmurs, no displaced apex
data_table.Investigations: ECG not yet performed; baseline bloods unremarkable
data_table.Family history: Father sudden cardiac death at 42 from documented arrhythmia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before initiating stimulant?

options.text: Refer to cardiology for ECG and echocardiogram review before commencing any stimulant medication
Commence methylphenidate 10 mg twice daily and review symptoms at four weeks with a BP recheck
Commence atomoxetine 40 mg daily as non-stimulant alternative without cardiology referral now
Order outpatient 24-hour Holter monitor alone without further cardiology input before treatment now
Defer all pharmacotherapy indefinitely and refer for ongoing CBT alone without further investigation

subtopic_detail: Recommended initial screening tool for refugee mental health in primary care first visit
stem: You are the refugee health GP reviewing a 28-year-old man from Syria three weeks after arrival on a humanitarian visa. He reports broken sleep, nightmares, irritability, and avoidance of crowds. He spent three years in transit including time in detention. He speaks limited English and an Arabic interpreter is present. He has no acute suicidal ideation and is engaged in the consultation but cautious.

data_table.Examination: Wary, intermittent eye contact, no current acute distress
data_table.Past history: Reported torture survivor; no diagnosed mental illness; nil regular medication
data_table.Social: Recent arrival; living with extended family; engaged with settlement service

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial mental health screening approach?

options.text: Use a translated PHQ-9 self-report tool today and book a six-week follow-up for routine review
Refer for inpatient psychiatric admission for diagnostic clarification and trauma therapy initiation
Start oral sertraline 50 mg daily empirically for presumed PTSD before any formal mental health assessment
Decline to discuss trauma and provide general lifestyle advice with social settlement support only today
Use a culturally validated screening tool such as the RHS-15 with an accredited interpreter and onward referral

subtopic_detail: Bicarbonate threshold and indication in tricyclic antidepressant overdose with widened QRS
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 22-year-old woman two hours after ingestion of an unknown quantity of amitriptyline tablets in a suicide attempt. She had a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure on arrival lasting one minute. ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 130 bpm with QRS 140 ms and right axis deviation in lead aVR with terminal R wave 4 mm. She is now drowsy with shallow breathing.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 130, RR 10, BP 86/54, SpO2 92 percent, GCS 9
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, dry mucosa, mydriasis, hyperreflexia, no focal weakness
data_table.Investigations: ECG QRS 140 ms with terminal R wave in aVR 4 mm; VBG pH 7.30 lactate 3.8 mmol/L; bedside glucose 5.2
data_table.Medications: No regular medications; ingestion 2 hours ago

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg bolus and titrate against conscious level for reversal
Administer intravenous adenosine 6 mg rapid push to terminate the wide complex tachycardia rhythm
Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg as a bolus to narrow the QRS interval
Administer intravenous glucagon 5 mg slow push for refractory hypotension and bradycardia presumed
Administer activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube for late presentation decontamination first

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing very late onset schizophrenia from delusional disorder in 72-year-old woman
stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatrist asked to review a 72-year-old woman with a six-month history of fixed persecutory belief that her neighbour is poisoning her water supply. She has installed cameras and tested her water. She has no hallucinations, no thought disorder, no negative symptoms, and remains otherwise able to manage her household and pay bills. There is no family history of schizophrenia, no recent drug use, normal MMSE, and unremarkable MRI brain.

data_table.Mental state: Calm, fixed non-bizarre delusion, no hallucinations, no thought disorder, mood euthymic, insight nil
data_table.Investigations: MMSE 28/30; MRI brain unremarkable; bloods normal; urine drug screen negative; TSH 2.4
data_table.Functional: Independent in activities of daily living, paying bills, shopping, driving

lead_in: What is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Very late onset schizophrenia-like psychosis with intact higher cognition and preserved function
Alzheimer disease with associated paranoid behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia first
Substance-induced psychotic disorder from her recent over-the-counter and prescription medications
Delusional disorder persecutory type with circumscribed non-bizarre belief and preserved function
Schizoaffective disorder with mood instability and persistent delusion across affective phases now

subtopic_detail: Valproate pregnancy prevention program in a woman with bipolar I disorder of childbearing potential
stem: You are the consultant psychiatrist reviewing a 28-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder maintained on sodium valproate 1500 mg daily for 4 years following a manic episode. She has had no further admissions and is now in a stable relationship. She is using condoms only as contraception. She raises the possibility of starting a family within the next 2 years. Liver function and full blood count are normal.

data_table.Bloods: Valproate level 350 micromol/L (therapeutic), LFTs normal, FBC normal, beta hCG negative
data_table.Reproductive history: Nulliparous, regular cycles, no fertility concerns
data_table.Current medications: Sodium valproate 1500 mg daily, no other psychotropics

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue valproate at current dose and review again in 6 months when pregnancy planning becomes active
Counsel on teratogenicity, switch to lithium, and enrol in the valproate pregnancy prevention program
Add high-dose folate 5 mg daily and continue valproate at the current dose throughout pregnancy
Reduce valproate to 750 mg daily and continue indefinitely as a safer dose in pregnancy
Cease valproate today without alternative and arrange community mental health follow-up review weekly

subtopic_detail: Anticholinergic burden when escalating tricyclic antidepressant in an older adult with comorbidities
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 76-year-old man with chronic neuropathic pain and depression maintained on amitriptyline 25 mg nocte for 3 months. He has had a partial mood response and his pain remains poorly controlled. He also takes oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily for urge incontinence, donepezil 10 mg daily for mild Alzheimer dementia, and citalopram 20 mg daily was ceased 2 months ago when amitriptyline was started.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 88, BP 132/80 mmHg supine, 110/72 mmHg standing
data_table.Cognitive status: MMSE 24 of 30, mild short-term recall impairment, attention intact
data_table.Bloods: Sodium 138 mmol/L, eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73m^2, ECG QTc 440 ms
data_table.Medications: Amitriptyline 25 mg nocte, oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily, donepezil 10 mg daily, ramipril 5 mg daily

lead_in: Which medication change is most appropriate?

options.text: Increase amitriptyline to 50 mg nocte for stronger antidepressant and neuropathic effect
Switch amitriptyline to duloxetine 30 mg daily and titrate based on response and tolerability
Increase donepezil to 23 mg daily to overcome the anticholinergic burden affecting cognition
Cease oxybutynin and review bladder symptoms with non-anticholinergic alternatives in 4 weeks
Substitute amitriptyline with nortriptyline 10 to 25 mg nocte and cease oxybutynin with bladder retraining

subtopic_detail: Lorazepam challenge in suspected catatonia complicating major depressive episode
stem: You are the consultant liaison psychiatrist asked to review a 22-year-old man with a known history of severe major depression admitted under medicine for 4 days of not eating or drinking, mutism, posturing, and waxy flexibility. He is medically cleared, with a normal CT brain, lumbar puncture, and metabolic screen. He has had no fevers, autonomic instability, or rigidity. He is not on any antipsychotic.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 88, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Mental state: Mute, immobile, waxy flexibility on right upper limb, no rigidity, no autonomic instability
data_table.Investigations: CK 230 U/L (normal), TSH normal, urine drug screen negative, CT brain and CSF normal
data_table.Bush-Francis catatonia rating: Score 16 with 6 of 14 screening items positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral olanzapine 10 mg daily and review the response again in 48 hours
Refer for urgent electroconvulsive therapy without a benzodiazepine trial in the next 24 hours
Administer parenteral lorazepam 1 to 2 mg and observe over 5 to 10 minutes for clinical response
Start scheduled diazepam 5 mg orally three times a day and review response again in 48 hours
Reassure the medical team this is psychogenic and arrange psychotherapy review in the community

subtopic_detail: DSM-5 timing rule discriminating schizoaffective disorder from bipolar disorder with psychotic features
stem: You are the consultant psychiatrist reviewing a 27-year-old man on an extended inpatient admission. Over the past 12 months he has had two confirmed episodes of mania each lasting around 2 weeks accompanied by persistent grandiose delusions. Between these manic episodes, the family describe approximately 6 weeks of continued grandiose delusions and auditory hallucinations without mood disturbance. He has had ongoing psychotic symptoms for most of the last 12 months. He is currently euthymic but continues to describe special abilities.

data_table.Substance use: Nil illicit substances on urine drug screen, no alcohol misuse
data_table.Medical workup: CT brain, full medical workup, autoimmune encephalitis screen negative
data_table.Mental state: Euthymic mood, hyperreligious content, paranoid persecutory delusions, no formal thought disorder
data_table.Family history: Father with bipolar I disorder, paternal aunt with schizophrenia

lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits the DSM-5 timing rule?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type is the best fit given the longitudinal pattern of symptoms
Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features is the most accurate single diagnosis
Schizophrenia with comorbid bipolar I disorder is the most accurate combined diagnosis
Brief psychotic disorder with marked stressor is the most accurate diagnosis presently
Delusional disorder grandiose type is the most accurate single diagnosis in this presentation

subtopic_detail: Discriminating cannabis-induced psychotic disorder from first-episode primary psychosis
stem: You are the registrar in the early psychosis service reviewing a 19-year-old man who is 7 days post-discharge from an inpatient unit following a first presentation with persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations and disorganised thinking. Symptoms began acutely 4 weeks ago after heavy daily cannabis use over 6 months. He has been abstinent from cannabis for 14 days under family supervision. Olanzapine 10 mg nightly was started during admission with marked improvement.

data_table.Mental state: Euthymic affect, persecutory ideas now overvalued not fixed, no hallucinations, fully oriented
data_table.Family history: Paternal cousin with schizophrenia, maternal grandmother with depression
data_table.Substance history: Daily high-potency cannabis 0.5 to 1 g for 6 months, no other substances, no withdrawal
data_table.Medical workup: Urine drug screen positive cannabis at admission, repeat now negative; CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan now?

options.text: Stop olanzapine immediately as it is no longer required following discharge from inpatient unit
Refer for a Mental Health Act community treatment order to enforce ongoing antipsychotic medication
Switch olanzapine to amisulpride to avoid future metabolic risk and review at 6 months only
Continue olanzapine for at least 6 months with brief structured cannabis use intervention and headspace follow-up
Provide reassurance and discharge to the GP for a single follow-up appointment in 3 months

subtopic_detail: Recognition of GHB overdose presenting with rapid fluctuation in conscious state
stem: You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 23-year-old woman brought in by ambulance from a music festival. She was found unresponsive in a portable toilet and on arrival has fluctuating GCS rapidly between 4 and 12 over 20 minutes. She has no signs of trauma, miosis, or pupillary asymmetry. Her vital signs are stable. Bystanders saw no injectables and no prescription containers. She has woken briefly, become agitated, and then dropped GCS again twice.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 64, BP 110/70 mmHg, RR 12, SpO2 99 percent on 4 L oxygen via Hudson
data_table.Examination: No trauma, pupils 4 mm reactive, no needle tracks, no neck rigidity
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.36, lactate 1.8, glucose 5.4 mmol/L, paracetamol and salicylate negative, ethanol 0.04
data_table.Urine toxicology: Pending; rapid amphetamine and opioid panel negative

lead_in: Which is the most likely cause of her presentation?

options.text: Acute opioid overdose despite negative urine drug screen and absence of typical examination signs
Gamma-hydroxybutyrate intoxication producing characteristic rapid fluctuation in conscious state
MDMA toxicity with serotonin syndrome accounting for the presentation and observed symptoms
Acute methamphetamine intoxication producing rapid swings between agitation and unresponsiveness
Cannabis intoxication producing acute psychosis with associated rapid fluctuation in conscious state

subtopic_detail: Discriminating functional neurological disorder from malingering and factitious disorder
stem: You are the neurology registrar consulted on a 38-year-old woman with sudden right-sided weakness on awakening 5 days ago. There was no headache, dysphasia, or facial droop. MRI brain and MR angiography are normal. Examination shows positive Hoover sign on the right leg, sudden weakness that reverses with distraction, and intact reflexes. She is distressed by the symptoms, has missed work, and is requesting a second neurological opinion. There is no ongoing legal claim and no external secondary gain identified.

data_table.Examination: Hoover sign positive, give-way weakness in right upper and lower limb, deep tendon reflexes 2+ symmetric, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain, MR angiography, glucose, electrolytes, CK all normal
data_table.Psychosocial: Distressed by symptoms, no compensation claim, no military or insurance context
data_table.Behaviour: Cooperative with examination, willing to engage with physiotherapy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnosis and next step?

options.text: Malingering: discharge with safety-net advice and no further follow-up needed at present
Factitious disorder imposed on self: refer for psychiatric management and avoid further investigation
Conversion disorder: order CT angiogram of the carotids to rule out a missed structural cause
Stroke mimic: admit for observation on stroke unit with 24-hour neurological observations performed
Functional neurological disorder: explain diagnosis using positive signs and refer for specialist FND physiotherapy

stem: A 28-year-old software engineer presents to your general practice clinic asking about adult ADHD assessment after his partner suggested it. He describes lifelong difficulty completing projects at work, frequently losing his keys, interrupting in meetings, and being unable to sit through long presentations since primary school. School reports from age 9 documented inattention and disruptive behaviour. He has used cannabis socially on weekends for years and drinks four to six standard drinks two nights per week, which he describes as helping his racing thoughts settle. There is no personal history of mood disorder or psychosis. His mother had similar inattention as a child.

data_table.Examination: Mildly fidgety, well groomed, normal mental state examination
data_table.Investigations: Adult Self-Report Scale (ASRS-v1.1) part A: 6 of 6 positive screening items

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his ADHD assessment?

options.text: Refer to a psychiatrist after a four-week substance-free observation period from alcohol and cannabis
Commence methylphenidate immediate release as a four-week diagnostic and therapeutic primary-care trial
Order brain MRI and quantitative EEG to confirm the diagnosis before any specialist referral
Reassure that adult ADHD is unlikely given his tertiary attainment and review routinely in twelve months
Refer directly for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting inattention without prior diagnostic clarification

stem: A 54-year-old taxi driver presents to your general practice clinic motivated to quit smoking. He has smoked 25 cigarettes per day for 35 years and his last serious quit attempt with patches alone failed at four weeks. He has stable major depressive disorder on sertraline 100 mg daily with no recent suicidal ideation. He has well-controlled hypertension and a history of recurrent vivid dreams when he tried mirtazapine briefly two years ago. He drinks alcohol occasionally, has no renal impairment, and asks for the most effective pharmacotherapy to combine with brief counselling.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 132/80, RR 14, SpO2 96% on room air
data_table.Examination: Mood euthymic, no current passive or active suicidal ideation; PHQ-9 score 5
data_table.Investigations: eGFR 88 mL/min/1.73m2; LFTs within reference range
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 100 mg daily; perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to recommend?

options.text: Nicotine patch 21 mg daily as monotherapy starting on his planned quit day without short-acting NRT
Varenicline with standard titration to 1 mg twice daily, commenced one to two weeks before a planned quit day
Bupropion titrating from 150 mg daily to 150 mg twice daily, commenced one week before a planned quit day
Nortriptyline 75 mg nocte for cessation after cross-tapering sertraline off over the preceding fortnight
Defer pharmacotherapy and refer for hypnotherapy and acupuncture as first-line cessation interventions

stem: A 27-year-old man with a first episode of schizophrenia commenced olanzapine 10 mg nightly six weeks ago in your community mental health clinic. He attends for routine review feeling more settled with reduced auditory hallucinations, but reports increased appetite and a 4 kg weight gain. He has no personal or family history of diabetes. He has not had any pre-treatment baseline metabolic bloods taken because he was acutely unwell at initiation. He smokes ten cigarettes per day and drinks no alcohol. He asks how often you will be checking his physical health.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84, BP 128/78, RR 14, SpO2 99%, weight 86 kg (baseline 82 kg), waist 96 cm
data_table.Examination: Morning sedation only, no abnormal movements, BMI 27.8
data_table.Investigations: Pending: fasting lipids, fasting glucose or HbA1c, prolactin

lead_in: Which metabolic monitoring schedule best matches Australian best-practice for olanzapine?

options.text: Fasting glucose or HbA1c, fasting lipids and waist at three months and then twelve-monthly while stable
Fasting lipids only at six months with weight and waist circumference checked at twelve-monthly intervals
Weight and waist at every visit; fasting glucose or HbA1c and fasting lipids at baseline, twelve weeks, then yearly
ECG and prolactin only at six and twelve months without routine glucose or lipid testing during the first year
Two-yearly OGTT only, with no routine fasting lipid, weight or waist monitoring required during the interval

stem:
A 52-year-old accountant is referred to your community mental health clinic by her GP. For the past 18 months she has held a fixed, unshakeable belief that her next-door neighbour is poisoning her water supply through the shared plumbing because she once parked across his driveway. She has had her water independently tested three times with normal results, but remains convinced.

Outside this single belief she works full time, manages her finances, maintains friendships, and presents at interview with normal speech, organised thought, and full affective range. She denies hallucinations, has no negative symptoms, and there has never been a manic or depressive episode. She does not use substances and her medical history is unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Mental state examination otherwise unremarkable apart from the persecutory belief; cognition intact; insight absent for the belief only
data_table.Investigations: TSH, B12, folate, electrolytes within reference range; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: Which DSM-5 diagnosis best fits the presentation?

options.text: Paranoid schizophrenia given the fixed persecutory belief and the disturbed neighbour interaction over months
Brief psychotic disorder, persecutory subtype, given the discrete structure of the delusional belief
Schizophreniform disorder, given the total symptom duration shorter than two years at presentation
Delusional disorder, persecutory type, given a single non-bizarre delusion for at least one month with preserved function
Obsessive-compulsive disorder with poor insight, given her sustained preoccupation with the neighbour situation

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 68-year-old woman admitted for severe major depressive disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features. She has lost 9 kg over six weeks, refuses food intermittently believing it is contaminated, and has stopped drinking adequately for the past 48 hours. She has not responded to sertraline 200 mg daily for six weeks. Past medical history includes essential hypertension on perindopril, mild aortic stenosis (peak gradient 28 mmHg, EF 60%), and degenerative cervical spine disease.

She was treated with right unilateral ECT 12 years ago for a similar episode with full recovery and no significant side effects. Family and patient consent for further treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88 sinus, BP 122/76, RR 16, SpO2 97%, Temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Profoundly slowed, food refusal, mute episodes, dry mucosae
data_table.Investigations: Na 132, K 4.0, urea 9.2, creatinine 86, eGFR 64, albumin 30, ECG sinus QTc 430 ms; recent transthoracic echocardiogram unchanged
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 200 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next treatment step?

options.text: Switch sertraline to an SNRI and review response over a further four weeks before considering escalation steps
Add olanzapine 5 mg nocte for psychotic features and reassess clinical response over four weeks of combination treatment
Commence intravenous ketamine 0.5 mg/kg over 40 minutes twice weekly as the principal antidepressant therapy
Proceed to bitemporal high-dose ECT first-line after anaesthetic review, given the severity and aim for fastest response
Proceed to right unilateral high-dose ECT after anaesthetic review and informed consent with cardiac and spine precautions

stem: A 34-year-old woman is intubated for a falling conscious state 45 minutes after ingesting about 3 g of dothiepin. Sodium bicarbonate has been given and a nasogastric tube sits in the stomach. Bowel sounds are reduced.

data_table.Investigations: Arterial pH 7.47, potassium 3.7 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Instil activated charcoal through the nasogastric tube
Start multiple-dose activated charcoal every four hours
Perform gastric lavage before any charcoal is given
Start whole bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol
Withhold decontamination and continue supportive care

stem:
A 24-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder is being followed in your community psychiatry team. She has been in dialectical behaviour therapy for nine months. Over the past two weeks she has presented to ED four times after superficial self-harm episodes, each precipitated by escalating arguments with her partner. She has skipped two of her last four group skills sessions because she found them dysregulating.

There has been no recent suicide attempt or hospitalisation, no substance use, and her mood has been reactive but no major depressive episode. She is on no psychotropics.

data_table.Examination: Healed superficial linear cuts to bilateral forearms; mental state - dysregulated affect, no current suicidal intent, full reality testing
data_table.Investigations: Nil indicated acutely

lead_in: Within standard DBT, which target should the next individual therapy session prioritise?

options.text: Sleep hygiene and exercise scheduling as foundational stage-one quality-of-life targets within DBT this week
Address life-threatening behaviours by completing a behavioural chain analysis of the most recent ED self-harm episode
Address therapy-interfering behaviours first by problem-solving her skipped skills group sessions before any other target
Address life-threatening behaviours first, then therapy-interfering behaviour (missed group), then quality-of-life targets
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily as the priority intervention for repeated affective dysregulation episodes leading to self-harm

subtopic_detail: Anorexia nervosa - medical risk and refeeding
stem:
A 17-year-old female presents to your hospital paediatric medical ward via ED at her parents' request after eight months of restrictive eating. Weight is 38 kg (BMI 13.6), with rapid weight loss of 6 kg in the past month. She is bradycardic at 38 bpm, normotensive supine but BP drops from 100/64 to 78/52 on standing with a 32 bpm rise.

She is cold, mildly slowed cognitively, and her ECG shows sinus bradycardia with QTc 470 ms. Bloods show K 3.0, phosphate 0.62 mmol/L, magnesium 0.68 mmol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L. The dietitian proposes initial caloric intake of 1400 kcal per day with stepwise increases.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 38 lying, BP 100/64 lying to 78/52 standing; postural HR rise 32; Temp 35.4; SpO2 97%
data_table.Examination: Significant muscle wasting, lanugo, peripheral oedema absent, mild bradypsychism
data_table.Investigations: K 3.0, phosphate 0.62, magnesium 0.68, glucose 3.2, urea 6.0, creatinine 70, eGFR 92, albumin 35, LFTs ALT 64, INR 1.1; ECG sinus bradycardia QTc 470 ms; ketones positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate refeeding plan in the first 48 hours?

options.text: Commence oral feeding at 2200 kcal per day from day one with no prophylactic electrolyte replacement and ward observation
Feed at 1400 kcal/day on cardiac-monitored bed with prophylactic phosphate, potassium, magnesium plus IV thiamine before feeds
Initiate parenteral nutrition via a central venous line as primary route given poor oral intake and severe malnutrition
Delay any feeding for 48 hours to allow serum electrolytes to fully normalise before nutrition is reintroduced safely
Discharge home with weekly outpatient dietitian and GP review given she is awake, cooperative and willing to engage

stem:
A 31-year-old female accountant attends your general practice clinic asking about adult autism assessment. She describes lifelong exhaustion after social events, scripting conversations in advance, intense interest in spreadsheet design since childhood, and sensory aversion to fluorescent lighting and clothing tags. She has never had developmental concerns flagged at school because she achieved high marks and modelled her behaviour on a chosen peer.

She presents now after her recently diagnosed nephew prompted her to read about autistic women. She has well-treated generalised anxiety on sertraline 100 mg daily. She is articulate, makes brief eye contact, and her PHQ-9 today is 6.

data_table.Examination: Calm engaged manner; mild fidgeting with pen; no thought disorder
data_table.Investigations: AQ-10 score 8 of 10; RAADS-14 screen score 28 (high)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her diagnostic pathway?

options.text: Refer to a multidisciplinary autism diagnostic service for full assessment including developmental history and standardised tools
Reassure her that autism is unlikely given her successful career and high educational attainment in adulthood
Request a single psychometric IQ assessment from a psychologist to clarify whether her presentation reflects autism
Increase sertraline to 150 mg daily and review in eight weeks before reconsidering any neurodevelopmental assessment
Order brain MRI and quantitative EEG to look for organic correlates of her sensory and social difficulties first

stem: A 26-year-old man is referred to your community mental health team after a third psychiatric admission in two years. During admissions he has presented with grandiose delusions, persecutory beliefs, decreased sleep and pressured speech responsive to olanzapine and lithium combination. Collateral history from his sister and chart review confirm that on two separate occasions between admissions, while euthymic with normal sleep, energy and goal-directed activity, he continued to hold fixed persecutory delusions for at least six weeks before any subsequent mood episode. He has no substance use disorder and his thyroid function is normal.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic mood today; no current psychotic symptoms; insight partial
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.8 mIU/L; urine drug screen negative on two occasions
data_table.Medications: Olanzapine 15 mg nocte; lithium 750 mg nocte (level 0.7 mmol/L)

lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits this longitudinal course?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features during manic episodes and full inter-episode remission
Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type given delusions persisting for at least two weeks outside the mood episodes documented
Schizophrenia with comorbid major depressive episodes superimposed during periods of severe negative symptom burden
Delusional disorder persecutory type with episodic comorbid bipolar I disorder requiring separate sequential treatment courses
Substance-induced psychotic disorder despite two negative urine drug screens given the episodic nature of his presentations

stem:
A 22-year-old apprentice mechanic is brought to your emergency department by his housemates after two days of paranoid beliefs that his employer is poisoning his food. He has been smoking high-potency cannabis daily for the past four months, with last use yesterday evening. He has no prior psychiatric admissions but reports brief paranoia after heavy use on three previous occasions, each lasting under 48 hours and resolving with sleep.

He has no first-degree family history of psychosis. He is alert and oriented, vital signs are stable, and his urine drug screen confirms cannabis without other substances detected.

data_table.Examination: Mildly agitated; pressured speech; persecutory delusional ideation
data_table.Investigations: UDS THC positive, methamphetamine and cocaine negative; ECG QTc 412 ms

lead_in: Which classification best fits his current presentation?

options.text: Cannabis intoxication only with paranoia expected to resolve once acute intoxication phase concludes within hours
First-episode schizophrenia with cannabis use as an aggravating environmental risk factor in this young adult man
Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder given two days of delusional symptoms developing during or soon after cannabis use
Brief psychotic disorder with marked stressor given recent workplace conflict precipitating the persecutory belief content
Delusional disorder persecutory type with substance use as an incidental finding unrelated to the persecutory delusion

subtopic_detail: BPD inpatient splitting and DBT principles
stem: You are the registrar covering an inpatient psychiatric unit overnight. A 24-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder admitted three days ago following a low-lethality overdose tells you the day team has been cruel to her and that you are the only doctor who has ever understood her. She asks you to immediately rewrite her discharge plan, prescribe diazepam at night and grant unescorted leave tomorrow, threatening that she will discharge against medical advice and harm herself if you do not. She has a structured DBT-informed care plan from her treating community team.

data_table.Examination: Tearful but engaged; no acute intoxication; mental state otherwise unchanged
data_table.Investigations: Bloods normal on admission; no current ECG concerns
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 150 mg daily; no benzodiazepines on regular chart

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate response?

options.text: Schedule her under the Mental Health Act tonight to prevent the threatened self-discharge and remove decisional autonomy
Prescribe diazepam 5 mg nocte tonight as a once-only dose to settle her distress and prevent self-discharge tonight
Rewrite the discharge plan now to grant unescorted leave tomorrow morning and document her request as informed choice
Empathically validate her distress, decline plan changes overnight and hand over to the day team for the next morning
Confront her about the manipulative nature of her request and document that her behaviour is attention-seeking only

stem:
A 48-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been on lithium 750 mg nocte for 14 years with stable mood and serum levels around 0.7 mmol/L. At routine review she reports increasing thirst over the last four months with polyuria of around 4 litres per day, nocturia twice nightly, and unchanged mood. She is on no other relevant medications, drinks one to two cups of tea per day, and has no recent infection.

Her GP has been monitoring six-monthly bloods. Today bloods show stable lithium level, mildly reduced eGFR from her baseline, normal calcium and glucose, and notably dilute urine.

data_table.Examination: Mucous membranes moist; no signs of dehydration; mood euthymic
data_table.Investigations: Li 0.7 mmol/L; Na 142, K 4.1, eGFR 58 (baseline 72) mL/min/1.73m2; corrected Ca 2.30, glucose 5.2, urine osm 180 mOsm/kg, serum osm 295
data_table.Medications: Lithium 750 mg nocte; quetiapine 100 mg nocte

lead_in: What is the most likely cause of her polyuria and best initial action?

options.text: Central diabetes insipidus from undiagnosed pituitary lesion; arrange pituitary MRI and copeptin level before any treatment
Primary polydipsia from psychotropic medication dry mouth; advise fluid restriction to 1.5 litres daily and review in eight weeks
New-onset type 2 diabetes mellitus from quetiapine; arrange fasting glucose, HbA1c and lipid panel before the next review
Lithium-induced hypercalcaemia driving polyuria; arrange parathyroid hormone level and outpatient endocrinology referral
Lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; arrange psychiatrist review for lithium dose reduction or switch to alternative mood stabiliser

stem:
A 29-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder presents to your community mental health clinic on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily prescribed by a previous psychiatrist three years ago, with stable mood and no current relationship. She tells you she has met a new partner and is considering trying for pregnancy in the next twelve months. She has not had pre-pregnancy counselling about her current mood stabiliser.

She has private health insurance and good engagement with services. She has no history of treatment-resistant illness and previously responded well to lithium during a first episode of mania six years ago.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic mood; no current psychotic, depressive or manic features
data_table.Investigations: Valproate level 520 micromol/L; LFTs normal; FBC normal; eGFR 88

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Plan a structured cross-taper from valproate back to lithium, with reproductive counselling and adherent contraception during transition
Continue sodium valproate at current dose and add high-dose folate 5 mg daily pre-conception to mitigate neural tube defect risk
Halve valproate dose to 500 mg daily as low-dose exposure abolishes teratogenic and neurodevelopmental concerns in pregnancy planning
Discontinue valproate immediately today without alternative mood stabiliser cover and review again at the next routine outpatient slot
Switch valproate to carbamazepine as a safer pregnancy option given carbamazepine has no major congenital malformation signal currently

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman admitted to the medical ward two days ago with reduced oral intake and minimal speech for one week. She has a history of recurrent severe major depressive disorder. On examination she lies in bed, makes no spontaneous movement, holds an arm in any position you place it for several minutes, and is mute.

She has resistance to passive limb movement that increases with examiner force. Bloods including creatine kinase are mildly elevated, infection screen is negative and CT brain is normal. The medical team has been giving small-volume nasogastric feeds.

data_table.Examination: Mutism, waxy flexibility (catalepsy), negativism, posturing; Bush-Francis 14
data_table.Investigations: CK 380 U/L (mildly elevated); WCC 7.2; CRP 6; CT brain normal; UDS negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Commence olanzapine 5 mg orally daily for presumed catatonic schizophrenia and reassess response after seven days of treatment
Administer a single dose of lorazepam 1 to 2 mg parenterally and reassess catatonic signs within 10 to 30 minutes after administration
Increase her existing sertraline back to 100 mg daily for the presumed underlying severe depressive episode currently driving symptoms
Arrange MRI brain with contrast and lumbar puncture before any pharmacological intervention to exclude an autoimmune encephalitic process
Refer urgently for inpatient electroconvulsive therapy without any preceding benzodiazepine trial regardless of the catatonia subtype

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents to your emergency department with new-onset right lower limb weakness developing over three hours, with no antecedent trauma. She works as a registered nurse and is currently on long-term workers compensation for a back injury. On examination she demonstrates 1/5 strength on direct testing of right hip flexion but contralateral hip extension produces strong synergistic activation in the right hip extensors that is inconsistent with the deficit, and her Hoover sign is positive. Sensation is intact. Reflexes and tone are normal. MRI brain and spine are unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: 1/5 right hip flexion; positive Hoover sign; normal tone and reflexes
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain and lumbar spine: no acute pathology; routine bloods normal
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol PRN for chronic back pain

lead_in: Which diagnosis is most consistent with the examination findings?

options.text: Factitious disorder imposed on self given her medical knowledge and unconscious sick role pursuit without external incentive present
Malingering given workers compensation context with deliberate symptom fabrication for external financial secondary gain on history
Functional neurological disorder (conversion type) based on positive Hoover sign and clinical inconsistency on internal validation
Acute ischaemic stroke despite a normal MRI given limb weakness can precede imaging changes within early acute ischaemic stroke windows
Subacute combined degeneration of the cord from undiagnosed pernicious anaemia with vibration loss and ataxia in lower limbs predominantly

stem: A 32-year-old man is brought to your emergency department by friends after 14 hours of severe agitation, tremor, profuse sweating and visual hallucinations. He attends regularly at dance events on weekends and his friends report he has been dosing 1,4-butanediol (a GHB precursor) every 2 hours around the clock for the past three months to maintain function. He last dosed approximately 18 hours ago. He drinks alcohol minimally and denies opioid use. His urine drug screen detects no opioids, benzodiazepines, amphetamines or alcohol on standard panel testing.

data_table.Examination: Tremor, diaphoresis, mydriasis, visual hallucinations; oriented; CIWA-Ar 24
data_table.Investigations: UDS negative on standard panel; FBC and UEC normal; CK 240

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological management?

options.text: Discharge home with referral to an outpatient drug and alcohol service for community-based GHB withdrawal management within seven working days
Administer naloxone 0.4 mg intravenously immediately for presumed concealed opioid withdrawal as the underlying cause of his autonomic instability
Use intravenous haloperidol as primary pharmacotherapy for agitation given his prominent visual hallucinations on initial presentation today
Commence high-dose oral diazepam titrated to symptom control with parenteral midazolam available for breakthrough agitation in resuscitation
Administer intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg as a diagnostic test for benzodiazepine intoxication given his presentation of prominent autonomic features

stem:
A 27-year-old man is admitted to your acute mental health unit with a four-day history of decreased sleep, grandiose religious beliefs and pressured speech. He has used crystal methamphetamine intermittently on weekends for two years and his last reported use was nine days ago. His urine drug screen is negative for amphetamines today and was negative on admission three days ago.

Hair testing is unavailable in your service area. He has no first-degree family history of bipolar disorder. After three days of olanzapine 10 mg nocte and observed abstinence on the ward, he remains overtly manic with grandiosity and minimal sleep.

data_table.Examination: Pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiose delusions, minimal need for sleep
data_table.Investigations: UDS amphetamines negative on admission and day 3; TSH 1.4; LFTs normal
data_table.Medications: Olanzapine 10 mg nocte for 3 days; no benzodiazepines

lead_in: Which diagnosis and management combination best fits the clinical course on day 4 of inpatient stay?

options.text: Methamphetamine-induced psychotic disorder with mood features; continue olanzapine, defer mood stabiliser pending one month of verified observed abstinence
Methamphetamine intoxication despite negative urine drug screening; observe further without any pharmacological intensification of treatment for a further 48 hours
Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type; continue olanzapine, plan early discharge to outpatient follow-up without inpatient mood stabiliser initiation today
Brief psychotic disorder with marked stressor of recent methamphetamine cessation; taper olanzapine over the next week prior to outpatient psychology referral
Bipolar I disorder current episode manic; add lithium 750 mg nocte as a mood stabiliser to current olanzapine and target serum level 0.6 to 1.0 mmol/L

stem: A 48-year-old woman attends a general practice appointment requesting help to quit smoking. She has smoked 25 cigarettes a day for 28 years and has tried lozenges twice in the past with relapse within 4 weeks. She is keen to set a quit date in the next fortnight and is open to medication. Her medical history includes well-controlled hypertension on perindopril and a remote episode of moderate depression treated with sertraline 6 years ago, now off all psychotropics. She is not pregnant, does not drink alcohol heavily, and has no history of seizures.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 132/82, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: PHQ-9 today 4; engaged, motivated; no current suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Exhaled carbon monoxide 22 ppm; eGFR 88; LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy to support her quit attempt?

options.text: Commence varenicline titrated over 7 days, starting 1 to 2 weeks before her chosen quit date, for 12 weeks
Prescribe combination nicotine replacement therapy with a patch plus oral form for 12 weeks from quit date
Prescribe bupropion 150 mg daily for 3 days then twice daily for 7 to 12 weeks starting before her quit date
Recommend e-cigarettes via a prescription model from her general practitioner for 12 weeks alongside counselling
Defer pharmacotherapy and provide brief advice with referral to Quitline only as initial behavioural support

stem: A 26-year-old man with a 9-month history of first-episode schizophrenia is reviewed by the early-psychosis team. He has been taking olanzapine 15 mg nightly for 7 months and is now in symptomatic remission. Since starting treatment his weight has increased from 78 kg to 92 kg and his waist circumference from 92 cm to 108 cm. He is otherwise well, walks his dog daily, and would prefer to stay on olanzapine because his mental state is settled. He has no chest pain, no thirst, and no polyuria. His family history includes type 2 diabetes in both parents.

data_table.Examination: Mental state stable; no involuntary movements; no acanthosis nigricans
data_table.Investigations: Random glucose 5.8 mmol/L; HbA1c 5.7%; LDL 4.2 mmol/L; triglycerides 2.4 mmol/L; ALT 56

lead_in: Which monitoring and management step is most appropriate at this point?

options.text: Continue olanzapine unchanged and reassess metabolic parameters in 12 months given his clinical stability
Refer to dietitian and exercise program, repeat fasting lipids and glucose, and consider switching to aripiprazole or amisulpride
Add metformin 500 mg twice daily to attenuate olanzapine-associated weight gain and ignore lipid abnormalities
Switch immediately to clozapine given the magnitude of metabolic change and his early stability on olanzapine
Reduce olanzapine to 7.5 mg, add a statin, and avoid switching to minimise relapse risk in early remission

subtopic_detail: Valproate in women of childbearing potential
stem: A 26-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is reviewed in the community mental health clinic. She has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 18 months following two manic episodes and remains in remission. She is in a stable relationship and is considering pregnancy in the next 12 months. She has no current depressive symptoms, no thyroid disease, and no recent admissions. Her general practitioner recently issued repeat scripts without discussing pregnancy planning. She is not on any reliable contraception currently and reports inconsistent condom use.

data_table.Examination: Mood euthymic; mental state stable; no involuntary movements
data_table.Investigations: Sodium valproate level 480 micromol/L (within range); LFTs normal; pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discuss the major risks of valproate in pregnancy, ensure highly effective contraception, and plan a cross-taper to lithium or lamotrigine
Continue valproate at the current dose and add high-dose folic acid 5 mg daily for pregnancy prophylaxis
Stop valproate abruptly today and start sertraline 50 mg as a safer alternative mood-stabiliser before pregnancy
Continue valproate and reassure her that the teratogenic risk is largely confined to the first trimester only
Refer to a perinatal psychiatry service and continue valproate unchanged pending tertiary review in 3 months

stem: A 34-year-old man attends his general practice seeking assessment for adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. He reports lifelong difficulty completing tasks, frequent job changes due to disorganisation, and being told he was disruptive at primary school. School reports from year 4 confirm restlessness and inattention. He scored highly on a self-administered Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS-v1.1). He has a remote past of cannabis use (ceased 5 years ago), no current substance use, no current depressive episode, and is otherwise medically well. He has no history of cardiac disease and his resting ECG is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 70, BP 122/78, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Engaged, fidgety, no thought disorder; affect bright; school reports support childhood symptoms
data_table.Investigations: ASRS-v1.1 part A positive (6/6); ECG sinus rhythm; thyroid function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his diagnostic pathway?

options.text: Commence a trial of methylphenidate immediate-release 10 mg three times daily for 4 weeks and reassess response
Refer to a psychiatrist or paediatrician with adult ADHD experience for diagnostic assessment and treatment authority
Refer for neuropsychological testing as a prerequisite to any specialist clinical assessment for adult ADHD
Provide reassurance, cognitive behavioural therapy referral, and reassess in 12 months without diagnostic workup
Prescribe atomoxetine 40 mg daily as a non-stimulant alternative bypassing the need for specialist diagnostic assessment

subtopic_detail: Bipolar I maintenance with depressive predominance
stem:
A 34-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder presents to your community psychiatry clinic 8 weeks after recovering from her most recent depressive episode. Her illness pattern over 6 years includes one hypomanic episode 5 years ago and four depressive episodes, the most recent requiring inpatient admission. She is currently euthymic and tolerated her acute treatment of quetiapine and sertraline well, but has gained 8 kg and complains of sedation.

Her renal function is normal. She is sexually active and uses a copper intrauterine device. She wants a single maintenance agent with the best evidence for preventing further depressive relapse.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 72, BP 124/78, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.5
data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no psychomotor change, no suicidal ideation; BMI 28.4 kg/m^2
data_table.Investigations: TSH 2.1; UEC normal; LFTs normal; eGFR > 90

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate maintenance pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Continue sertraline as the sole maintenance agent and review every 3 months in psychiatry clinic
Switch to carbamazepine titrated to a target serum level for relapse prevention
Continue quetiapine 300 mg nocte indefinitely as the established maintenance choice in bipolar I disorder
Initiate sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily and titrate to a maintenance serum trough level
Initiate lamotrigine with slow titration to a target maintenance dose with monitoring for skin reaction

subtopic_detail: Continuing treatment after a positive lorazepam challenge
stem: A 45-year-old woman with catatonia complicating major depression spoke and moved freely ten minutes after a lorazepam challenge. Four hours later she is again mute and immobile.

data_table.Observations: HR 84, BP 118/74, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Regular oral lorazepam 2 mg three times daily, reviewed daily
Further parenteral doses only if she deteriorates again overnight
Oral olanzapine 10 mg at night with the lorazepam ceased
Refer today for electroconvulsive therapy instead of drugs
Observation alone, as the response confirms the diagnosis

subtopic_detail: Shock unresponsive to fluid and alkalinisation in poisoning
stem: A 41-year-old man ingested amitriptyline four hours ago. He is intubated, has received 30 mL/kg of sodium chloride 0.9 percent and enough sodium bicarbonate to reach an arterial pH of 7.52, and his QRS has narrowed. He remains hypotensive.

data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.1 mmol/L, sodium 149 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start an intravenous noradrenaline infusion
Start an intravenous dobutamine infusion
Start an intravenous dopamine infusion
Give a further intravenous crystalloid fluid bolus
Give intravenous lipid emulsion therapy

subtopic_detail: Psychosis tied to stimulant use and abstinence
stem: A 24-year-old man has had three episodes of persecutory delusions and hostility over two years. Each began within two days of a methamphetamine binge and settled within a fortnight of stopping. He was well throughout six months in custody and during a year of abstinence.

data_table.Collateral: Custodial health records document no psychotic symptoms
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for methamphetamine, TSH 1.9 mIU/L

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Methamphetamine-induced psychotic disorder
Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type
Brief psychotic disorder, recurrent episodes
Schizophrenia with comorbid substance misuse
Delusional disorder, persecutory subtype

stem: A 44-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium 1000 mg nocte for 6 years with steady-state levels of 0.7 mmol/L. He attends for his routine review with you as his community psychiatry registrar. His baseline 6 years ago showed normal renal function with creatinine 78 micromol/L. He has no new symptoms, takes no nephrotoxic medications, drinks alcohol minimally, and adheres well to his lithium regimen. Today's bloods are reviewed alongside his historical trends.

data_table.Examination: No tremor; no oedema; mental state stable euthymic
data_table.Investigations: Lithium level 0.7 mmol/L; Cr 102 micromol/L (baseline 78); eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73m2 (baseline 92); TSH 3.2 mIU/L; calcium 2.42 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding his renal monitoring?
