options.text: Continue 6-monthly U+E and increase frequency only when the eGFR falls below the routine clinical action threshold
Repeat U+E and eGFR within 4 weeks, calculate the rate of decline, and arrange nephrology review for shared planning
Cease lithium today and start sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily as the immediate substitute mood stabiliser regimen
Add an angiotensin receptor blocker to reduce intraglomerular pressure and continue the existing lithium dose unchanged
Halve the lithium dose now to reduce nephrotoxic exposure and target a level of 0.4 mmol/L at the next steady state

stem: A 29-year-old woman attends her first antenatal visit at 10 weeks. She has smoked for 12 years, currently 15 cigarettes daily, and asks what she can take to stop.

data_table.Smoking: 15 cigarettes daily; first within 30 minutes of waking; no previous quit attempt

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer to Quitline for structured behavioural support and review her in one week
Start varenicline titrated to 1 mg twice daily from a nominated quit date
Start bupropion 150 mg daily, increasing to twice daily after three days
Supply a 21 mg nicotine patch worn continuously for the next twelve weeks
Advise that cutting down without treatment is sufficient during the first trimester

stem: A 24-year-old woman is referred to community mental health by her general practitioner after her third presentation in 6 months with non-suicidal self-harm and emotional dysregulation. She meets DSM-5-TR criteria for borderline personality disorder, with affective instability, intense interpersonal relationships, identity disturbance, and recurrent suicidal gestures. She is not currently psychotic, not in a major depressive episode, and is not using substances problematically. She is motivated to engage with structured treatment and has stable housing. She works part-time.

data_table.Examination: Linear superficial cuts on forearm; reactive mood; intact insight; no acute psychotic features; no suicidal intent today
data_table.Investigations: Routine bloods and TSH normal; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line intervention for the disorder itself?

options.text: Long-term hospitalisation in a specialist personality disorder inpatient unit for 6 to 12 months of intensive containment
Lifelong second-generation antipsychotic such as quetiapine 200 mg nightly as the primary therapeutic intervention
Brief solution-focused cognitive behavioural therapy over 6 weeks targeted only at self-harm reduction at presentation
Structured psychological therapy such as dialectical behaviour therapy for at least 12 months with case management support
Discharge to primary care with crisis line contact details and an SSRI prescription for emotional dysregulation

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic metabolic monitoring at baseline and 12 weeks
stem: A 27-year-old man with first-episode schizophrenia was commenced on olanzapine 10 mg nocte 12 weeks ago. He has had a good clinical response with reduction in positive symptoms and minimal extrapyramidal effects. He attends today for the 12-week metabolic review. His baseline measurements showed normal weight, fasting glucose 4.8, lipids unremarkable, and BP 118/72. He has gained 6 kg since commencing treatment. He has no family history of diabetes or premature cardiovascular disease and has otherwise stayed well.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 134/88, weight 86 kg (baseline 80), waist 102 cm
data_table.Examination: No EPS; mental state stable; no acute distress; no acanthosis nigricans
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 5.8 mmol/L (baseline 4.8), HbA1c 5.6 percent, total cholesterol 5.4 mmol/L, LDL 3.5, HDL 1.1, TG 2.4, ECG QTc 442 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue olanzapine unchanged and rely on routine 12 monthly reviews because no parameter exceeds a threshold for action
Add metformin 500 mg twice daily empirically and continue olanzapine without further behavioural or dietary intervention
Cease olanzapine abruptly and start ziprasidone 80 mg twice daily today as a metabolically neutral antipsychotic option
Stop all antipsychotic therapy because metabolic adverse effects outweigh symptomatic response in a first episode case
Implement lifestyle intervention, consider switch to aripiprazole given metabolic trajectory, and arrange repeat metabolic panel in 12 weeks

stem: A 31-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 4 years. She presents to your community psychiatry clinic having recently entered a new relationship and wishes to consider pregnancy in the next 12 to 24 months. She has been counselled previously about valproate risks but asks for a detailed plan. Her mood has remained euthymic with no episodes for 3 years on valproate monotherapy. She is otherwise well, takes no other medications, and has no contraindications to alternative mood stabilisers. She has no children.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic mental state; no tremor; full insight; capacity preserved
data_table.Investigations: Valproate level 540 micromol/L; LFTs normal; FBC normal; pregnancy test negative; folate level adequate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue valproate at the current dose with prescribed high-dose folate 5 mg daily for 3 months before conception
Reduce valproate to 500 mg daily to lessen teratogenic exposure during planned conception while maintaining mood stability
Switch to carbamazepine 400 mg twice daily as an alternative mood stabiliser with comparable mood-stabilising properties
Cross-taper to a safer mood stabiliser such as lamotrigine, document highly effective contraception throughout, and refer to perinatal psychiatry
Stop valproate today without substitution and rely on psychological therapy alone until pregnancy is confirmed

subtopic_detail: SSRI discontinuation syndrome recognition versus relapse
stem:
A 34-year-old woman returns to her GP 6 days after stopping paroxetine 20 mg daily, which she has taken for 14 months for a single episode of major depression now in stable remission. She stopped after running out of script while travelling and forgot to refill. She reports vivid 'electric shock' sensations in her head when she moves her eyes, dizziness when standing, nausea, vivid disturbing dreams, and feeling anxious and irritable.

Her mood is reactive, she is enjoying her usual activities, sleeps well after initial dreaming subsides, eats normally, and denies anhedonia, hopelessness, or suicidal thoughts.

data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented, full affect range, eye movements normal, no focal neurology, gait normal
data_table.Investigations: Nil performed today
data_table.Medications: Paroxetine 20 mg daily ceased 6 days ago; combined oral contraception

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Switch to fluoxetine 20 mg daily as a long half-life bridge then taper fluoxetine over 4 weeks instead of paroxetine
Commence prochlorperazine 5 mg three times daily and ondansetron 8 mg three times daily for symptomatic relief of nausea and dizziness
Reassure that symptoms will resolve spontaneously within 7 days and recommend continued cessation without resuming any medication
Diagnose major depressive recurrence and restart paroxetine 20 mg with referral for outpatient psychiatry assessment within 4 weeks
Restart paroxetine 20 mg daily and taper over 4 to 6 weeks once symptoms resolve, with close follow-up to monitor for recurrence

subtopic_detail: Borderline personality disorder acute self-harm crisis management
stem:
A 24-year-old woman with established borderline personality disorder under a community mental health team (currently in week 14 of an 18-month dialectical behaviour therapy program) presents to the emergency department after taking 14 paracetamol tablets at 9 pm following an argument with her boyfriend. It is now 11 pm. She immediately told her mother who brought her in. She has had three similar low-lethality overdoses in the past 18 months.

She is calm now, regrets the act, and says she 'just wanted to feel something stop'. She denies current suicidal intent and has agreed verbally to use her crisis card and call her DBT therapist tomorrow morning. Her therapist is contactable now if needed.

data_table.Examination: Alert, full conversation, no signs of intoxication, no fresh self-harm wounds, mood reactive, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Paracetamol level pending (4 h sample at 1 am); ALT 22, INR 1.0, creatinine 68
data_table.Medications: Currently nil regular; trialled three SSRIs previously with no benefit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management approach after treating the paracetamol overdose?

options.text: Treat the overdose, liaise with her DBT and crisis teams, activate her agreed safety plan, and discharge home with mother and 24-hour follow-up
Commence quetiapine 100 mg nocte as ongoing mood stabilisation and discharge with a 7-day pharmacy supply for self-administration
Request an inpatient Mental Health Act assessment for involuntary admission to enforce safety despite her stated agreement to use the crisis plan
Admit to an acute mental health inpatient unit for at least 7 days for observation, behavioural stabilisation, and medication review
Discharge without communication to the community mental health team and advise her to call Lifeline if distress returns at any point

subtopic_detail: Anorexia nervosa medical admission threshold criteria
stem: A 19-year-old woman is reviewed at her university health service after losing 14 kg over 6 months. She has restricted intake and exercises 2 hours daily. She denies binge or purge behaviour. Her menses ceased 3 months ago. Today she felt dizzy on standing and her family is alarmed. She is intelligent, insightful that her behaviour is harmful, but ambivalent about gaining weight. There is no suicidal ideation. She has no prior psychiatric history and is not on medication.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 38 supine and 62 standing, BP 86/52 supine and 76/40 standing, RR 16, T 35.4, weight 38 kg, height 1.66 m (BMI 13.8)
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, dry skin, lanugo, cold peripheries, no focal neurology, alert, oriented, no thought disorder, mood low-normal reactive
data_table.Investigations: Na 132, K 3.0, phosphate 0.62, magnesium 0.62, glucose 3.4, urea 8.2, creatinine 88, LFT mildly raised, FBC normal, ECG QTc 478 ms with U waves

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange day-program treatment with structured meals and group therapy three times weekly with regular weight and electrolyte monitoring
Admit to a medical or eating disorders inpatient unit for cardiac monitoring, cautious nutritional rehabilitation and electrolyte correction
Initiate olanzapine 2.5 mg nocte to promote appetite and weight gain and review in 2 weeks to assess the effect on eating behaviour
Refer to the community eating disorders team for weekly outpatient review with weight checks and food diary for the next 6 weeks
Discuss using the Mental Health Act to detain her for treatment given the high risk of death without immediate involuntary intervention at this stage

subtopic_detail: ECT indication in severe depression with food refusal and psychomotor retardation
stem: A 68-year-old man is admitted involuntarily under the Mental Health Act with severe psychotic depression. He has lost 8 kg in 6 weeks, refuses food and drink for the past 4 days, has stopped speaking, lies motionless in bed and is incontinent. He has had two adequate trials of antidepressants (sertraline 200 mg for 8 weeks, then venlafaxine 300 mg for 6 weeks) augmented with quetiapine and lithium in turn over the past 14 months with no improvement. He has no significant comorbidities other than hypertension. His son provides next-of-kin consent and the consultant psychiatrist is requesting urgent treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 64, BP 138/82, T 36.2, weight 62 kg (was 70 kg)
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, reactive to noxious stimuli only, no rigidity or waxy flexibility, no focal neurology, dehydrated
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 138, urea 9.4, creatinine 102, glucose 4.2, LFT and TFT normal, ECG normal QTc 410, CT brain age-related atrophy only
data_table.Medications: Venlafaxine 300 mg, lithium 800 mg nocte (level 0.7), perindopril 4 mg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in this patient's treatment?

options.text: Refer for transcranial magnetic stimulation in a private centre as the next evidence-based step before considering electroconvulsive therapy
Continue venlafaxine, increase lithium target to 0.8 to 1.0 mmol/L, and review response in 4 weeks at outpatient follow-up appointment
Trial intranasal esketamine 84 mg twice weekly in a registered TGA Risk Management program centre while continuing current oral antidepressants
Refer for an urgent course of electroconvulsive therapy with anaesthetic preassessment and bridging intravenous fluids while awaiting first session
Switch venlafaxine to tranylcypromine 30 mg daily after washout and add olanzapine 10 mg as augmentation for treatment-resistant depression

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia with amenorrhoea switch strategy
stem: A 27-year-old woman with schizophrenia in clinical remission for 18 months on risperidone 4 mg daily presents to her community psychiatrist with secondary amenorrhoea of 7 months, galactorrhoea, loss of libido, and bone pain in the hips. She has had no positive or negative symptoms during this remission. She is not pregnant. She has been adherent to risperidone with good clinical response and is reluctant to change because of previous relapses on quetiapine. Her bone densitometry shows a Z-score of -1.8 at the lumbar spine.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral galactorrhoea, no thyroid mass, normal visual fields, normal neurological examination, intact secondary sexual characteristics
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 2640 mU/L (upper normal 500); TSH normal, beta-hCG negative, FSH and LH suppressed, oestradiol low, MRI pituitary normal
data_table.Medications: Risperidone 4 mg daily, vitamin D 1000 IU

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Halve the risperidone dose to 2 mg daily to lower prolactin while accepting the increased risk of psychotic relapse for the next several months
Switch directly from risperidone to amisulpride 400 mg daily as the next antipsychotic and reassess prolactin and bone density in 6 months
Continue risperidone unchanged and add cabergoline 0.5 mg twice weekly to normalise prolactin while preserving the current antipsychotic response
Cross-titrate risperidone down while introducing aripiprazole 10 to 15 mg daily to lower prolactin while maintaining symptomatic control
Refer to endocrinology for transsphenoidal pituitary biopsy to exclude prolactinoma despite the normal magnetic resonance imaging study

stem:
A 32-year-old man with schizophrenia has had persistent auditory hallucinations and paranoid delusions causing significant functional impairment over the past 3 years despite treatment. He completed an adequate 8-week trial of risperidone 6 mg daily (with documented adherence on long-acting injectable for 6 months), then an adequate 10-week trial of olanzapine 20 mg daily, both with minimal response. He has gained 14 kg on olanzapine and has impaired fasting glucose.

He has no other major comorbidities and lives with his parents who support treatment. He has read about clozapine and is willing to engage with monitoring.

data_table.Examination: Mildly thought-disordered, third-person auditory hallucinations described, paranoid ideation, no acute risk
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal (neutrophils 4.2 x10^9/L), HbA1c 5.8 percent, lipids LDL 3.1, LFT normal, ECG QTc 410 ms
data_table.Medications: Olanzapine 20 mg nocte, metformin 1 g BD

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his pharmacological management?

options.text: Commence clozapine titration under monitoring with weekly FBC for 18 weeks then monthly, plus baseline ECG and lipid panel before titration begins
Add lithium 500 mg nocte to the current olanzapine regimen as augmentation and review response over the next 8 weeks at outpatient clinic
Trial repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation targeted at the temporoparietal cortex for auditory hallucinations before any further drug change
Continue olanzapine at maximum 30 mg daily and add high-dose sertraline as augmentation for the residual positive symptoms over the next 12 weeks
Switch directly to long-acting paliperidone palmitate monthly injections to ensure adherence before considering clozapine in 6 months

subtopic_detail: Timing of smoking cessation during alcohol dependence treatment
stem: A 47-year-old man is two weeks into treatment for alcohol dependence, abstinent on acamprosate with weekly counselling. He smokes 30 cigarettes daily and asks to stop smoking as well.

data_table.Smoking: 30 cigarettes daily; first within five minutes of waking

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Offer cessation pharmacotherapy with behavioural support starting now
Defer smoking treatment for twelve months to protect his alcohol abstinence
Offer behavioural support alone until he completes his alcohol program
Advise gradual reduction in cigarettes without medication for now
Refer him for residential withdrawal before addressing his smoking

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation in established mental illness
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 46-year-old man with chronic schizophrenia stable on clozapine for 8 years. He smokes 30 cigarettes daily, wants to quit, and is asking what works best. He has no past suicide attempts but had one major depressive episode in his 20s. He has no cardiovascular disease, no renal impairment, and no current substance use. His mental state is stable with no recent psychotic symptoms. His care coordinator and treating psychiatrist support the plan to quit. He has tried nicotine gum unsuccessfully twice in the past.

data_table.Examination: Settled mood, no thought disorder, no psychotic symptoms, no extrapyramidal signs, smoker's cough
data_table.Investigations: Clozapine trough level 480 ng/mL on 350 mg nightly, eGFR 85, ECG normal, fasting glucose 5.4, LDL 3.0

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy is most appropriate?

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg daily titrated to 150 mg twice daily commenced 1 to 2 weeks before quit date, with reassurance that this antidepressant has no interactions with the antipsychotic regimen
Varenicline 0.5 mg daily titrated over 1 week to 1 mg twice daily commenced 1 week before quit date, with monitoring for mood change and proactive clozapine level review after he has quit
Combination nicotine replacement therapy with 21 mg patch plus rapid release lozenges on cravings, with reassurance that no monitoring of clozapine level is required after he successfully quits
Refer for hypnotherapy and acupuncture as primary therapy without pharmacological cover, given the lack of robust evidence for medication efficacy in patients with chronic psychotic illness
Switch clozapine to olanzapine to reduce the smoking-clozapine interaction, then prescribe varenicline 1 mg twice daily without further clozapine monitoring during the cessation attempt

subtopic_detail: Borderline personality disorder - acute distress in ED
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 25-year-old woman with known borderline personality disorder brought in after superficial forearm cuts following an argument with her partner. She is engaged in a DBT program and has a safety plan. She is calm now and apologetic, says she does not want to die, can identify the trigger, and feels regretful. She is housed, has supportive friends, and the GP is contactable in the morning. The wounds do not need suturing. She has had multiple similar presentations over the past 12 months.

data_table.Examination: Superficial linear lacerations to left forearm, dressed, no neurovascular compromise; mental state: euthymic, congruent affect, no thought disorder, no current suicidal ideation or plan, oriented
data_table.Investigations: None required
data_table.Medications: Quetiapine 25 mg PRN nocte; sertraline 100 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Admit voluntarily for 72 hours to the acute psychiatric inpatient unit to provide safety and reset her crisis plan, with daily DBT individual sessions for the duration of admission
Commence regular oral diazepam 5 mg three times daily for 2 weeks to reduce emotional reactivity, then have the GP gradually wean it once her mood stabilises and crises become less frequent
Discharge home with wound care advice, review her DBT crisis plan together using a chain analysis approach, ensure outpatient DBT therapist follow-up, and arrange GP review the following day

Apply an inpatient treatment order under the Mental Health Act for involuntary admission given the repeated pattern of self-harm presentations, then transfer her to the acute unit overnight for safety
Increase sertraline to 200 mg daily and add olanzapine 10 mg at night as augmentation given the recurrent self-harm pattern, with psychiatrist outpatient appointment within 2 weeks for review

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 28-year-old IT worker who requests assessment for ADHD after reading about it online. He describes lifelong difficulty completing tasks, frequent job changes, chronic disorganisation, losing items and being easily distracted. School reports from primary school describe him as bright but unable to focus and impulsive. He has no current substance use, no past psychosis, and his mood is stable. He sleeps adequately. He has not previously been on any psychiatric medication. He is now in a stable relationship.

data_table.Examination: Alert, restless, normal mental state otherwise, no thought disorder, no psychotic symptoms
data_table.Investigations: Not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence a trial of dexamfetamine 5 mg twice daily for 4 weeks and review symptom response, with referral to specialist ADHD service only if the medication trial does not show clear benefit
Order brain MRI, sleep study, urine drug screen, and thyroid function to exclude organic mimics of inattention before any referral to mental health services is initiated by primary care
Reassure the patient that adult-onset ADHD does not exist and arrange counselling for procrastination, with cognitive behavioural therapy as the primary intervention for organisational difficulty
Refer to a psychiatrist or paediatrician credentialed in adult ADHD assessment to confirm diagnosis using DSM-5 criteria, collateral history, and validated rating scales before any pharmacotherapy
Prescribe atomoxetine 40 mg daily for 4 weeks as a non-stimulant trial, since it requires no authority script in adults and is safe to initiate in general practice without specialist input

subtopic_detail: Excess sedation during benzodiazepine treatment of catatonia
stem: A 34-year-old woman receiving lorazepam for catatonia has improving motor signs but is now drowsy and difficult to rouse two hours after her last dose.

data_table.Observations: RR 9, SpO2 92% room air, HR 62, BP 106/64, temperature 36.5

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Withhold the next lorazepam dose and observe her with oxygen
Give intravenous flumazenil to reverse the benzodiazepine effect
Continue the same dose and add oxygen by nasal cannulae only
Stop the lorazepam and refer her for electroconvulsive therapy
Change to intramuscular midazolam at an equivalent daily dose

stem:
You are the GP reviewing a 34-year-old female paramedic 4 months after a fatal multi-casualty incident on a highway. She describes intrusive flashbacks several times daily, nightmares, avoidance of driving past the site, hypervigilance at work, irritability and low mood. She is no longer enjoying activities she once loved. There is no substance misuse. She had a brief depressive episode in her 20s.

She is functioning at work with difficulty and has supportive family. She is not suicidal and has no current self-harm. She has not previously had psychotherapy.

data_table.Examination: Mood low, affect reactive, hypervigilant during interview, no thought disorder, no psychotic symptoms, oriented
data_table.Investigations: Not required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line therapy?

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily as first-line pharmacotherapy and provide psychoeducation, with referral for psychological therapy only if symptoms have not responded after 12 weeks of medication
Refer for trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing, either delivered by a trained therapist over 8 to 12 sessions as first-line management
Prescribe benzodiazepine clonazepam 0.5 mg twice daily for anxiety and sleep disturbance, combined with stress management techniques and lifestyle advice in primary care without further referral
Provide single-session psychological debriefing focused on the index incident, with review at 4 weeks to determine whether additional structured therapy will be needed for any persisting symptoms
Refer for inpatient psychiatric admission for stabilisation and intensive group therapy given the severity of intrusive symptoms and the operational role she holds in emergency services

stem: You are the ED registrar on the late shift when security calls for help. A 30-year-old man with known schizophrenia is shouting, pacing, threatening staff and refusing to engage. He has been brought in by police under emergency apprehension for self-neglect. He has previously responded to oral olanzapine in similar presentations. Verbal de-escalation by senior nursing staff over 20 minutes has not reduced agitation, and the team is now concerned for the safety of other patients and staff in the department. He has no known allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Not yet measurable, observed alert with regular respirations, no pallor, no diaphoresis
data_table.Examination: Pacing, shouting, raised arms, persecutory and grandiose content, refusing assessment
data_table.Investigations: Not yet performed
data_table.Medications: Documented past response to oral olanzapine; on community paliperidone depot, last dose 5 weeks ago (overdue)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Restrain physically and administer intramuscular zuclopenthixol acetate 100 mg for sustained tranquillisation, then re-dose after 24 hours if behavioural disturbance has not fully settled
Administer intramuscular droperidol 10 mg plus midazolam 5 mg without offering oral therapy, given the level of disturbance and the risk to other patients in the department
Administer intravenous ketamine 200 mg as procedural sedation by the consultant, with rapid sequence intubation prepared because of the level of agitation and refusal to engage with staff
Administer intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg with promethazine 50 mg as a single combination injection, then commence regular oral antipsychotic once cooperative for the remainder of the admission
Offer oral olanzapine wafer 10 mg as the first pharmacological step alongside continued de-escalation, accepting that intramuscular medication is offered only if oral is refused

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 38-year-old man with bipolar I disorder, well-controlled on lithium for the last six years at a stable level. He has had no manic or depressive episodes in three years. He attends today asking for a script for ibuprofen for two weeks for an acute mechanical back strain after lifting at work. He has no past history of renal disease, hypertension or peptic ulceration. He is on no other regular medications and is otherwise well.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/74 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, T 36.6°C, weight 84 kg
data_table.Examination: Lumbar paraspinal tenderness only, no neurology, no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Last lithium level 4 weeks ago: 0.7 mmol/L, eGFR 92 mL/min/1.73 m^2, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, sodium 138 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe oral celecoxib 200 mg daily as a COX-2 selective alternative without lithium monitoring
Prescribe oral ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily and recheck lithium level after the two-week course
Prescribe oral paracetamol 1 g four times daily and topical diclofenac gel rather than oral NSAID
Prescribe oral oxycodone 5 mg as required and review back pain weekly for the next month
Withhold lithium for two weeks while the patient uses oral ibuprofen and resume lithium afterwards

stem: You are the psychiatry registrar in an early intervention clinic seeing a 19-year-old man with a four-month history of social withdrawal, persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations. He has not used illicit substances and screens negative for cannabis, methamphetamine and synthetic cannabinoids. He is medication-naive and has no relevant past medical history. He is engaged in shared decision-making and is willing to start an antipsychotic but is concerned about weight gain because his older brother gained 18 kg on olanzapine.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/72 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, T 36.7°C, BMI 22 kg/m^2
data_table.Examination: Calm, formal thought disorder, persecutory delusions, second-person auditory hallucinations, no insight
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, total cholesterol 4.2 mmol/L, ECG normal sinus rhythm with QTc 410 ms, prolactin within normal range

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antipsychotic choice?

options.text: Oral clozapine 12.5 mg daily titrated according to protocol with weekly FBC monitoring
Oral aripiprazole 10 mg daily titrated weekly with monthly metabolic monitoring
Oral olanzapine 10 mg daily titrated weekly with monthly metabolic monitoring
Oral haloperidol 5 mg daily titrated weekly with extrapyramidal symptom monitoring
Oral lorazepam 1 mg three times daily as monotherapy until clear diagnosis is established

stem: You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 26-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia who started clozapine 18 days ago and is on day 18 of titration at 200 mg daily. The community nurse phones because he reports increasing fatigue, mild central chest discomfort and a low-grade temperature. He has had no respiratory symptoms and his clozapine clinic baseline ECG was normal. He has no past cardiac history. Examination shows sinus tachycardia and mild bibasal crackles.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 122 bpm, BP 108/62 mmHg, T 37.6°C, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air
data_table.Examination: Mild bibasal crackles, no murmurs, no peripheral oedema, JVP not raised
data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 380 ng/L (baseline less than 14), CRP 78 mg/L, ECG sinus tachycardia with non-specific T wave changes, FBC unchanged, ferritin within normal range

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add oral prednisolone 50 mg daily and continue clozapine 200 mg daily with weekly troponin and CRP checks
Reduce clozapine to 100 mg daily and recheck troponin and CRP in 72 hours as outpatient at the clozapine clinic
Continue clozapine at 200 mg daily and review with the general practitioner at 7 days for symptom progression
Cease clozapine today, admit for cardiac monitoring and arrange urgent transthoracic echocardiogram and cardiology review
Switch to oral olanzapine 20 mg daily and ignore the cardiac investigations pending outpatient psychiatry review

stem: You are the perinatal psychiatry registrar urgently called to the postnatal ward to assess a 30-year-old woman on day 3 after an uncomplicated vaginal birth of her first baby. The midwives report 24 hours of insomnia, pressured speech, religious grandiosity and now disorganised thought. She is breastfeeding and is reluctant to be separated from the baby. She has a family history of bipolar disorder in her sister. She has been medication-naive throughout pregnancy and has had no obstetric complications.

data_table.Examination: Pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiose religious delusions, partial insight, no acute medical findings, no fever, no neurology
data_table.Investigations: FBC, urea, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, TSH all within normal limits, urinalysis clear, no infective focus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Admit to a general adult psychiatry ward, commence oral diazepam 5 mg three times daily and suspend breastfeeding
Discharge home with the baby on oral lithium 600 mg daily with paediatric monitoring of the breastfed infant
Admit to a mother-baby unit, commence oral olanzapine 5 mg at night and arrange consultant psychiatry review in 24 hours
Arrange community perinatal psychiatry follow-up in 48 hours with no medication changes made today
Admit for urgent unilateral electroconvulsive therapy today as the first-line treatment without an oral antipsychotic trial

subtopic_detail: Depression with psychotic features in older adults
stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 76-year-old woman admitted under geriatrics with weight loss of 8 kg over 2 months, reduced oral intake and persistent low mood. She has nihilistic delusions that her bowels have rotted and refuses food because of this. She has tried sertraline at 100 mg daily for 8 weeks and mirtazapine at 30 mg daily for 6 weeks as outpatient with no response. She has no past history of psychosis. She has retained capacity and is willing to consider further treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/68 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, T 36.5°C, weight 48 kg, BMI 18 kg/m^2
data_table.Examination: Psychomotor retardation, nihilistic delusions, MMSE 28 of 30, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, B12, folate, calcium all within normal limits, ECG normal sinus rhythm with QTc 440 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in treatment?

options.text: Switch mirtazapine to oral venlafaxine 75 mg daily titrating over 4 weeks and review at 8 weeks
Add oral aripiprazole 5 mg daily to existing mirtazapine and continue for 8 weeks before reassessment
Refer for bilateral electroconvulsive therapy after written informed consent and anaesthetic assessment
Commence oral lithium 250 mg twice daily for augmentation aiming for level 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L
Refer for transcranial magnetic stimulation as outpatient over the next 6 weeks

stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 22-year-old woman admitted with mutism, immobility and refusal to eat or drink for 4 days. She has a first presentation of a probable mood disorder. Medical workup including computed tomography of the brain, lumbar puncture, autoimmune encephalitis panel and toxicology has been unremarkable. An intramuscular lorazepam 2 mg trial 48 hours ago produced a brief partial improvement that lasted 2 hours. She has since had two further 2 mg doses without sustained benefit. She has developed pressure areas and has stopped passing urine.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/86 mmHg, HR 110 bpm, T 37.4°C, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale 28 of 69, mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, no rigidity, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 480 U/L, Na 134 mmol/L, K 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 110 micromol/L, lactate 1.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence intravenous amantadine 200 mg twice daily as the next step in management while continuing lorazepam
Increase lorazepam to 8 mg orally over 24 hours and continue for a further 5 days before considering ECT referral
Commence oral olanzapine 10 mg daily as the next step in management and re-evaluate at 7 days for response
Refer for bilateral electroconvulsive therapy starting within 24 hours with daily anaesthetic and physical review
Stop all psychotropic medications and continue supportive care for 7 days before reassessment of catatonic features

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 26-year-old man with first-episode schizophrenia commenced on risperidone 3 mg daily 12 weeks ago. Symptoms are improved and he tolerates the medication. He has gained 6 kg since starting treatment. He smokes 10 cigarettes per day, drinks no alcohol and has no family history of cardiovascular disease. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. Baseline metabolic parameters were normal. He is asymptomatic and lives independently.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/82, HR 78, RR 16, BMI 28, waist circumference 99 cm
data_table.Examination: Well-appearing, no extrapyramidal signs, no tardive dyskinesia, no orthostatic hypotension
data_table.Investigations: Baseline (12 weeks ago) fasting glucose 5.0 mmol/L, lipids normal, HbA1c 33 mmol/mol, ECG normal

lead_in: What metabolic monitoring is most appropriate at this visit?

options.text: Repeat fasting glucose and lipids at 12 months from baseline review and not before then
Check serum prolactin and weight only because metabolic risk is minimal in young men
Check fasting glucose, lipids, weight, waist and blood pressure and review the lifestyle plan
Switch to aripiprazole now to reduce future metabolic risk even though he is tolerating risperidone
Order oral glucose tolerance test plus 24-hour urinary cortisol to exclude secondary causes today

subtopic_detail: Sertraline in third-trimester pregnancy and neonatal adaptation
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 31-year-old at 34 weeks pregnant with a history of moderate depression. She has been on sertraline 100 mg daily for 18 months and is well, with no current symptoms. She is anxious about effects on the baby and considering stopping the medication before delivery. She has no other medications, no risk of postpartum psychosis and has supportive family. She has booked at a tertiary centre.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74, HR 78, T 36.6 °C, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Soft uterus, cephalic, fetal heart 138 reassuring, no oedema, EPDS score 7
data_table.Investigations: Not required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding sertraline continuation in late pregnancy?

options.text: Stop sertraline now to reduce neonatal adaptation syndrome risk and restart after delivery completed
Continue sertraline 100 mg daily and arrange neonatal adaptation review at 24 to 48 hours after birth
Halve the sertraline dose now and stop it completely two weeks before the expected date of delivery
Switch sertraline to fluoxetine to maintain a longer half-life and reduce neonatal withdrawal effects
Substitute psychological therapy alone now and discontinue sertraline before the third trimester begins

subtopic_detail: Valproate pregnancy prevention in bipolar disorder
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 23-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder who has been stable for 18 months on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily. She has a long-term partner and uses condoms only. She is not currently planning pregnancy but is unsure about her contraception. She is aware valproate has risks in pregnancy. She has no other psychiatric or medical conditions and her last manic episode required hospital admission.

data_table.Examination: Stable mood, euthymic, no extrapyramidal signs, no tremor
data_table.Investigations: FBC, LFTs, valproate level within range; beta-hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding her treatment plan?

options.text: Reassure that condoms are adequate contraception and continue valproate at the current dose long-term
Plan a slow valproate taper over four weeks and start lamotrigine 25 mg daily titrating up cautiously
Switch to lithium today and provide both verbal and written information about teratogenicity risks
Continue valproate and add a combined oral contraceptive without other contraceptive review or plan
Insert an etonogestrel subdermal implant today and document the pregnancy prevention program plan

stem: A 29-year-old man with schizophrenia has taken risperidone for three weeks. Over two days he has become mute and immobile and holds imposed postures. He is afebrile.

data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 150, electrolytes and full blood count normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Withhold risperidone while the catatonia is assessed and treated
Increase the risperidone dose to treat the residual psychosis
Substitute haloperidol for risperidone to settle the presentation
Continue risperidone unchanged and add an anticholinergic drug
Cease risperidone and commence dantrolene for muscle rigidity

subtopic_detail: TCA overdose with QRS widening management
stem: You are the ED registrar at a metropolitan hospital seeing a 28-year-old man brought in 90 minutes after ingestion of about 40 amitriptyline 25 mg tablets in a suicide attempt. He is drowsy but responsive, with dry mouth and dilated pupils. His ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS of 140 ms and right axis deviation of the terminal R wave in aVR. He has no seizures and a single dose of activated charcoal has been administered. Toxicology has been notified.

data_table.Vital signs: GCS 13, HR 124, BP 96/58, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, T 36.7 °C, BSL 6.2
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, dry mucous membranes, mydriasis, no focal neurological deficit, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia, QRS 140 ms, terminal R in aVR >3 mm; venous blood gas pH 7.30, lactate 3.2 mmol/L, K 3.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus and reassess QRS width and pH
Commence intravenous lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg as a first-line antidote prior to alkalinisation therapy
Give intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg titrated until alert as the immediate next reversal step today
Begin intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 10 minutes as the recommended sodium channel antidote
Commence intravenous procainamide 17 mg/kg to control sinus tachycardia and prevent further conduction loss

subtopic_detail: Discrimination of NMS from serotonin syndrome with hyperthermia
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 24-year-old man with treatment-resistant depression on phenelzine. He took two doses of tramadol from his mother's medication this evening. Two hours later he is agitated, sweating, with hyperthermia, hypertension, ocular clonus, hyperreflexia and inducible lower limb clonus. His muscles are not lead-pipe rigid and his mental status fluctuates with marked agitation. No antipsychotic exposure. CK is 220 IU/L. Toxicology has been contacted and ICU is aware.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.6 °C, HR 132, BP 168/102, RR 24, SpO2 98% room air, BSL 6.4
data_table.Examination: Agitated, mydriasis, hyperreflexia greater in lower limbs, sustained clonus at ankles, ocular clonus, sweating
data_table.Investigations: CK 220 IU/L, lactate 3.6 mmol/L, creatinine 92, sodium 138, ECG sinus tachycardia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate specific therapy in addition to supportive care?

options.text: Give intramuscular adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg and intravenous methylprednisolone for autonomic crisis
Start oral bromocriptine 2.5 mg three times daily and intravenous dantrolene for muscle rigidity now
Administer intravenous haloperidol 5 mg for control of agitation and continue all current medications
Restart phenelzine immediately and add oral mirtazapine to block serotonin syndrome symptoms tomorrow
Cease serotonergic drugs, give midazolam titrated and oral cyproheptadine 12 mg loading dose now

stem: You are the GP seeing a 42-year-old man who smokes 25 cigarettes a day, has done so for 20 years, and is highly motivated to quit. He has a Fagerstrom score of 7 indicating high dependence. He had one mild depressive episode treated with sertraline 5 years ago, has been off SSRI for 4 years and reports no current depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation or cardiovascular disease. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular and respiratory examination unremarkable; no signs of liver disease; PHQ-9 score 3
data_table.Investigations: FBC, LFTs, eGFR all normal; ECG unremarkable; carbon monoxide breath test elevated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy plan?

options.text: Combination nicotine patch and bupropion together with weekly counselling
Nicotine 21 mg/24 hour patch alone with as needed lozenges for cravings
Bupropion 150 mg twice daily combined with nortriptyline 25 mg at night
Hypnotherapy alone without pharmacological support and a quit date in 4 weeks
Start varenicline 0.5 mg daily titrating to 1 mg twice daily with quit date in week 2

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD pathway with childhood symptom evidence
stem: You are the GP seeing a 30-year-old man with long-standing inattention, distractibility, poor organisation, frequent lateness, and recent loss of his job after repeated forgotten deadlines. His mother provides childhood school reports from age 8 documenting 'does not pay attention in class' and 'difficulty completing tasks'. PHQ-9 is 4 and GAD-7 is 3. He drinks 2 standard drinks a week and has no illicit drug use. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular examination unremarkable; no thyroid mass; cognitive screen unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: TFTs normal; B12 and ferritin normal; ECG unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a psychiatrist for formal ADHD diagnostic assessment using DSM-5 criteria and collateral
Commence a trial of methylphenidate 10 mg twice daily from the GP and review in 4 weeks
Order thyroid function tests alone and review again with a working diagnosis at 2 weeks
Refer to occupational therapy for cognitive strategies and defer any psychiatric assessment
Trial of methylphenidate sustained release as a diagnostic-therapeutic probe in clinic

subtopic_detail: First-line treatment of borderline personality disorder
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 22-year-old woman with a formal diagnosis of borderline personality disorder confirmed by a public mental health service. She describes recurrent self-harm by cutting, intense unstable relationships, fear of abandonment and chronic emptiness. She is currently on sertraline 100 mg with no significant change in symptoms after 4 months. She has no active suicidality today, no psychotic features and no substance use disorder. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Examination: Faint linear scars on volar forearms; no acute injuries; engaged with cooperative manner; no thought disorder
data_table.Investigations: TFTs and FBC normal; PHQ-9 score 12; GAD-7 score 10

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Increase sertraline to 150 mg daily and review in 4 weeks for further response
Refer for structured dialectical behaviour therapy with a trained therapist or program
Add quetiapine 200 mg at night for affective instability and sleep disturbance
Commence lithium 600 mg at night targeting a serum level of 0.6-0.8 mmol/L
Refer for electroconvulsive therapy given persistent symptoms despite an SSRI trial

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 28-year-old woman with schizophrenia stabilised on risperidone 4 mg daily for 18 months. Over the last 3 months she has developed amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and reduced libido. Beta-hCG is negative. TFTs are normal. Pituitary MRI shows no mass. Serum prolactin is 1850 mIU/L. Her positive psychotic symptoms have remained well controlled and she has good insight. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Examination: Galactorrhoea on bilateral expression; no visual field defect; normal thyroid; no acanthosis nigricans
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 1850 mIU/L (high), beta-hCG negative, TSH normal, MRI pituitary normal, fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue risperidone unchanged and add cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly for prolactin
Reduce risperidone to 1 mg daily to lower prolactin while accepting reduced antipsychotic cover
Stop the antipsychotic entirely given the side effect and review again in 6 weeks
Switch risperidone to aripiprazole with cross-titration and monitor for relapse and prolactin
Refer to gynaecology for combined oral contraceptive to mask symptoms with risperidone

subtopic_detail: Medical admission threshold for severe anorexia nervosa
stem: You are the inpatient psychiatric registrar reviewing a 16-year-old girl referred from her GP. She has restricting-type anorexia nervosa with 30 percent weight loss over 6 months and now refuses any oral intake. She presents with severe bradycardia, postural hypotension and significant electrolyte derangement. She is fully oriented but expresses distorted body image and intense fear of weight gain. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 38 supine, BP 80/50 with 30 mmHg postural drop, T 35.6 °C, SpO2 99% room air, BMI 13.5
data_table.Examination: Marked muscle wasting; lanugo hair; cool peripheries; dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Investigations: K 2.8 mmol/L, phosphate 0.6 mmol/L, magnesium 0.6 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L; ECG QTc 480 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Discharge home with outpatient family-based therapy and weekly weight monitoring
Commence olanzapine 5 mg at night and arrange outpatient psychiatry follow-up next week
Admit for cardiac monitoring, electrolyte correction and supervised refeeding under refeeding precautions
Refer to a dietitian only for outpatient meal planning and review at the GP in 2 weeks
Discharge with weekly weight checks and contingency plan if she loses more weight at home

subtopic_detail: Preventing venous thromboembolism during catatonic immobility
stem: A 52-year-old woman has been immobile and mute on the mental health unit for four days while her catatonia is treated. Her renal function is normal.

data_table.Observations: HR 78, BP 122/70, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate additional measure?

options.text: Subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg daily with compression stockings
Aspirin 100 mg orally daily until she is mobilising again
Passive limb physiotherapy twice daily without drug cover
Duplex ultrasound of both legs every 48 hours while immobile
Warfarin 5 mg daily targeting an international normalised ratio of 2 to 3

subtopic_detail: Delusional disorder community management without involuntary admission
stem: You are the community psychiatric registrar reviewing a 52-year-old woman with an 18-month history of a fixed belief that her next-door neighbour is poisoning the water supply to her house. She has no auditory or visual hallucinations, no thought disorder, no negative symptoms and no mood disorder. Her husband reports she works, drives and socialises normally except for this belief. She uses no substances and her mini-mental status examination is normal. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Examination: Cooperative, well-groomed; no thought disorder; circumstantial speech around the persecutory belief; no perceptual disturbance; insight is poor for the belief but preserved elsewhere
data_table.Investigations: TFTs, B12, syphilis serology, HIV negative; urine drug screen negative; MRI brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Admit involuntarily under the Mental Health Act despite there being no risk of harm to others
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily for likely psychotic depression with predominant delusions
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis alone without any pharmacotherapy
Refer for electroconvulsive therapy given treatment resistance and chronicity of belief
Initiate aripiprazole 10 mg daily and arrange outpatient community psychiatric follow-up

stem: You are the community mental health registrar reviewing a 24-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia who started clozapine 8 weeks ago. He has tolerated the titration with mild constipation and sedation. He returns today for routine review. He reports no fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers. He has had blood tests done weekly since commencement under the central monitoring system.

data_table.Examination: Alert, no oropharyngeal lesions, no cervical lymphadenopathy, chest clear, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Latest FBC: Hb 144 g/L, WCC 6.2 x10^9/L, neutrophils 3.4 x10^9/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L. Previous weekly results all within green-traffic-light range.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing haematological monitoring schedule?

options.text: Continue weekly full blood examinations for the duration of his clozapine treatment because the agranulocytosis risk does not change over the course of the first year
Continue weekly full blood examinations until 18 weeks of treatment, then space to fortnightly until 12 months and monthly thereafter while clozapine is continued
Reduce to monthly full blood examinations now that he has completed 8 weeks because his neutrophil counts have been stable through the first two months of treatment
Stop routine full blood examinations and rely on patient-reported symptoms of fever, sore throat or mucosal ulcers to trigger any further investigations during clozapine treatment
Add weekly C-reactive protein and procalcitonin to the existing full blood examination to capture early signs of cytokine-mediated myocarditis during titration through this period of treatment

subtopic_detail: First-line psychological therapy for post-traumatic stress disorder
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 33-year-old woman with intrusive memories, nightmares, hypervigilance and avoidance for the past six months. The symptoms began after a serious motor vehicle accident in which a passenger died. She avoids driving and feels emotionally numb. She has no current suicidal ideation, no psychosis and no alcohol or substance misuse. She has not been on any psychotropic medication.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: anxious affect, congruent mood, intact thought form, no perceptual disturbance, future-oriented
data_table.Investigations: PCL-5 score 48 of 80. PHQ-9 score 12 of 27.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Refer for trauma-focused cognitive behaviour therapy with a clinical psychologist over 8 to 12 weekly sessions and review her response in primary care after the course
Start oral diazepam 5 mg three times daily for symptomatic control of hyperarousal and review at four weeks for response and tolerance with possible dose adjustments
Commence quetiapine 50 mg at night for sleep and intrusive symptoms with planned uptitration to 200 mg over 4 weeks if tolerated by the patient at clinical review
Provide supportive psychoeducation only and review in 12 weeks because spontaneous remission occurs in most adults within the first six months of post-trauma symptoms
Start mirtazapine 30 mg at night and refer for generic supportive counselling sessions in the community over a course of weekly meetings spanning the next several months

subtopic_detail: Long-term lithium monitoring schedule for renal and thyroid function
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 45-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder who has been on lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte for 4 years. She is euthymic and continues to work full time. She takes no other regular medications and has no recent illnesses. Her last formal lithium level monitoring was nine months ago. She asks how often she needs ongoing tests.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic mood and affect, no tremor at rest, no peripheral oedema, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Latest serum lithium 0.7 mmol/L (12-hour trough), TSH 2.4 mIU/L, creatinine 68 micromol/L, eGFR 92 mL/min/1.73 m^2, corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing monitoring schedule?

options.text: Repeat serum lithium, urea and electrolytes and thyroid function tests now and then again every three months for the foreseeable course of treatment with this medication
Stop routine monitoring because she has been stable for four years and lithium levels have remained therapeutic at the most recent 12-hour trough level measurement
Order serum lithium, urea, electrolytes, calcium and thyroid function every six months and an annual eGFR, with prompt repeat if dose, illness or new medications change
Switch to lamotrigine 200 mg daily as long-term maintenance therapy because lithium causes inevitable progression to chronic kidney disease over more than 5 years of continuous use
Continue annual serum lithium only because all other organ-system tests for this medication can be reasonably deferred when the patient is clinically euthymic and well

subtopic_detail: Opioid agonist therapy initial agent choice and safety
stem: You are the addiction medicine registrar reviewing a 28-year-old man with heroin use disorder for the past three years. He injects daily and wants to start opioid agonist therapy. He has hepatitis C antibody positive, but liver function and synthetic function are preserved. He has had no overdoses but has been using alone. He has no chronic respiratory disease or current benzodiazepine use. He has unstable housing and limited transport.

data_table.Examination: Mild withdrawal symptoms with dilated pupils, piloerection and yawning; no track marks of skin and soft tissue infection
data_table.Investigations: ALT 48 U/L, AST 52 U/L, bilirubin 14 micromol/L, INR 1.0, albumin 38 g/L. Urine toxicology positive for heroin; negative for benzodiazepines and methadone.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial opioid agonist therapy?

options.text: Start oral methadone 80 mg daily today and continue at this dose until next review with daily supervised dosing at his community pharmacy of usual choice
Trial extended-release oral naltrexone 50 mg daily from tomorrow for relapse prevention because of its low risk of accumulation and once-daily oral dosing convenience
Start oral diazepam 10 mg three times daily and oral clonidine for autonomic features and arrange community-based residential rehabilitation in the next available place
Defer pharmacotherapy and refer to weekly cognitive behaviour therapy and peer support group meetings as the initial treatment of his opioid use disorder before any agonist therapy
Induce sublingual buprenorphine-naloxone 4 mg when he is in objective withdrawal, uptitrate to 8 to 16 mg over the first day and arrange a depot formulation when stable

subtopic_detail: Discriminating serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome
stem: You are the medical registrar called to a 38-year-old woman on the psychiatric ward with sudden agitation, tremor and fever. She has bipolar I disorder and was started on tramadol 50 mg four-hourly for back pain yesterday in addition to her usual sertraline 100 mg and lithium 750 mg nocte. Symptoms began 6 hours ago and have worsened in the last hour. She has had no recent dose change of her antipsychotic.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 °C, HR 132, BP 168/96, RR 28, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Examination: Agitated, diaphoretic, mydriasis, hyperreflexia and sustained clonus more marked in lower limbs, mild tremor, no lead-pipe rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 482 U/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L, WCC 11.8 x10^9/L, Na 138, K 4.0, creatinine 78 micromol/L, lithium 0.9 mmol/L. ECG: sinus tachycardia.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease the offending serotonergic agents, give intravenous benzodiazepines for agitation, commence active cooling and admit for monitoring and supportive care
Start bromocriptine 2.5 mg orally three times daily and intravenous dantrolene 1 mg/kg as definitive treatment for neuroleptic malignant syndrome before any other escalation
Administer intravenous physostigmine 1 to 2 mg over 5 minutes targeting reversal of anticholinergic delirium and persisting tachycardia in this acutely confused febrile patient
Give intravenous haloperidol 5 mg for the acute behavioural disturbance and increase her usual sertraline to 150 mg today to address mood-related agitation in this acute presentation
Hold lithium for 24 hours, continue sertraline and tramadol unchanged and recheck the lithium level in the morning before considering further changes to her medication regimen

subtopic_detail: Acute mania with psychotic features adjunctive antipsychotic choice
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar on the consultation-liaison service reviewing a 36-year-old man with known bipolar I disorder. He has been on lithium 1000 mg nocte for two years with previous good response. He presents in florid mania for the past four days with grandiose delusions, reduced sleep and hyperactivity. He is medication adherent and his lithium level is in range. He has no diabetes or known cardiac disease. He has no acute medical issues.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 110, BP 132/82, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiose delusions, no perceptual disturbance reported, no extrapyramidal signs
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 0.9 mmol/L. TSH 2.2 mIU/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, eGFR 95 mL/min/1.73 m^2, fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, fasting lipids unremarkable. ECG QTc 412 ms.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Increase his lithium dose to target a level of 1.2 mmol/L and continue this as monotherapy without addition of any antipsychotic agent during this episode
Switch his lithium to sodium valproate 1 g twice daily and reassess his response over a fortnight after a routine therapeutic drug level has been obtained from his bloods
Add oral olanzapine 10 mg daily to his existing lithium and review the response over the following week with weekly weight, lipid and glucose monitoring
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily in addition to current therapy to address irritability and mood lability that may be driving his presenting acute behavioural disturbance
Add lamotrigine 25 mg daily, titrate over six weeks to 200 mg and continue ongoing monthly serum monitoring of his lithium level during the titration period

stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 15-year-old non-Aboriginal girl with a four month history of persistent low mood, anhedonia, fatigue and reduced school attendance. She has had no manic features. She has been engaged in weekly trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy for eight weeks without improvement. She denies active suicidal ideation but has fleeting passive thoughts of being better off dead. Her parents are present and supportive of medication.

data_table.Examination: Mood low, affect restricted, no psychomotor agitation, thought form linear, no perceptual disturbance, denies plan or intent
data_table.Investigations: TSH normal, FBE normal, ferritin normal, urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological choice?

options.text: Sertraline 25 mg orally daily titrated to 50 mg after 1 week with weekly clinical review for 4 weeks and shared safety planning
Mirtazapine 15 mg orally at night titrated weekly with regular face-to-face review and explicit safety planning that includes a written crisis plan
Continue psychological therapy alone for a further 8 weeks before reconsidering pharmacotherapy because medication carries a suicidality warning in adolescents
Venlafaxine 37.5 mg orally daily titrated weekly with face-to-face review at one week and explicit safety planning agreed with family and patient
Fluoxetine 10 mg orally daily increased to 20 mg after one week, weekly clinical review for four weeks with explicit safety planning and continued psychological therapy

stem: You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 28-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with bipolar I disorder, currently euthymic six weeks after a manic episode requiring brief admission. She has been stable on quetiapine 600 mg daily but has gained 7 kg. She and her consultant agree to switch to lithium for relapse prevention. She is in a relationship and has had a Mirena IUD inserted last year. She has no past renal, thyroid or cardiac disease.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no abnormal movements, thyroid not palpably enlarged
data_table.Investigations: U&E pending, TSH pending, calcium pending, ECG pending, beta-hCG today negative

lead_in: Which baseline workup is required before commencing lithium?

options.text: Full blood examination, liver function tests and serum prolactin level before commencing lithium therapy at an initial dose of 250 mg twice daily
Urea, electrolytes and creatinine; thyroid function; serum calcium; ECG; weight and a pregnancy test before commencing lithium at an initial low dose
Urea, electrolytes and creatinine alone without other tests because lithium's main adverse effect is nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and reduced glomerular filtration rate
Echocardiogram and exercise stress test to assess cardiac function before commencing lithium because of conduction abnormalities and risk of cardiomyopathy progression
MRI brain and electroencephalogram to assess baseline neurological status before commencing lithium because of neurotoxicity risk and tremor reporting in many users

stem: You are the addiction medicine registrar reviewing a 48-year-old non-Aboriginal man on day one of planned community alcohol detoxification. He has been drinking 200 g alcohol daily for 10 years. He has had two previous unprovoked alcohol withdrawal seizures. He has no liver decompensation and is keen to remain at home with carer support. His last drink was 12 hours ago and he is mildly tremulous but oriented.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 96, BP 142/86, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Mild tremor, anxious, no diaphoresis, oriented to time and place, no asterixis, no jaundice
data_table.Investigations: LFTs mildly deranged GGT 240 U/L, ALT 62, AST 70, INR 1.0, FBE normal, BSL 5.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate prescription?

options.text: Oral thiamine 300 mg daily and outpatient detox without sedative cover because his withdrawal severity is currently mild and he has carer supervision at home
Oral diazepam loading 20 mg every 2 hours symptom-triggered using CIWA-Ar scoring with thiamine cover and admission to hospital because of his seizure history
Oral lorazepam 1 mg every 6 hours for 5 days at home with general practitioner review every second day and thiamine 100 mg orally daily as outpatient support
Oral carbamazepine 200 mg three times daily as primary withdrawal therapy and outpatient detoxification with daily clinic review and oral thiamine supplementation
Oral chlordiazepoxide 25 mg every 6 hours fixed-schedule for 5 days at home with no thiamine because of his preserved nutritional status and normal full blood count

stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar called to the emergency department to assess a 42-year-old non-Aboriginal man brought in with confusion and rigidity. He was started on haloperidol 10 mg three days ago for acute psychosis. He had received no other psychotropic medication. On arrival he is sweating, mute, and stiff with cogwheeling in all four limbs. Family deny illicit drug use and there has been no recent infection.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 °C, HR 132, BP 168/96, RR 28, SpO2 95% room air, GCS 12
data_table.Examination: Generalised lead-pipe rigidity, tremor, diaphoresis, no clonus, no neck stiffness, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 6200 U/L, WCC 13.5 x10^9/L, urea 9.2, creatinine 142 micromol/L, K 4.4, Na 142, urine myoglobin positive, CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue haloperidol at reduced dose with paracetamol and active cooling because pyrexia is from the acute psychosis rather than from the medication
Add lorazepam 2 mg orally and observe for response with no other change in psychotropic medication because rigidity is characteristic of catatonia not NMS
Cease haloperidol immediately, transfer to intensive care for active cooling, intravenous hydration, dantrolene or bromocriptine and electrolyte monitoring with myoglobinuric renal protection
Switch haloperidol to olanzapine 10 mg, continue current observation in the medical ward and reassess in 24 hours after a single trial of cyproheptadine 12 mg orally
Administer intramuscular procyclidine 10 mg as the first-line antidote and continue haloperidol in expectation that cogwheel rigidity will resolve within an hour

subtopic_detail: Borderline personality disorder with recurrent self-harm
stem: You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 26-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with known borderline personality disorder who presents after superficial wrist lacerations following an argument with her partner. She is engaged in weekly dialectical behaviour therapy. She has had four similar presentations this year. She is now calm, engaged, declines admission and has a written safety plan in her phone. Her partner is present and supportive.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 78, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Superficial linear lacerations to left forearm, no neurovascular compromise, no tendon injury; mood reactive, no current suicidal intent reported
data_table.Investigations: Bedside urine drug screen negative, BSL 5.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Admit involuntarily to the psychiatric unit under the relevant Mental Health Act because the repeated self-harm episodes constitute risk of serious harm
Prescribe diazepam 5 mg three times daily for two weeks and arrange general practitioner review without communication with her existing DBT therapist about the presentation
Wound care, review and update of the existing safety plan, communication with her DBT therapist, and discharge with planned follow-up within 24 to 48 hours
Initiate quetiapine 100 mg at night to reduce emotional dysregulation and arrange a private psychiatrist review within 6 weeks without contacting her current treating team
Refer for an inpatient electroconvulsive therapy course because of the chronic and recurrent nature of the self-harm and limited response to weekly psychotherapy

stem: You are the early psychosis service registrar reviewing a 23-year-old non-Aboriginal man 3 months after starting olanzapine 15 mg nightly for a first episode of schizophrenia. Symptoms have improved and he is adherent. He has gained 5 kg since starting treatment. He smokes 10 cigarettes daily, eats takeaway most nights and walks only briefly. His parents and partner are supportive and he is back at his apprenticeship. He has no known cardiovascular disease and no family history of premature heart disease.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/82 mmHg, HR 84, RR 14, T 36.7 °C, BMI 27 kg/m2 (up from 25 baseline)
data_table.Examination: Mildly increased waist circumference 96 cm, no acanthosis nigricans, no peripheral oedema, no extrapyramidal signs
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 5.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.6%, total cholesterol 5.4 mmol/L, LDL 3.4 mmol/L, HDL 1.0 mmol/L, triglycerides 2.4 mmol/L, prolactin 380 mIU/L (normal up to 500), ECG QTc 432 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange dietitian and exercise physiologist input, schedule repeat fasting lipids and glucose at 6 months, and review olanzapine choice with the prescriber if metabolic indices worsen
Commence metformin 500 mg twice daily immediately to prevent further weight gain, continue olanzapine 15 mg unchanged, and review the FBC and renal function in 3 months
Switch immediately to risperidone 4 mg daily without dietitian input, withhold metabolic re-screening for 6 months, and review in psychiatric outpatient clinic in 12 weeks
Refer to cardiology for stress echocardiography given the elevated triglycerides and rising BMI, defer further psychiatry follow-up until that result is available
Cease olanzapine, prescribe diazepam 5 mg twice daily for symptom control, and refer back to the general practitioner for ongoing care of the metabolic side effects without psychiatry review

subtopic_detail: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder vs first-episode schizophrenia
stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar called by ED about a 21-year-old non-Aboriginal man brought in by his housemates with 5 days of persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations. He has used high-potency cannabis daily for 18 months and increased intake markedly over the past month. He has no past psychiatric history and no family history of psychosis. He is calm in the cubicle. Urine drug screen is positive for cannabinoids and negative for amphetamines.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/72 mmHg, HR 88, RR 16, T 36.6 °C, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented to person and time, mildly perplexed, no extrapyramidal signs, no fever, normal cardiovascular and neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, CRP all normal, urine drug screen positive cannabinoids only, ECG QTc 410 ms, CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Order overnight observation in ED with diazepam 5 mg twice daily for sedation only, withhold antipsychotic and AOD counselling, and discharge in the morning to GP follow-up
Discharge home with instructions to cease cannabis, withhold antipsychotic treatment, and review in early psychosis clinic in 2 weeks once a baseline assessment is complete
Detain under the Mental Health Act for compulsory inpatient treatment and commence intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg every 6 hours for symptom control on admission
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily for the perplexity and persecutory thoughts, recommend cannabis cessation, and arrange GP review in 1 week for medication titration
Admit voluntarily, commence olanzapine 10 mg nightly, arrange brief alcohol and other drug counselling, and plan psychiatric review in 4 weeks with abstinence advice

stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar called to the medical ward to see a 28-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with bipolar I disorder admitted 4 days ago for refusing food and fluids. She has been mute, immobile and maintaining odd postures. She has not eaten or drunk anything. She has not had recent neuroleptic dose change. Medical causes have been excluded by neurology consult. She is on lithium 750 mg nightly.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.0 °C, HR 96, RR 18, BP 116/72 mmHg, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Mute, eyes open without engagement, waxy flexibility with arms remaining where placed, mild echopraxia of examiner gestures, Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale score 14, no rigidity or pyrexia
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs normal, lithium level 0.72 mmol/L, CK 320 U/L, CRP 4 mg/L, CT brain normal, EEG without epileptiform activity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg twice daily for the immobility and mutism, observe for further extrapyramidal features, and review the response after 48 hours
Administer a lorazepam challenge with 1 mg intramuscularly and reassess at 30 minutes, planning ongoing scheduled lorazepam if responsive and ECT referral if not
Increase the lithium dose to 1000 mg nightly, recheck the level in 5 days, and continue ward observation pending mood stabiliser optimisation over the next week
Commence intravenous valproate loading at 20 mg/kg in addition to lithium, withhold benzodiazepines, and reassess catatonic features after 4 hours of observation
Refer for nasogastric tube insertion for feeds and rehydration, withhold psychotropic intervention until oral intake resumes, and review with psychiatry team in 24 hours

subtopic_detail: Valproate teratogenicity and pregnancy prevention in a woman of reproductive age
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar in the mood disorders clinic reviewing a 27-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with bipolar I disorder who has been stable for 18 months on sodium valproate 1000 mg nightly. She is in a new relationship and has stopped using contraception because she wants to start trying for a baby in the next 6 months. She has had no episodes for 18 months and is otherwise well. She works as a primary school teacher and has supportive parents nearby. There is no other medical or psychiatric history.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/76 mmHg, HR 76, RR 14, T 36.6 °C, BMI 24 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Euthymic mental state, normal neurological examination, no signs of polycystic ovary syndrome, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, valproate level 480 micromol/L (therapeutic 350 to 700), LFTs normal, urine pregnancy test negative, TSH 1.6 mIU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch to carbamazepine 400 mg daily as an alternative mood stabiliser with the rationale that it has a more favourable fetal safety profile in pregnancy planning settings
Continue valproate at the current dose, add folic acid 5 mg daily, and reassure that the medication is safer for the baby than a relapse during pregnancy in this stable patient

Counsel that valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy planning, arrange specialist review to transition to a safer mood stabiliser such as lamotrigine, and continue effective contraception during the switch
Cease valproate immediately without replacement therapy, commence cognitive behavioural therapy fortnightly, and review for relapse with monthly mood diaries and clinic visits
Continue valproate during the periconceptional period only, switch to lamotrigine after the first trimester, and arrange detailed morphology scan at 20 weeks

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose with QRS widening
stem: You are the emergency registrar called to resus for a 32-year-old non-Aboriginal woman brought in 90 minutes after a deliberate overdose of approximately 50 amitriptyline 50 mg tablets. She is drowsy with a GCS of 11. Her partner found her with the empty bottle. She has a 5-year history of depression and previous self-harm by cutting. There is no other prescribed medication and no recreational drug use disclosed.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.5 °C, HR 132 sinus tachycardia, RR 16, SpO2 96% room air, BP 92/56 mmHg, GCS 11 (eyes 2, verbal 4, motor 5)
data_table.Examination: Dry mouth, mydriasis with sluggish pupils, dry warm skin, urinary retention, hyperreflexia, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: ECG QRS 132 ms with terminal R wave in aVR over 3 mm, QTc 480 ms, ABG pH 7.30 pCO2 30 mmHg HCO3 17 mmol/L, paracetamol level under 10 mg/L, alcohol negative, salicylate not detected, potassium 3.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus targeting QRS narrowing and arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55, intubate to protect the airway, and arrange ICU admission
