Administer activated charcoal 50 g orally, place on telemetry in the resus bay, and reassess the ECG and conscious state in 2 hours before deciding on further intervention
Administer intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg over 30 seconds for the reduced level of consciousness and reassess airway protective reflexes after each dose titration
Administer intravenous physostigmine 1 mg slow push to reverse the anticholinergic syndrome and arrange continuous cardiac monitoring with intensive care liaison after dose
Administer intravenous amiodarone 300 mg over 20 minutes for the sinus tachycardia and broadening QRS, continue oxygen and intravenous fluids, and admit to a monitored ward bed

stem: You are the on-call psychiatry registrar in ED with a 26-year-old non-Aboriginal man brought in by police for violent and threatening behaviour in the community. He has a 3-year history of schizophrenia. He is shouting, intermittently striking the walls and refuses oral medication. De-escalation by experienced ED nursing staff has not reduced his agitation. He has no known medical conditions, no allergies and is otherwise physically well. Six security staff are present.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 124, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, BP 142/88 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Highly agitated, no signs of intoxication, no head injury, no needle marks, no pyrexia, no clonus, no rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 5.4 mmol/L, urine drug screen pending, ECG QTc 410 ms on previous admission

lead_in: What is the single best initial pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg with promethazine 25 mg as a combined dose, no cardiac monitoring required, and admit to the psychiatric assessment unit immediately afterwards
Intramuscular midazolam 10 mg as a single dose without antipsychotic, observe airway and oximetry in the resus bay, and repeat at 10 minute intervals as needed
Oral olanzapine 20 mg wafer with lorazepam 2 mg by mouth and observe in the cubicle, repeating doses at 30 minute intervals if cooperation continues to improve
Intramuscular droperidol 10 mg as a single dose with continuous pulse oximetry and cardiac monitoring, repeat dose available at 15 minutes if needed
Intravenous ketamine 100 mg as a sedative dose with anaesthetic standby, intubation kit prepared, and direct admission to ICU once sedated

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD with comorbid stimulant use disorder
stem: You are the addiction psychiatry registrar in a tertiary clinic seeing a 29-year-old non-Aboriginal man referred for assessment of adult ADHD with comorbid methamphetamine use disorder. He has used methamphetamine intermittently for 6 years and was abstinent for the past 4 weeks following a residential withdrawal admission. He describes lifelong inattention, distractibility and impulsivity, with school records confirming attentional difficulties from age 8. His mother has untreated ADHD. He is engaged with an outpatient drug and alcohol service. He drives a delivery truck for work.

data_table.Examination: Normal cardiovascular and neurological examination, no signs of intoxication or withdrawal, no peripheral stigmata of long-term stimulant use
data_table.Investigations: Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) score 18 of 24 inattentive features, structured diagnostic interview meets DSM-5 ADHD criteria with childhood symptom evidence, urine drug screen negative, ECG QTc 405 ms with normal sinus rhythm, FBC, UEC, LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological plan?

options.text: Commence guanfacine extended release 4 mg daily as a non-stimulant alternative, with the understanding that this is the preferred non-stimulant choice over atomoxetine in adults
Commence immediate-release dexamfetamine 5 mg twice daily and titrate weekly to symptom response, with monthly urine drug screens and direct supply through a single prescriber
Commence lisdexamfetamine 30 mg morning dose immediately with daily pharmacy dispensing and weekly urine screens, plus continued outpatient drug and alcohol engagement throughout therapy
Defer ADHD pharmacotherapy until 12 months of abstinence, continue cognitive behavioural therapy and addiction support, and review at the end of that period for treatment planning
Commence atomoxetine titrated to 80 mg daily, continue addiction medicine engagement, and reassess in 8 weeks before considering stimulant trial if symptoms persist

subtopic_detail: Anorexia nervosa medical admission criteria and refeeding syndrome
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 19-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with a 3-year history of anorexia nervosa restricting subtype. Her parents have brought her in because of progressive fatigue, dizziness on standing and one syncopal episode while showering this morning. She has been eating around 400 kcal per day for the past month. She is medically stable but markedly underweight. She has been seeing an outpatient psychologist weekly but has not been admitted before.

data_table.Vital signs: T 35.6 °C, HR 38 supine resting, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, BP 86/52 lying 70/40 standing, weight 38 kg height 168 cm BMI 13.5 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, lanugo on arms and back, cool peripheries, no oedema, alert and orientated but withdrawn, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Na 134 K 2.9 Cl 96 HCO3 28 mmol/L, phosphate 0.65 mmol/L, magnesium 0.62 mmol/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L, ALT 78 ALP 88 albumin 32 g/L, ECG QTc 478 ms, FBC unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Discharge home with daily dietitian and psychologist input, immediate commencement of a high calorie oral nutritional supplement plan of 3000 kcal/day and review by adolescent psychiatry in the eating disorders day program within 48 hours

Admit to a general medical ward for cardiac monitoring, commence high-calorie nasogastric feeding at 30 kcal/kg/day, correct potassium and phosphate aggressively and start a benzodiazepine at night to manage refeeding anxiety

Admit to a monitored medical bed, commence oral thiamine 200 mg daily and a multivitamin, replace potassium phosphate and magnesium before feeding, start cautious refeeding at 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day and increase under daily electrolyte monitoring

Admit to the high-dependency unit, commence rapid parenteral nutrition at 40 kcal/kg/day to restore weight gain, correct electrolytes intravenously and request urgent compulsory inpatient treatment under the relevant state Mental Health Act

Refer urgently to a private eating disorders inpatient program with daily outpatient electrolyte monitoring at her general practice surgery while a private psychiatric admission is being arranged over the next 7 days

subtopic_detail: Complex PTSD therapy and pharmacotherapy choice
stem: You are the general practitioner reviewing a 34-year-old non-Aboriginal woman 4 months after a violent assault. She has nightmares, hypervigilance, intrusive flashbacks during the day, avoidance of public transport and difficulty sleeping. She has tried sertraline at 50 mg daily for the last 6 weeks with partial response on mood symptoms but persistent flashbacks. She is engaged with a clinical psychologist for supportive counselling and is willing to consider trauma-focused therapy. She has no current suicidal ideation and is working part-time.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 84, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, BP 122/76 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Anxious affect with intermittent tearfulness, no psychomotor retardation, intact insight and judgement, no current suicidality
data_table.Investigations: PCL-5 score 48 (moderate-severe), PHQ-9 score 18 (moderate-severe), thyroid function and FBC within reference ranges, no substance use on history or urine drug screen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Switch sertraline to mirtazapine 30 mg nocte targeting sleep and appetite improvement, and continue supportive counselling with the clinical psychologist as the sole talking therapy intervention going forward

Add olanzapine 5 mg nocte for adjunctive sleep and re-experiencing symptom control, and review SSRI dose titration in 4 weeks before considering any psychological therapy referral or non-pharmacological intervention

Increase sertraline to 100 mg daily, add prazosin 1 mg nocte for nightmares titrated to 5 mg over 4 weeks and review in 4 weeks for further dose adjustment without any change to her current psychological treatment

Refer for trauma-focused CBT or EMDR with an experienced clinician, continue sertraline at 50 mg with a planned review of dose at the next appointment and arrange GP review in 4 weeks to monitor symptoms

Recommend a 6-week course of mindfulness-based stress reduction in a community group program as the primary therapy and discontinue sertraline because of the partial response and intolerance of medication side effects

stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 56-year-old non-Aboriginal man with a 30-year history of heavy alcohol use. He has been on the ward for 36 hours after self-presenting for detoxification and stopped drinking 48 hours ago. He is now confused, tremulous, sweating profusely and has had a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure 30 minutes ago. He is intermittently agitated and seeing animals on the curtains. He has had two previous episodes of complicated alcohol withdrawal.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.2 °C, HR 132, RR 26, SpO2 96% room air, BP 168/108 mmHg, capillary glucose 4.8 mmol/L
data_table.Examination: Disoriented to time and place, marked tremor, profuse diaphoresis, visual hallucinations, GCS 14, no focal neurology, soft non-tender abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Na 132 K 3.2 Mg 0.62 phosphate 0.7 mmol/L, glucose 4.8 mmol/L, urea 7.2 creatinine 92 micromol/L, ALT 96 GGT 540 U/L, INR 1.4, FBC platelets 102 x10^9/L, head CT no acute pathology

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence oral diazepam 20 mg every 2 hours by symptom-triggered CIWA-Ar protocol on the general ward and arrange routine medical review by the consultant on the morning ward round in approximately 12 hours from now

Administer haloperidol 5 mg intramuscular for agitation, continue oral thiamine 100 mg daily and observe for further seizures on the ward with intramuscular diazepam available for clinician-initiated breakthrough as needed

Start phenytoin loading dose 18 mg/kg over 30 minutes for ongoing seizure prevention and continue an oral benzodiazepine taper with no need to escalate the level of care beyond the current general medical ward bed

Transfer to the intensive care unit for sedation with continuous propofol infusion and elective intubation to control airway and autonomic features given the established delirium tremens with seizure and pyrexia

Transfer to a high-dependency or intensive care bed, give intravenous diazepam 10 mg titrated to RASS minus 1, administer parenteral thiamine 300 mg three times daily for 3-5 days before any glucose-containing fluids and replace magnesium and potassium

stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 28-year-old non-Aboriginal man who presents requesting an assessment for adult ADHD. He describes lifelong difficulties with sustained attention, frequent forgetfulness, restlessness, impulsivity at work, and three traffic infringements in the past 12 months for inattention while driving. He has not been previously assessed. Collateral from his mother confirms problems since primary school. He drinks alcohol on weekends only and uses no other substances. He has no current depression or anxiety on screening.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 76, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, BP 124/78 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Engaging in conversation, mildly restless, no thought disorder, no psychotic features, GCS 15, normal cardiac and neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: DIVA-5 structured interview supports ADHD combined presentation, ASRS-v1.1 screener positive in both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive domains, no medical contraindications on baseline ECG and bloods, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before initiating stimulant medication?

options.text: Refer to a psychiatrist or paediatrician with an authority to prescribe stimulant medication for confirmation of diagnosis and treatment initiation, and counsel on Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive obligations including notifying the driver licensing authority

Commence methylphenidate immediate release 10 mg twice daily under your own prescription, with cardiac and blood pressure monitoring at 2 and 4 weeks, and continue community follow-up before any psychiatry referral is considered

Trial atomoxetine 40 mg daily for 6 weeks first and refer for stimulant prescriber only if atomoxetine has failed to control core ADHD symptoms because stimulants carry abuse potential and cardiovascular risk concerns

Recommend cognitive behavioural therapy alone for 12 weeks with no pharmacotherapy until psychological therapy completion and review CBT outcomes before considering whether stimulant medication will be necessary at that future review

Advise the patient that ADHD diagnosis in adulthood requires symptoms appearing before age 7 years and cannot be diagnosed with first presentation at 28 years even with childhood history confirmed by collateral parental information

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective vs bipolar with psychosis discrimination
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 26-year-old non-Aboriginal man brought in by his family after 8 weeks of bizarre behaviour. He describes persistent persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations of voices commenting on his actions. Over the last 3 weeks he has also developed elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech and grandiose plans to start a new tech company.

His delusions persisted during a 5-week period when his mood and energy were normal earlier in this episode. He has had two previous similar episodes. There is no substance use confirmed on urine drug screen.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 92, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, BP 124/76 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Pressured speech, distractible, grandiose, persistent auditory hallucinations of commentary type, persecutory delusions; no formal thought disorder, oriented to person place and time, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, FBC UEC LFT TSH within reference ranges, head CT no acute findings, fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, lipids fasting cholesterol 4.6 mmol/L LDL 2.4 HDL 1.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder (bipolar type) given two or more weeks of psychotic symptoms occurring in the absence of a major mood episode together with current concurrent manic and psychotic symptoms over the course of this illness

Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features given the current manic episode with mood-congruent grandiose delusions and the absence of any persistent psychotic symptoms outside discrete mood episodes during the course of his illness

Schizophrenia given the 8 week duration of psychotic symptoms with persistent auditory hallucinations and delusions of persecution and the absence of negative symptoms that have lasted at least 6 months at this present time

Substance-induced psychotic disorder given the relatively rapid onset of psychotic symptoms with concurrent mood elevation and the typical pattern observed in stimulant and cannabis use in young men of his age and demographic

Brief psychotic disorder given the rapid onset of psychotic symptoms with full return to premorbid functioning expected within one month and no requirement for ongoing antipsychotic maintenance therapy beyond resolution of symptoms

stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 79-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with a 6-week history of anhedonia, early morning waking, 4 kg weight loss and pervasive low mood since the death of her husband. Her past medical history includes well-controlled type 2 diabetes, atrial fibrillation on apixaban and stage 3 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 42 mL/min/1.73 m2). She lives alone, has good social supports through her church and has no current suicidal ideation. Her GDS-15 score is 11/15. There is no cognitive impairment on MoCA.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6 °C, HR 72 irregularly irregular, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, BP 132/78 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Tearful, psychomotor slowing, intact insight, no thought disorder, no psychotic features, GCS 15, MoCA 28/30
data_table.Investigations: Na 136 K 4.4 urea 6.8 creatinine 122 micromol/L eGFR 42, ALT 24 albumin 38 g/L, HbA1c 7.0%, TSH 2.4 mU/L, ECG sinus rhythm with QTc 460 ms, FBC within reference ranges

lead_in: Which antidepressant is the most appropriate first-line option?

options.text: Amitriptyline 25 mg nocte titrated to 75 mg over 4 weeks because tricyclic antidepressants have a long evidence base in older adults with biological depression features including early morning waking and significant weight loss

Sertraline 25 mg daily, titrating to 50 mg after 1 week with monitoring of serum sodium at 2 and 4 weeks, sleep and appetite, and review for response at 4 to 6 weeks before considering further dose adjustment

Mirtazapine 30 mg nocte targeting appetite stimulation, weight gain and sleep restoration in geriatric depression with prominent vegetative features and minimal pharmacokinetic interaction with currently prescribed apixaban therapy at this stage

Citalopram 20 mg daily titrated to 40 mg over 2 weeks for fastest response with regular ECG monitoring to track QTc changes during dose increases over the next 6 weeks of antidepressant initiation and titration

Venlafaxine extended release 75 mg daily titrated to 150 mg over 4 weeks combining SNRI efficacy with daily blood pressure monitoring and electrolyte review at 1 and 4 weeks for any hyponatraemia or treatment-emergent hypertension

subtopic_detail: Clozapine red-result neutrophil threshold and immediate action
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on a community clozapine clinic. A 34-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been on clozapine 400 mg daily for 18 months with full symptom remission. His weekly FBC for the first 18 weeks was normal; after the first 6 months he was on 4-weekly monitoring and his most recent FBC 5 weeks ago was a green result.

Today's FBC, taken because of 2 days of sore throat and rigors, shows WBC 2.1 x10^9/L (was 6.8 x10^9/L last month), absolute neutrophil count 1.1 x10^9/L (was 4.2 x10^9/L last month), platelets 240 x10^9/L, Hb 142 g/L. He is afebrile (37.8 °C) but well in himself with no localising signs of infection.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8 °C, BP 120/76 mmHg, HR 88, SpO2 98% room air, RR 18
data_table.Examination: Mild pharyngeal erythema, no exudate or tonsillar swelling, no cervical adenopathy, chest clear, no other findings
data_table.Investigations: WBC 2.1, ANC 1.1, plt 240, Hb 142, CRP 18; viral PCR pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Continue clozapine at current dose, repeat FBC in 24 hours and reassure that an isolated mild drop is common with viral illness in the first 18 months of treatment and resolves spontaneously without dose change

Halve clozapine to 200 mg daily as a precautionary dose reduction, repeat FBC in 7 days and review at the next routine clinic appointment after the protocol-required interval has elapsed for medication adjustment review

Cease clozapine, admit to a medical ward for haematology consultation, take blood cultures, commence broad-spectrum IV antibiotics empirically and consider granulocyte colony-stimulating factor if ANC falls below 0.5 x10^9/L

Switch to olanzapine 20 mg daily today and arrange weekly FBC for 8 weeks to ensure recovery of haematological parameters before considering rechallenge with clozapine or alternative antipsychotic options

Continue clozapine at current dose, escalate to twice-weekly FBC monitoring until two consecutive green results, review for infection (chest X-ray, blood cultures if febrile or focal signs), and notify the clozapine coordinator and prescribing psychiatrist

subtopic_detail: Lithium long-term monitoring schedule for renal, thyroid and calcium function
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community mental health clinic seeing a 45-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder maintained on lithium carbonate 1000 mg nocte for 8 years. She has been euthymic on this dose throughout. Her last set of routine bloods 6 months ago showed lithium level 0.7 mmol/L (target 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L for maintenance), eGFR 78 mL/min/1.73m^2, TSH 3.4 mIU/L, corrected calcium 2.42 mmol/L.

She drinks 1.5 to 2 litres of water daily, no NSAID use, no recent dehydration, no new medications. She has no current symptoms of toxicity.

data_table.Examination: No tremor, normal reflexes, no goitre, no signs of dehydration
data_table.Investigations: Last set 6 months ago as above

lead_in: What is the recommended routine monitoring schedule for her stable maintenance lithium therapy?

options.text: Lithium level every 6 months together with UEC, TFTs and corrected calcium every 6 months; review for new medications (NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors, diuretics) and dehydration at every appointment
Lithium level monthly, UEC monthly, TFTs annually, corrected calcium annually; review for drug interactions at every visit because of the narrow therapeutic index of lithium therapy in older adults

Lithium level annually, UEC annually, TFTs annually, corrected calcium 2-yearly; counsel on hydration and to report tremor, nausea or polyuria immediately as warning signs of impending lithium toxicity
Lithium level every 3 months, UEC every 3 months, TFTs every 6 months, corrected calcium annually; review medication interactions, dehydration risk and lithium toxicity signs at every visit
Lithium level 4-weekly until 6 months from any dose change then 6-monthly thereafter, TFTs and UEC only if clinically symptomatic, corrected calcium not routinely required for long-term lithium

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose ECG criteria for sodium bicarbonate
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar managing a 28-year-old woman brought in by ambulance 90 minutes after a witnessed ingestion of around 2 grams of dosulepin tablets with vodka. She is drowsy but rousable to voice, agitated when stimulated. Her partner reports she took the tablets after an argument and a long history of depression. Initial GCS 13, BP 92/58 mmHg, HR 128, T 36.6 °C, SpO2 95% room air.

The ECG just performed shows sinus tachycardia at 128 bpm, QRS duration 142 ms with a prominent R wave in aVR of 5 mm and a deep S wave in lead I.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 92/58 mmHg, HR 128, RR 22, SpO2 95%, T 36.6 °C, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, agitated on stimulation, dry mucous membranes, dilated pupils 6 mm reactive, no focal neurology, no seizure activity
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia 128, QRS 142 ms, R in aVR 5 mm; VBG pH 7.32, pCO2 41, HCO3 21; Na 138, K 3.6; paracetamol level pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube and obtain repeat ECG and serum drug levels in 4 hours before any additional pharmacological intervention beyond standard supportive measures

Administer sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol (100 mL of 8.4%) IV bolus, repeat to keep QRS under 100 ms and serum pH 7.45 to 7.55, intubate for airway protection given GCS 13 and start IV crystalloid 1 L bolus
Commence IV metoprolol 5 mg slow bolus to control the tachycardia and reduce myocardial oxygen demand, repeat ECG in 30 minutes and titrate further beta-blockade based on heart rate response
Administer flumazenil 0.2 mg IV titrated to GCS over 15 and avoid sodium bicarbonate unless clearly seizing because rapid alkalinisation may precipitate cardiac arrhythmia in TCA toxicity
Administer IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 10 minutes to suppress polymorphic ventricular ectopy and reserve sodium bicarbonate for QRS over 160 ms or established ventricular tachycardia

subtopic_detail: Lorazepam challenge for diagnosis and treatment of catatonia
stem:
You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar called to the medical ward to see a 22-year-old woman with a recent first episode of psychotic depression on the psychiatric unit who was transferred to medicine 36 hours ago for poor oral intake. She has eaten almost nothing and drunk very little for 5 days. The medical team are concerned she may have an organic encephalopathy.

On examination she shows marked psychomotor retardation, will not respond to verbal commands, has waxy flexibility with maintenance of posed positions for over a minute, intermittent grimacing, mutism with occasional brief echolalia and posturing of the right arm. T 37.1 °C, BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 92. Bloods show no infection or metabolic cause; CT head is unremarkable. CK is 290 U/L.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.1 °C, BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 92, RR 16, SpO2 98%, GCS reported as 14
data_table.Examination: Waxy flexibility, mutism, posturing, grimacing, echolalia, Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale 18
data_table.Investigations: Bloods unremarkable, CK 290, CT head unremarkable, EEG pending, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence olanzapine 10 mg orally daily and review for response after 72 hours given that catatonia in psychotic depression usually resolves with effective antipsychotic monotherapy at adequate doses

Initiate enteral feeding via nasogastric tube to address nutritional compromise from 5 days of minimal intake, monitor electrolytes daily for refeeding syndrome and delay specific catatonia treatment until oral intake is restored

Refer for empirical immunotherapy with high-dose methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily for 5 days and consider plasma exchange given the possibility of NMDA receptor encephalitis presenting with catatonia and mutism

Administer lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV (lorazepam challenge), observe over 10 to 15 minutes for partial or complete remission of catatonia (around 50% rate), then commence scheduled lorazepam 2 mg three times daily and refer for ECT if no response within 48 to 72 hours

Continue current management without specific pharmacotherapy and arrange daily Bush-Francis Rating Scale assessment, planning ECT only if catatonia persists beyond 14 days and not responding to supportive care

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD diagnosis confirmation pathway and driving notification under Austroads
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman who self-presented requesting assessment for adult ADHD after seeing content online. She describes lifelong inattention, distractibility and impulsivity that she now believes contributed to her difficulties at school and her current poor work performance at her professional services firm. She reports six or more inattentive symptoms (loses focus mid-task, forgets appointments, struggles to start tasks) and four hyperactive-impulsive symptoms with onset in primary school.

Her teachers' reports document poor concentration from age 8. She has no current substance use, no current depression or anxiety meeting criteria, and no medical comorbidities. She holds an unrestricted Australian car licence and drives daily to work.

data_table.Examination: Normal physical exam, no cardiovascular abnormality
data_table.Investigations: Hospital ECG normal; thyroid function normal; iron studies normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence a trial of methylphenidate immediate-release 10 mg twice daily and review response at 4 weeks to assess symptom improvement before referring to a psychiatrist for formal diagnosis and ongoing prescribing

Reassure her that adult-onset ADHD is uncommon and that her symptoms are more likely to reflect anxiety or burnout; provide CBT referral and reassess in 6 months without specific ADHD pathway investigation

Commence atomoxetine 40 mg daily titrated to 80 mg as a non-stimulant ADHD pharmacotherapy that does not require psychiatrist authority and can be initiated in GP practice for clear adult ADHD presentations

Order EEG, MRI brain and overnight polysomnography in primary care to exclude differential diagnoses including absence seizures, structural intracranial lesion and obstructive sleep apnoea before any referral for ADHD assessment

Refer her to a psychiatrist for diagnostic confirmation by structured interview, screen with a validated adult ADHD tool (DIVA-5 or ASRS-v1.1), assess comorbidity, and counsel on the Austroads requirement to disclose untreated symptomatic ADHD if it impairs safe driving

subtopic_detail: Varenicline versus NRT versus bupropion choice in post-myocardial infarction smoker
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 56-year-old man 8 weeks after an inferior NSTEMI treated with primary PCI to the right coronary artery. He smokes 25 cigarettes daily and has been on aspirin, ticagrelor, atorvastatin, ramipril and metoprolol since discharge. He started smoking at 16 and has had 3 prior cessation attempts using cold turkey alone, each relapsing within 3 weeks.

His mood is stable and he has no history of seizures, depression or self-harm. He has no renal impairment. He scores 8 on the Fagerstrom test for nicotine dependence (high). He wants to quit and asks what works best for him given his recent heart attack.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/76 mmHg, HR 64, BMI 28, SpO2 98%, expired CO 28 ppm
data_table.Examination: Healthy male, no cardiac signs of decompensation, no neurological abnormality
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs normal; recent echocardiogram LVEF 50%; HbA1c 5.8%

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation?

options.text: Prescribe nicotine inhalator alone titrated to cravings, suggest he sets a quit date 2 weeks from now and provide brief advice plus a self-help quit booklet for behavioural support over the next 12 weeks

Defer pharmacotherapy until 6 months post-MI because both varenicline and bupropion have been associated with neuropsychiatric and cardiovascular adverse events in the immediate post-infarct period and only NRT is appropriate now

Commence varenicline 0.5 mg daily for 3 days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily from day 8 for 12 weeks with quit date at day 8 to 14 and Quitline behavioural support throughout therapy

Prescribe bupropion 150 mg daily for 3 days then 150 mg twice daily for 12 weeks with quit date at day 8 to 14 and Quitline support, choosing bupropion because it has the best efficacy and safety profile in post-MI patients

Prescribe combination NRT (21 mg/24h patch plus 4 mg gum as needed) with no behavioural support given his prior failed attempts and ask him to return only if cessation fails at 4 weeks for escalation of therapy

subtopic_detail: Acute severe behavioural disturbance pharmacological choice in young adult male
stem: You are the emergency department registrar called to the resuscitation bay where a 25-year-old man with first-presentation psychosis is acutely agitated, threatening staff and other patients, attempting to leave despite an Inpatient Treatment Order. De-escalation by an experienced nurse and security has failed over 15 minutes. He is not currently taking any psychotropic medication and has no documented allergies. Collateral suggests no significant alcohol or substance use in the past 24 hours but possible methamphetamine use 3 days ago. He weighs around 80 kg and is haemodynamically stable. The duty psychiatrist has authorised chemical restraint.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/88 mmHg, HR 118, T 37.0 °C, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, ECG sinus tachycardia QTc 430 ms
data_table.Examination: Pacing, fists clenched, verbally threatening, no signs of intoxication, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 5.2 mmol/L, urine drug screen pending, FBC and UEC pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate single first-dose chemical restraint?

options.text: Administer droperidol 10 mg intramuscularly, monitor continuous cardiac monitoring and SpO2, repeat 10 mg IM at 15 minutes if not settled, and review for further treatment after 30 minutes from the second dose
Administer haloperidol 5 mg with promethazine 25 mg IM together as a combined sedation regimen, monitor for extrapyramidal effects and lower the threshold for ECG monitoring given the QT interval

Administer midazolam 10 mg IM as a single agent without monitoring beyond intermittent vitals given that benzodiazepine monotherapy avoids the cardiac and extrapyramidal risks of antipsychotic chemical restraint
Administer ketamine 4 mg/kg intramuscularly under anaesthetic supervision as the first-line agent for severe behavioural disturbance in a stimulant-related agitation given recent methamphetamine use

Offer oral olanzapine wafer 20 mg with a glass of water and observe for cooperation before escalating to any parenteral medication, regardless of the failed de-escalation by experienced staff already attempted

subtopic_detail: First-line structured psychotherapy choice for established borderline personality disorder
stem:
You are the community mental health team registrar following up a 24-year-old woman with a 4-year history of borderline personality disorder confirmed on structured assessment 12 months ago. She has had three psychiatric admissions for self-harm and suicidal ideation in the past 2 years. She has been on sertraline 200 mg daily and quetiapine 100 mg at night for over a year with limited benefit.

Self-harm by cutting occurs around weekly. She is engaged in care, attends appointments and is keen to try therapy. She is not currently psychotic, severely depressed or in active crisis. She lives independently and has a part-time job.

data_table.Examination: Healed self-harm scars to forearms, no fresh wounds; mental state stable
data_table.Investigations: Routine bloods normal, no current intoxication

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Increase sertraline to 250 mg daily and add lithium 250 mg twice daily for emotion dysregulation and consider a long-acting injectable antipsychotic if self-harm persists at the next 3-month review

Refer for an evidence-based structured psychotherapy program (dialectical behaviour therapy or mentalisation-based therapy or schema-focused therapy) with a target of 12 months of treatment and review pharmacotherapy aiming to rationalise prescribing

Plan a hospital admission for behavioural containment of self-harm with a 4 to 6 week structured ward program, ECT consideration and graded leave because community management has failed over the last 12 months
Discharge to GP-led management with a written safety plan and crisis line numbers, on the basis that BPD generally responds best to non-specialist supportive care with minimal medical intervention

Trial open-label naltrexone 50 mg daily and topiramate 100 mg twice daily for impulsivity and self-harm and reassess at 12 weeks before considering psychotherapy referral if symptoms persist on combination pharmacotherapy

subtopic_detail: Anorexia nervosa long-term hypogonadism and bone mineral density management
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 22-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa restrictive subtype diagnosed at age 15. She has had two prior medical admissions for bradycardia and electrolyte derangement; her last admission was 14 months ago. She is now stable at BMI 17.2 and engaged with a community eating disorder specialist team for 18 months. Menses have been absent for 5 years; she has never tried to conceive.

Recent bloods show normal electrolytes, oestradiol low, LH and FSH low. DEXA scan from 3 months ago shows lumbar spine T-score -2.4 and femoral neck T-score -1.9.

data_table.Examination: No bradycardia symptoms, no lanugo, mild peripheral cyanosis, no fractures
data_table.Investigations: Oestradiol low, LH 1.2, FSH 1.8 (both low), TSH 1.8, prolactin 360 mIU/L, vitamin D 42 nmol/L, corrected calcium 2.30, PTH 4.2 pmol/L, urine pregnancy negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her bone health?

options.text: Commence a combined oral contraceptive pill 30 microgram ethinylestradiol/levonorgestrel as the primary treatment for low bone mineral density to provide systemic oestrogen replacement and improve T-scores over 12 months of therapy

Commence alendronate 70 mg weekly as a first-line bisphosphonate for low T-score in a young woman with hypothalamic amenorrhoea regardless of nutritional restoration progress or her stated plans for future pregnancy in coming years

Refer to endocrinology for consideration of teriparatide 20 micrograms subcutaneously daily for 2 years as a bone-anabolic agent given her premenopausal age and persistent low BMD despite treatment of her primary eating disorder

Continue to support weight restoration as the primary intervention, optimise vitamin D and calcium, consider physiological oestrogen replacement via transdermal oestradiol with cyclical progesterone if BMD does not improve or fractures occur, and repeat DEXA in 12 months

Commence denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months as an antiresorptive agent because it has rapid onset compared with bisphosphonates and is not deposited in bone matrix to give long-term fetal risk

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing conversion (functional neurological) disorder from factitious disorder and malingering
stem:
You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 32-year-old woman in clinic with a 6-month history of intermittent left-sided weakness, episodes of unresponsiveness with eye closure and convulsive activity. MRI brain, EEG (including ictal recordings of 4 typical events), and CSF are all normal. She is not seeking financial compensation and there is no medico-legal context. On examination, the left-sided weakness shows Hoover's sign and give-way pattern; her grip strength is variable when distracted.

Her symptoms began after the death of her father from a stroke. She is distressed by the symptoms and wishes to return to work as a nurse. She does not knowingly produce symptoms and is not seeking medical attention as the primary motivator.

data_table.Examination: Hoover's sign positive on the left, give-way weakness, variable grip when distracted, normal cranial nerves, sensory exam non-anatomical distribution
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain, EEG (4 ictal recordings), CSF all normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Malingering, because the symptoms are inconsistent with any organic neurological process and the variability of weakness on examination indicates intentional production of symptoms for personal gain

Factitious disorder imposed on self because the production of seizure-like events without any organic correlate on EEG suggests deliberate symptom feigning to assume the sick role rather than for any external incentive

Functional neurological disorder (conversion disorder) because the symptoms are not consciously produced, are inconsistent with neurological examination, have positive rule-in signs (Hoover's, variable weakness) and are associated with psychological precipitants

Generalised anxiety disorder with somatic symptoms because chronic worry can manifest as motor and sensory symptoms in the absence of an underlying organic neurological cause and CBT for anxiety would be first-line

Multiple sclerosis with normal initial MRI, because MS can present with motor symptoms and atypical seizure-like episodes for years before brain lesions become radiologically apparent on standard imaging sequences

subtopic_detail: Sodium valproate pregnancy prevention program and switch in woman of reproductive age
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 27-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder maintained on sodium valproate 1500 mg daily for 4 years. She is euthymic, currently studying full-time, in a stable relationship and not actively planning pregnancy but does not use any reliable contraception. She does not want to use combined hormonal contraception due to a family history of VTE.

She has tried lithium previously but stopped due to fine tremor and weight gain, and tried quetiapine briefly with sedation. She asks for your advice about staying on valproate.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable, no tremor, no acne, no hirsutism
data_table.Investigations: Valproate level 540 micromol/L (therapeutic), FBC, LFTs, UEC normal, urine pregnancy negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue sodium valproate at current dose, advise her of teratogenic risks and document discussion in the medical record, and recommend she contacts you within 24 hours of any positive pregnancy test result for review

Switch to carbamazepine 200 mg twice daily over 4 weeks as a safer mood stabiliser option in pregnancy planning with lower teratogenic risk than sodium valproate and continue with regular review of mood symptoms during the transition period from valproate to carbamazepine over the next month

Discontinue valproate today and start lamotrigine 25 mg daily with rapid titration to 200 mg daily over 2 weeks to avoid bipolar relapse during transition and minimise the window of unprotected reproductive exposure to teratogenic valproate during the changeover period

Continue valproate at her current dose but enrol her in the formal pregnancy prevention program with monthly pregnancy testing and document a risk discussion review annually; if she fails to comply with the program transition to a non-teratogenic alternative

Counsel on teratogenic risks of valproate (around 10% major malformation, 30 to 40% neurodevelopmental delay), arrange psychiatric review to plan transition to lamotrigine or olanzapine, and recommend a long-acting reversible contraceptive such as an IUD in the interim

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective disorder versus bipolar I with psychotic features diagnostic discrimination
stem: You are the inpatient psychiatry registrar reviewing a 32-year-old man with a 6-year illness history with recurrent psychotic episodes. Records confirm: 2017 first episode lasting 7 weeks of grandiose delusions and auditory hallucinations of God speaking to him, accompanied by elevated mood, decreased sleep, pressured speech and overspending; 2019 a 6-week depressive episode with low mood, anhedonia and suicidal ideation, during which auditory hallucinations persisted; 2022 a 4-week period of persistent persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations with no concurrent mood symptoms (no mania, no depression). Between episodes he has had mild residual negative symptoms but no severe mood disturbance.

data_table.Examination: Mental state on admission: psychotic with ideas of reference, currently low mood and reduced sleep over 10 days
data_table.Investigations: Bloods routine; no substance use on urine screen; no organic cause identified

lead_in: Which diagnosis is most consistent with his longitudinal illness pattern?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type, because his illness includes mood episodes (mania, depression) with concurrent psychosis and a 4-week period of psychosis in the absence of mood symptoms during the lifetime of the illness

Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features, because the psychosis is part of his mood episodes (mania and depression) and the periods of inter-episode psychosis are unrelated negative symptoms rather than schizoaffective psychosis

Schizophrenia with comorbid mood episodes, because his persistent residual negative symptoms between episodes are more consistent with schizophrenia and the mood episodes are reactive demoralisation rather than primary affective illness

Major depressive disorder with mood-incongruent psychotic features, because his current presentation includes low mood and the persistent delusions and hallucinations represent treatment-resistant psychotic depression following inadequate antidepressant therapy

Substance-induced psychotic and mood disorder because chronic substance use produces both psychotic and mood phenomena and the patient's current presentation likely represents withdrawal-related affective and psychotic symptoms

subtopic_detail: First-episode schizophrenia antipsychotic selection and monitoring
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar in an early-psychosis service reviewing a 21-year-old engineering student who was admitted involuntarily 2 weeks ago after a first-episode psychosis with 6 months of persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations. He has fully cooperated with treatment, has no medical comorbidities and his BMI is 24. He has gained 1 kg in two weeks and his symptoms are partially improved on oral olanzapine 10 mg nocte. He smokes 10 cigarettes per day and has no family history of diabetes or cardiac disease.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72, HR 84, BMI 24, weight 76 kg (up from 75)
data_table.Examination: Affect blunted but engaged, no EPS, no abnormal involuntary movements, normal cardiovascular and neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: Baseline ECG QTc 412 ms, FBC, UEC, LFTs normal, fasting lipids: total cholesterol 4.6, LDL 2.8, fasting glucose 5.0 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.4%, prolactin 410 mIU/L (slightly elevated)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue oral olanzapine at the current dose, provide brief smoking cessation advice with nicotine replacement therapy and arrange baseline-plus-3-monthly metabolic monitoring with weight, waist circumference, fasting lipids and glucose for at least the first year of treatment

Switch immediately to first-generation haloperidol 5 mg daily because second-generation antipsychotics in young adult males consistently produce greater metabolic and prolactin morbidity than first-generation agents at equivalent symptomatic doses

Add a mood stabiliser such as sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily as augmentation for partial response at 2 weeks because combination therapy from the outset shortens time to remission in first-episode schizophrenia and reduces relapse risk

Discontinue antipsychotic medication entirely and commence weekly cognitive behavioural therapy alone because psychological therapy is now first-line in first-episode psychosis if symptoms partially improve during the initial 2-week admission period

Start a long-acting injectable depot antipsychotic such as paliperidone palmitate 150 mg deep IM at first dose, omit further oral antipsychotic and discharge home without further specialist follow up because depot reduces relapse risk most effectively

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome from SSRI plus tramadol
stem: You are the consult-liaison psychiatry registrar called by the emergency department about a 48-year-old man on sertraline 200 mg daily for major depressive disorder who attended his general practitioner two days ago for low back pain and was prescribed tramadol 50 mg three times daily. Today he presents with tremor, agitation, sweating, dilated pupils and inducible ankle clonus that is more marked on the right. His vital signs show hyperthermia at 38.6 degrees C, tachycardia and hypertension. He has had no recent alcohol or illicit drug use.

data_table.Examination: Tremor, hyperreflexia greater in lower limbs, inducible ankle clonus, dilated pupils, diaphoretic, agitated and restless, mild abdominal hyperactive bowel sounds
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, CK 320 U/L, UEC normal, ECG sinus tachycardia QTc 420 ms, toxicology screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g infusion and oral propranolol 40 mg three times daily as first-line therapy for serotonin syndrome and continue both serotonergic agents at reduced doses with ongoing twice-daily monitoring of vital signs

Continue both medications because tramadol plus an SSRI does not produce clinically significant serotonin syndrome at standard doses and treat the autonomic features with intravenous beta blocker and oral paracetamol for the hyperthermia

Treat as neuroleptic malignant syndrome with intravenous dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg and oral bromocriptine 2.5 mg every 8 hours and arrange transfer to intensive care because the autonomic instability is identical to NMS in clinical presentation

Cease sertraline and tramadol immediately, provide intravenous benzodiazepine sedation with diazepam or midazolam, active cooling and supportive intravenous fluids, and consider oral cyproheptadine 12 mg as a serotonin antagonist if symptoms persist

Administer single dose intravenous physostigmine 1 mg over 5 minutes as the specific cholinergic antidote for serotonin syndrome and continue intravenous hydration only with no further pharmacological cessation or substitution of any kind

subtopic_detail: Inpatient alcohol withdrawal management with CIWA-Ar guidance
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 52-year-old man with daily heavy alcohol use (estimated 14 standard drinks per day for 12 years) who has come in for elective inpatient detoxification. His last drink was 14 hours ago. He has no history of seizures or delirium tremens. He is fully oriented but tremulous and anxious. His CIWA-Ar score is 18 currently. He has no other medical comorbidities, no known liver disease and no pregnancy is possible.

data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor of outstretched hands, mildly anxious, mild diaphoresis, oriented to time place and person, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, LFTs ALT 78 AST 96 GGT 240, INR 1.0, UEC normal, BSL 5.4, ethanol level 0.04% on admission, CIWA-Ar 18

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence symptom-triggered oral diazepam 10 to 20 mg every 1 to 2 hours guided by CIWA-Ar score, plus intramuscular thiamine 300 mg daily for 3 days before oral thiamine 100 mg three times daily, and monitor for delirium tremens or seizure

Commence oral chlorpromazine 100 mg every 6 hours as first-line therapy because chlorpromazine treats both the autonomic features and any subsequent delirium tremens with a lower risk of respiratory depression than benzodiazepines

Commence intravenous 10% dextrose at maintenance rate prior to thiamine and continue without benzodiazepine cover because adequate carbohydrate restoration alone will prevent Wernicke encephalopathy and reduce the severity of subsequent withdrawal symptoms

Commence oral baclofen 10 mg three times daily and oral acamprosate 666 mg three times daily for relapse prevention before the patient develops further withdrawal features and as initial monotherapy without benzodiazepine cover during the acute period

Commence a small daily ration of oral alcohol via 30 mL whisky four times daily and gradual taper over 14 days as the safest method of avoiding the GABAergic rebound seen with abrupt cessation of long-term heavy alcohol use

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant choice in pregnancy after MDD relapse
stem: You are the perinatal psychiatry registrar reviewing a 31-year-old G2P1 at 10 weeks gestation with recurrent moderate to severe major depressive disorder. Her current episode began 6 weeks ago. She stopped citalopram 20 mg daily 4 weeks ago when she discovered she was pregnant, after which her mood, sleep and appetite have deteriorated and she now reports passive suicidal ideation without plan or intent. She has a history of postpartum depression after her first child. She is breastfeeding-naive currently. She has no other mental or physical health diagnoses.

data_table.Examination: Anxious mood, congruent affect, slowed speech and thought, no perceptual disturbance, no active suicidal ideation or intent, oriented
data_table.Investigations: FBC, TFTs, UEC normal; routine antenatal bloods unremarkable, beta-hCG appropriate for gestation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence paroxetine 20 mg daily as first-line because paroxetine has the largest sample of pregnancy outcome data of any SSRI and has been used successfully across all trimesters in international guidelines without major safety concerns

Defer all pharmacotherapy until after delivery because antidepressant exposure in the first trimester causes major congenital malformations and the safest approach is psychological therapy alone for the duration of the pregnancy

Restart citalopram at the previous 20 mg daily dose because she had a documented good response to citalopram before pregnancy and any switch of agent at the start of pregnancy risks unnecessary delay in symptom remission with second-line agents

Restart antidepressant therapy with sertraline 50 mg daily, refer to a perinatal mental health service and arrange combined obstetric and psychiatric follow up, with brief psychological therapy as a concurrent adjunct over the next 6 weeks

Commence venlafaxine 75 mg modified-release daily as first-line because SNRIs are more effective than SSRIs for moderate to severe MDD and the cardiovascular and persistent pulmonary hypertension risks in the neonate are reassuringly negligible

stem:
You are the on-call psychiatry registrar called by the obstetric team to review a 29-year-old G1P1 day 8 postpartum who was discharged 5 days ago after an uncomplicated normal vaginal delivery. Her partner reports she has had two days of progressively reduced sleep, perplexity, fluctuating mood, and tonight she has been talking about the baby having a special spiritual purpose she must protect.

She is bewildered and has trouble following conversation. She has no past psychiatric history but her mother had bipolar I disorder. The baby is currently with the grandmother.

data_table.Examination: Perplexed, restless, intermittent thought blocking, mood labile, fleeting persecutory and grandiose delusions about the infant, no objective auditory hallucinations elicited, cognitively impaired on bedside testing, no neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, TFTs, B12/folate, calcium, magnesium, BSL all normal; urine drug screen negative; CT head unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate plan?

options.text: Diagnose postpartum thyroiditis presenting with neuropsychiatric features and commence oral propranolol 40 mg three times daily while awaiting repeat thyroid function tests at 6 weeks postpartum before consideration of psychiatric pharmacotherapy

Diagnose severe postnatal depression with psychotic features and prescribe sertraline 50 mg daily with brief community psychological therapy by the perinatal mental health team while continuing her exclusive home care with her infant

Reassure the family that this presentation is consistent with severe baby blues that affect up to 80 percent of women in the first two weeks postpartum and arrange general practitioner review in 7 days if symptoms persist

Arrange urgent involuntary admission to a mother-baby unit (or psychiatric ward if MBU unavailable), commence a second-generation antipsychotic such as olanzapine and consider lithium for prophylaxis under specialist psychiatric supervision

Recommend her partner takes parental leave and provides 24-hour supervision at home while she initiates community lithium under shared general practitioner and community psychiatric team care for the coming 6 to 8 weeks of recovery

subtopic_detail: Dementia with Lewy bodies antipsychotic sensitivity
stem: You are the consult-liaison registrar reviewing a 76-year-old man with progressive cognitive decline over 18 months, fluctuating attention, recurrent vivid visual hallucinations of cats in his bedroom, and recent-onset rest tremor with bradykinesia. His GP started haloperidol 1.5 mg twice daily five days ago for the hallucinations. Today he is hyperthermic, has marked rigidity in all limbs, is mute and barely responsive. His baseline cognition four months ago showed a MoCA of 19 out of 30 with prominent visuospatial deficits. He has no other psychotropic medications.

data_table.Examination: Severe cogwheel rigidity in all 4 limbs, mute, barely responsive, marked diaphoresis, no clonus, brisk reflexes
data_table.Investigations: CK 4800 U/L, WCC 12.4, UEC creatinine 122 (baseline 88), CT head old age-related changes only, urinalysis negative, blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase haloperidol to 5 mg three times daily for refractory psychosis, add a benzodiazepine for the rigidity and transfer to a closed dementia ward for ongoing antipsychotic titration and behavioural containment over the next 7 days

Cease haloperidol immediately, treat as neuroleptic malignant syndrome with intravenous fluids and active cooling, transfer to a high-dependency setting, and once stabilised commence rivastigmine for the underlying dementia with Lewy bodies

Switch to risperidone 1 mg twice daily because risperidone is a safer antipsychotic in older patients with parkinsonian features than haloperidol and is recommended first-line for behavioural and psychological symptoms in dementia

Add oral carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 three times daily as treatment for newly recognised idiopathic Parkinson disease and continue haloperidol for the psychotic symptoms until levodopa shows benefit in the limbs over the next fortnight

Continue haloperidol at the current dose but add intravenous dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg six-hourly and oral bromocriptine 5 mg three times daily as specific antidotal therapy for ongoing NMS rather than ceasing the precipitating agent

stem:
You are the adult psychiatry registrar in an outpatient clinic seeing a 26-year-old man referred for assessment of long-standing inattention, distractibility and disorganisation that have persisted from childhood and now substantially impair his postgraduate study and ability to hold steady employment. A structured diagnostic interview using DIVA confirms adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder with childhood-onset symptoms documented on school reports.

Comorbid depression and anxiety have been excluded on screening. He drinks under 4 standard drinks weekly, uses no other substances, has no personal or family history of cardiac disease, and his cardiovascular and neurological examinations are entirely normal with no resting tachycardia, no murmur, and no documented hypertension.

data_table.Examination: Normal cardiovascular and neurological examination, no tremor, no thyromegaly, no Cushingoid features, alert and cooperative
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus rhythm rate 76, normal axis, QTc 412 ms; routine bloods and TFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg daily as off-label augmentation given its dopaminergic and noradrenergic profile, with monthly blood-pressure monitoring and an expectation of a clinically meaningful response within 4 to 6 treatment weeks

Atomoxetine 40 mg daily with uptitration to 80 mg daily over 2 weeks as a noradrenergic non-stimulant first-line option given the duration of his symptoms and the long-acting nature of this pharmacological treatment choice

Methylphenidate immediate-release starting at 10 mg twice daily with structured uptitration to a therapeutic dose, with monitoring of weight, blood pressure, heart rate and sleep, and a discussion about driving and stimulant-class diversion risks

Defer all pharmacotherapy and commence 12 sessions of cognitive behavioural therapy specifically adapted for adult ADHD, then reassess for pharmacotherapy if his symptoms persist following completion of the therapy course

Clonidine 50 microgram twice daily titrated to effect with weekly blood pressure monitoring at home and ongoing review for postural symptoms or fatigue or any clinically meaningful changes in his sleep architecture

subtopic_detail: Borderline personality disorder self-harm crisis management
stem:
You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24-year-old woman with established borderline personality disorder, currently engaged in a structured DBT program, who has self-presented to ED after a self-inflicted superficial right forearm laceration in the context of a relationship conflict 4 hours ago. She is calm now, expresses regret and embarrassment, denies current suicidal intent or plan, has no access to means at home, and asks to be discharged so she can attend her individual DBT session in the morning.

Wound assessment shows superficial linear cuts requiring closure with steristrips only. She has a supportive housemate at home, attends regular skills group, and her DBT therapist is contactable for handover within working hours.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72, HR 78, SpO2 99% in air, T 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Superficial right forearm lacerations closed with steristrips, no tendon or neurovascular involvement, no other injuries on torso or limbs, no signs of intoxication
data_table.Investigations: Bedside alcohol breath test negative; urine drug screen not indicated; routine bloods not required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Admit her voluntarily for 72 hours to the psychiatric short stay unit for crisis stabilisation and arrange a clozapine titration to begin during the inpatient stay to address her recurrent self-harm pattern observed today

Discharge her home without further follow-up and advise her to ring 000 if she has any further self-harm or suicidal thoughts; the wound has been dressed and her observations are within normal limits today

Arrange involuntary admission to a closed psychiatric unit under the Mental Health Act for ongoing risk management and recommend a trial of quetiapine 50 mg twice daily as a chemical containment intervention for the next 4 weeks

Discharge home with a written DBT-aligned safety plan, contact her DBT therapist by phone with her consent now to hand over and arrange a clinic review the next morning, and provide acute care service contact numbers for overnight use

Refer for an electroconvulsive therapy work-up given the recurrent self-harm and a probable underlying treatment-resistant depressive component, and admit her until the first ECT treatment can be scheduled during the week

subtopic_detail: Dementia with Lewy bodies recognition and antipsychotic avoidance
stem:
You are the geriatric psychiatry registrar reviewing a 76-year-old man brought in by his wife with 12 months of progressive cognitive decline characterised by marked fluctuations in attention and arousal, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations of small animals and children, and a recently diagnosed REM sleep behaviour disorder confirmed on polysomnography. Over the last 4 months he has developed mild Parkinsonian signs with bradykinesia and rigidity.

He has had two falls in the past month. On the ward he has become agitated overnight and his treating team is asking your advice. He has no preceding psychiatric history; his Addenbrooke's Cognitive Examination score has fallen from 86 to 72 over 12 months, with relative preservation of memory but impaired visuospatial function.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/82 lying with 22 mmHg systolic drop on standing, HR 78, T 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Bradykinesia, mild cogwheel rigidity bilaterally, no tremor, soft visual hallucinations described non-distressingly, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: mild generalised atrophy, no significant vascular load, no hippocampal predominance; DAT scan: bilateral reduced striatal uptake; routine bloods normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of his cognitive symptoms and overnight agitation?

options.text: Commence rivastigmine starting at 1.5 mg twice daily with stepwise dose titration, avoid first-generation and most second-generation antipsychotics due to severe neuroleptic sensitivity, and address modifiable triggers for his nocturnal agitation

Commence memantine 5 mg daily titrated to 20 mg daily over 4 weeks and add a benzodiazepine such as diazepam 2 mg at night to address both his cognitive symptoms and the overnight behavioural agitation episodes

Defer all pharmacotherapy and arrange a 4-week trial of one-on-one behavioural therapy and a structured cognitive stimulation program before considering any specific pharmacological interventions in this clinical presentation today

Commence levodopa-carbidopa for the Parkinsonian signs and add risperidone 0.5 mg at night for the visual hallucinations and the overnight agitation, with periodic review of both treatments at the local clinic

Commence haloperidol 0.5 mg orally twice daily for the visual hallucinations and agitation, and add donepezil 5 mg daily for the cognitive component once the agitation has been brought under reasonable control over time

subtopic_detail: Severe anorexia nervosa refeeding syndrome prevention
stem:
You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 19-year-old woman admitted to the general medical ward 2 hours ago with severe restrictive anorexia nervosa. Her current BMI is 13.1 with a 12 kg weight loss over 4 months and a daily intake estimated at 350 kcal for the past 3 weeks. Pulse is 42 sitting, blood pressure 88/52 lying with 22 mmHg systolic postural drop, and her temperature is 35.4 degrees C.

Her phosphate is 0.62 mmol/L, magnesium 0.66 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L; ECG shows a prolonged QTc of 488 ms; her glucose is 3.3 mmol/L. She is medically and cognitively cooperative, accepts the plan in principle, and wishes to engage with the eating-disorders service team during admission.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 88/52 lying (postural drop 22 mmHg systolic), HR 42, T 35.4 degrees C, SpO2 99% in air
data_table.Examination: BMI 13.1, severe muscle wasting, dry skin, lanugo, no peripheral oedema, alert and cooperative, normal cranial nerve exam
data_table.Investigations: Phosphate 0.62 (RR 0.8-1.5), Mg 0.66 (RR 0.7-1.0), K 3.1 (RR 3.5-5.0), Na 134, glucose 3.3, albumin 32, INR 1.2, ECG: sinus bradycardia, QTc 488 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial nutritional and electrolyte plan?

options.text: Defer the nutritional plan until she has been transferred to a tertiary eating-disorders unit for inpatient psychiatric admission under the Mental Health Act, maintaining her on a clear-fluids-only diet without electrolyte replacement

Commence oral feeding at 35 kcal/kg/day from the first meal with structured supervised meal support and replace phosphate and magnesium and potassium only after the first 48 hours of feeding to allow biochemical re-equilibration

Commence full nutritional rehabilitation with nasogastric feeding at 50 kcal/kg/day from admission to reverse her catabolic state as quickly as possible and replace electrolytes only if her biochemistry confirms deficits beyond initial values

Start at approximately 20 kcal/kg/day with the multidisciplinary team, supplement oral phosphate and magnesium and potassium before significant feeding, give intravenous thiamine 300 mg daily for 5 days, monitor electrolytes 12-hourly initially

Commence intravenous 10% dextrose at maintenance rate for the next 24 hours to correct her low blood glucose and only commence oral feeding once her electrolytes have been fully normalised on biochemistry without further loading

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose with QRS prolongation
stem:
You are the ED registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman brought in by paramedics 90 minutes after a witnessed ingestion of approximately 50 tablets of amitriptyline 25 mg from her own prescription. On arrival she is drowsy but rousable, has dilated pupils, dry warm skin and decreased bowel sounds. Her observations show tachycardia, mild hypotension and a wide-complex tachycardia on the cardiac monitor with the 12-lead ECG showing sinus tachycardia at 132/min with a QRS of 128 ms, an R wave in aVR of 6 mm, and a rightward terminal axis.

She has been intubated for airway protection. Activated charcoal was not given pre-hospital due to her drowsiness. There is no co-ingestion history of paracetamol or alcohol on initial assessment.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 92/56, HR 132, T 37.6 degrees C, SpO2 100% on FiO2 0.4 (intubated and ventilated)
data_table.Examination: Drowsy then intubated, dilated pupils, dry skin, decreased bowel sounds, no clonus, no rigidity, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia QRS 128 ms, R wave aVR 6 mm, terminal R wave rightward axis; ABG pH 7.32, pCO2 4.6 kPa, HCO3 18, Na 140, K 3.8, BSL 7.8, paracetamol level pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg as a bolus and repeat to narrow the QRS to under 100 ms while monitoring blood pH between 7.45 and 7.55 and titrating ongoing infusion to clinical and ECG response

Administer intravenous physostigmine 1 to 2 mg slowly to reverse the central anticholinergic syndrome and improve her drowsiness, with continuous cardiac monitoring and resuscitation equipment available throughout administration of the medication

Commence intravenous lipid emulsion 20% as a 1.5 mL/kg bolus followed by an ongoing infusion at 0.25 mL/kg/min as the first-line specific antidote intervention for amitriptyline-associated cardiotoxicity in this overdose presentation

Administer intravenous amiodarone 300 mg over 20 minutes for the wide-complex tachycardia and prepare for synchronised DC cardioversion if there is no improvement in the cardiac rhythm or her haemodynamic status

Administer intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg titrated to reverse her drowsiness and improve her airway protection so she can be extubated promptly and avoid the morbidity associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation in the ED

stem:
You are the perinatal psychiatry registrar reviewing a 29-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, stable for 4 years on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily as monotherapy with two prior depressive episodes and one manic episode in her early 20s. She has been in a stable relationship for 3 years and is now planning a first pregnancy within the next 6 to 12 months.

She uses no other medications, has no contraindications to lithium, has had no thyroid or renal disease, and her family history is unremarkable. She has read patient information that suggests valproate carries risks in pregnancy and asks for your advice on what to do. She is a non-smoker, drinks no alcohol, and her partner is supportive of her decisions.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic affect, normal speech, no thought disorder, no perceptual disturbance, no parkinsonism, mood elevated to baseline range
data_table.Investigations: Routine bloods including TFTs, eGFR, valproate level 460 micromol/L (RR 300-700) all within target range

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue valproate at the current dose throughout pregnancy and add high-dose folic acid 5 mg daily preconceptionally, and arrange detailed second-trimester anatomy ultrasound to detect any neural-tube or other structural anomalies that may arise

Continue valproate at a reduced dose of 500 mg daily and add lamotrigine titrated to 200 mg daily, hoping that the combination will protect against relapse while halving the dose-dependent teratogenic risk profile during pregnancy planning today

Plan a switch from valproate to lithium pre-conception with overlap and gradual cross-titration, baseline thyroid and renal function with ongoing therapeutic drug monitoring, and high-dose folic acid 5 mg daily preconceptionally

Switch from valproate to topiramate 100 mg twice daily as a non-teratogenic mood stabiliser alternative and arrange detailed pre-conception genetic counselling before any further changes to her medication regimen at this stage in her care

Cease valproate abruptly and rely on lifestyle measures and structured psychological therapy for relapse prevention until she has completed her pregnancy and lactation period before resuming maintenance pharmacotherapy at any later point

stem:
You are the acute psychiatry registrar reviewing a 22-year-old man brought in by police after he was found running through traffic shouting at unseen voices and accusing strangers of conspiring against him. Collateral from his housemate confirms 12 months of daily high-potency cannabis use with a sharp escalation in the past 3 weeks coinciding with a relationship breakdown. He has no prior psychiatric history, no family history of psychotic illness, no other substance use beyond occasional alcohol, no head injury, and a normal medical and neurological examination.

Urine drug screen is positive for THC only. Acute behavioural disturbance has now settled with calm verbal de-escalation in the ED; he is paranoid but able to engage with the interview process today.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/84, HR 96, T 36.9 degrees C, SpO2 98% in air
data_table.Examination: Alert, paranoid, mild psychomotor agitation, conjunctival injection, no nystagmus or rigidity, no neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen: THC positive, all other drugs of abuse negative; routine bloods unremarkable; CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Discharge home with his housemate, prescribe diazepam 5 mg three times daily for 7 days for sedation and arrange follow-up with the local alcohol and other drug service within the next 2 weeks for cannabis cessation support

Admit him under the Mental Health Act involuntarily for 4 weeks of inpatient stabilisation with risperidone 4 mg daily and a low-dose sodium valproate mood stabiliser added from admission as a substance-induced episode mood stabiliser

Discharge with a 4-week supply of olanzapine 10 mg daily and rely on his general practitioner to arrange specialist mental health follow-up, with reattendance only if there are any further psychotic symptoms after the discharge today

Commence clozapine 12.5 mg daily titrated as inpatient and continue for at least 6 months given the severity of the psychotic episode and the high risk of relapse with ongoing cannabis use after his discharge from hospital

Admit him voluntarily for short-term observation, commence olanzapine 10 mg orally daily, arrange brief intervention and motivational interviewing for cannabis cessation, and plan early community mental health team follow-up after discharge

subtopic_detail: Gamma-hydroxybutyrate withdrawal recognition and inpatient management
stem:
You are the addiction medicine registrar called to ED for a 32-year-old man with a 4-year history of daily gamma-hydroxybutyrate use, dosing every 2 to 3 hours including overnight, who ran out of supply 18 hours ago. He has been profoundly anxious, tremulous and diaphoretic; in the last 4 hours he has become confused with visual hallucinations of insects on the wall and a brief generalised seizure self-terminating after 60 seconds.

Standard alcohol-withdrawal-style diazepam loading at 60 mg over the past 2 hours has produced only modest improvement in his agitation and autonomic features. He has no past psychiatric history, no other substance use beyond moderate alcohol, and no metabolic, neurological or infective focus identified on a comprehensive bedside workup.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/104, HR 132, T 38.3 degrees C, SpO2 96% in air, RR 24
data_table.Examination: Confused, GCS 14 with intermittent worsening, diaphoretic, coarse tremor, hyperreflexia without sustained clonus, visual hallucinations
data_table.Investigations: Routine bloods, CK, lactate, BSL, electrolytes within acceptable limits; CT brain normal; LP not yet performed; urine drug screen GHB-positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer haloperidol 5 mg intramuscularly with promethazine for behavioural control and arrange a CT brain and lumbar puncture before any further sedation is given, in case there is an undetected intracranial cause for delirium

Escalate to high-dose benzodiazepine loading guided by sedation and seizure response, add a GABAergic adjunct such as baclofen, and discuss urgent ICU transfer for ongoing sedation, airway monitoring and ventilation if required

Commence clonidine 75 microgram four times daily and dexmedetomidine infusion in a monitored bed, with hourly observations and a low threshold for repeating his routine bloods overnight if his agitation has not improved on this regimen

Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g over 30 minutes and intravenous thiamine 300 mg daily for 5 days as the primary pharmacological intervention for his withdrawal syndrome and assess his progress 12 hours after this loading regimen

Discharge him to a community withdrawal facility with twice-daily nursing review and oral diazepam taper over the next 7 days, with explicit instructions about return precautions for seizures or worsening behaviour after the discharge

subtopic_detail: Varenicline initiation for smoking cessation in a patient with treated depression
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 52-year-old man who has decided to make another quit attempt after smoking 20 cigarettes per day for 30 years. His depression has been stable on sertraline 100 mg daily for the past three years with no recent suicidal ideation, self-harm, or psychiatric admission, and his GP-led mental health plan is current. He has no history of seizures, no significant renal impairment (eGFR 88), and no cardiovascular events.

He has previously tried nicotine replacement therapy patches alone for two weeks but resumed smoking due to severe cravings. He asks for the most effective evidence-based pharmacotherapy.

data_table.Examination: Mood euthymic on sertraline, no current suicidal ideation, normal cardiovascular and respiratory exam, no recent cardiac events documented
data_table.Investigations: Recent eGFR 88, normal LFTs, normal ECG, exhaled CO 28 ppm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Varenicline 0.5 mg daily for three days then 0.5 mg twice daily for four days then 1 mg twice daily for a 12-week course, with quit date in week two and monitoring for neuropsychiatric symptoms and abnormal dreams at routine review

Bupropion sustained release 150 mg daily for three days then 150 mg twice daily for nine weeks with quit date in week two, and counsel on the increased seizure risk if he has any past head injury or eating disorder history
Nicotine patch 21 mg per 24 hours alone, restarted for 8 to 12 weeks, with weekly review and gradual tapering of the patch dose over the final four weeks of treatment

Nortriptyline 25 mg nocte titrated to 75 mg nocte commencing two weeks before quit date for a 12-week course, with baseline ECG to assess QTc and monitoring for orthostatic hypotension and anticholinergic adverse effects

Brief motivational counselling alone without pharmacotherapy with structured weekly review for the first month and referral to the Quitline 13 78 48 telephone counselling service to consolidate the patient's stated motivation to quit

subtopic_detail: Long-term lithium monitoring with renal decline and parathyroid disturbance
stem: You are the community psychiatrist reviewing a 35-year-old woman on lithium 750 mg nocte for 8 years for bipolar I disorder, who is currently euthymic with no relapse during this time.
