Her routine annual monitoring shows progressive renal decline (eGFR fallen from 95 three years ago to 65 today), a lithium level within range at 0.7 mmol/L, subclinical hypothyroidism with TSH 7.2 and normal free T4, mildly elevated corrected calcium 2.68 mmol/L with raised PTH 9.8 pmol/L, BMI 28 and BP 130/82. She is asymptomatic, takes no other medications, and is planning a family within 12 months.

data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L, eGFR 65 (95 three years ago), TSH 7.2 (RR 0.4-4.0) free T4 normal, corrected calcium 2.68 (RR 2.20-2.60), PTH 9.8 (RR 1.6-6.9), urine ACR 4 mg/mmol, fasting glucose 5.2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue lithium at current dose and recheck eGFR, lithium level, TSH and calcium in 12 months as part of standard annual monitoring, with no immediate change to therapy given her euthymia and lithium level within range

Discuss with the patient cross-titration from lithium to an alternative mood stabiliser (e.g., quetiapine), continue lithium until the new agent is at therapeutic dose and stable for at least 6 weeks, and refer to nephrology and endocrinology for parallel management

Reduce lithium dose to 500 mg nocte to limit further renal injury and recheck eGFR and lithium level in 4 weeks while continuing the same drug as lower dose is generally renoprotective with preserved mood stabilising effect

Add amiloride 5 mg daily as prophylaxis against lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and continue lithium at current dose, with no other change to therapy or referral and routine reassessment in 6 months

Stop lithium abruptly today and commence sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily as alternative mood stabiliser with serum level check at 1 week, while accepting some risk of mood relapse from abrupt change in maintenance therapy

subtopic_detail: IM rapid tranquillisation for severe acute behavioural disturbance
stem: You are the emergency department registrar called to a 25-year-old man brought in by police on a Mental Health Act order following methamphetamine use earlier today. He is paranoid, threatening security staff, pacing, shouting and has thrown a chair. Verbal de-escalation by the senior nurse over 20 minutes has been unsuccessful and he is refusing oral medication. He has no past medical history, takes no regular medications, and there is no known QT prolongation or cardiac disease, but he will not allow ECG, vital sign measurement or IV cannulation. The team has decided to administer parenteral medication for safety.

data_table.Vital signs: Refusing measurement; visibly agitated, tachypnoeic, sweating
data_table.Examination: Aggressive, paranoid, pacing, shouting threats, throwing furniture, no obvious injury, no recent ETOH ingestion known
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen pending; no ECG available; collateral from family confirms first presentation, no known cardiac history or QT prolonging medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate parenteral pharmacological choice?

options.text: Intramuscular droperidol 10 mg as a single dose with continuous physical observation for sedation, repeat 10 mg dose at 15 minutes if behaviour has not de-escalated, and arrange cardiac monitoring as soon as it can be safely applied

Intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg plus IM lorazepam 2 mg given concurrently into separate sites with cardiac monitoring planned as soon as possible, and clinical observation for extrapyramidal adverse effects over the following 4 hours

Intramuscular diazepam 10 mg as a single agent with intensive observation for respiratory depression and resedation, with consideration of additional doses every 30 minutes until sedation is achieved and assessment can proceed

Intravenous midazolam 5 mg titrated against sedation in 2 mg aliquots with continuous pulse oximetry and respiratory monitoring, and IV access established under restraint by the security team before drug administration

Intramuscular zuclopenthixol acetate 100 mg as a longer-acting agent to control behaviour over several days while a longer-term plan is made, with observation for prolonged extrapyramidal adverse effects and slowed elimination

subtopic_detail: Functional neurological disorder diagnosis with positive Hoover sign
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to review a 28-year-old woman with sudden onset left-sided 'paralysis' three days ago following an argument with her partner. Detailed neurological examination demonstrates a positive Hoover sign (involuntary left hip extension when contralateral hip flexion is tested against resistance), inconsistent power across formal versus distracted testing, normal reflexes and tone with no atrophy, and dragging non-physiological gait.

MRI brain and whole spine are normal, EMG and nerve conduction studies are normal. She is genuinely distressed by her symptoms, is not seeking compensation, has no pending legal matters, has not deliberately produced symptoms for medical attention, and has no prior psychiatric history.

data_table.Examination: Inconsistent power on distraction, positive Hoover sign on left, normal reflexes and tone, no muscle wasting, dragging non-physiological gait, intact sensation in non-anatomical pattern
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain and spine normal, EMG and NCS normal, CSF examination normal, autoimmune encephalitis panel pending and unlikely given chronology

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Malingering with deliberate production of motor symptoms for an external secondary gain such as financial compensation, time off work, or avoidance of an ongoing legal or relational obligation by the patient

Factitious disorder imposed on self with deliberate falsification of motor symptoms in order to assume the sick role and receive medical attention, in the absence of any obvious external incentive other than the sick role itself

Functional neurological symptom disorder (also known as conversion disorder) diagnosed on positive clinical signs including a positive Hoover sign and inconsistency on distraction, with normal structural neurological investigations and an identifiable stressor

Somatic symptom disorder with one or more distressing physical symptoms accompanied by excessive disproportionate thoughts feelings and behaviours focused on those symptoms persisting more than six months in the typical clinical course

Acute stress reaction with psychomotor manifestations occurring within the first month after an interpersonal stressor and resolving spontaneously within four weeks without specific intervention beyond psychoeducation about the natural course

subtopic_detail: Postpartum depression with active suicidal ideation requiring inpatient mother-baby admission
stem:
You are the GP reviewing a 28-year-old woman 8 weeks postpartum after her first baby, a healthy term boy now exclusively breastfed. She presents with low mood, anhedonia, marked guilt about being 'a bad mother', insomnia beyond infant sleep disruption, and weight loss. EPDS score today is 22 with item 10 endorsed. On further interview she describes recurrent suicidal thoughts with a tentative plan involving medications at home.

She denies any intent or thoughts to harm the baby. Her husband works long hours and there is no extended family nearby. She has no prior psychiatric history and is taking no medications.

data_table.Examination: Flat affect, tearful, slowed speech, denies psychotic symptoms, denies thoughts to harm baby, infant settled and well-cared-for at this visit
data_table.Investigations: EPDS 22 with positive item 10, TSH 1.8 (normal), Hb 122, ferritin 38, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence oral fluoxetine 20 mg daily, arrange community perinatal mental health team review tomorrow and ensure husband is aware to provide support, with discharge home today and follow-up safety planning by phone in 48 hours

Arrange same-day admission to a mother-baby unit for combined inpatient assessment and treatment, commence sertraline as the SSRI most compatible with breastfeeding, and involve the perinatal psychiatry team for ongoing management

Refer for outpatient cognitive behavioural therapy through the Better Access program with focus on cognitive restructuring and behavioural activation, with weekly EPDS reassessment by GP for the next 6 weeks before considering medication or admission

Admit to general adult psychiatry inpatient unit with separation of mother and baby for the duration of admission, commence sertraline 50 mg daily, and arrange community follow-up with paediatric review for the infant after discharge

Commence diazepam 5 mg twice daily for anxiety and insomnia, with brief sleep advice, and reassess in 1 week with view to commencing antidepressant therapy once sleep has been restored and mood appears more stable on benzodiazepine cover

subtopic_detail: Continuing lithium in pregnancy for bipolar I with manic relapse history
stem:
You are the perinatal psychiatry registrar providing pre-conception counselling to a 32-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, well controlled on lithium 750 mg nocte for the past 5 years with no mood episodes during this time. Her recent lithium level is 0.8 mmol/L, eGFR 90, TSH 2.4, corrected calcium normal. Three years ago she self-discontinued lithium for 6 weeks because of weight concerns and developed a severe manic episode requiring involuntary admission with psychosis.

She has had two earlier hospitalised manic episodes pre-lithium. She and her partner plan to commence trying to conceive within 2 months and she asks for advice on her medication during pregnancy.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no current suicidal ideation, no psychotic symptoms, insightful, motivated for pregnancy planning
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.8 mmol/L, eGFR 90, TSH 2.4, corrected calcium 2.40, FBC and UEC normal, urine bHCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pre-conception plan for her mood stabiliser?

options.text: Switch immediately to lamotrigine 25 mg daily with planned titration to 200 mg over 6 weeks as a safer mood stabiliser during conception and pregnancy, since lamotrigine has the most reassuring safety profile in pregnancy

Switch to sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily for the duration of pregnancy and the postpartum period, accepting some teratogenic risk in exchange for superior mood stabilisation across both manic and depressive episodes

Continue lithium at the lowest effective dose throughout pregnancy with fetal echocardiography at 18-20 weeks, monthly lithium levels with rising frequency near term, hydration counselling, and planned dose adjustment around delivery to avoid toxicity

Stop lithium abruptly at confirmation of pregnancy and restart only at the beginning of the second trimester after organogenesis is complete, with close monitoring for early mood relapse and re-titration of lithium dose at that time

Switch to quetiapine 300 mg nocte as a non-teratogenic atypical antipsychotic with mood-stabilising effect, with cross-titration off lithium over 4 weeks prior to conception and ongoing monitoring for metabolic adverse effects in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Lorazepam challenge for catatonia in a patient on aripiprazole
stem: You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to review a 24-year-old woman with chronic schizophrenia on aripiprazole 30 mg daily, brought in by her family with one week of progressive mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility on examination, echolalia, and refusal of food and fluids. Examination shows BFCRS score 14 with prominent immobility, mutism, posturing, staring and grimacing. She is afebrile and haemodynamically stable. CK is 1200 with normal renal function and otherwise normal investigations including TSH, calcium, and a non-contrast CT brain.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 88, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, BFCRS 14
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, posturing with waxy flexibility, echolalia, staring, grimacing, no fever, no autonomic instability, no muscular rigidity beyond posturing
data_table.Investigations: CK 1200 (RR <200), eGFR 95, TSH 1.8, corrected calcium 2.38, FBC and UEC normal, urine drug screen negative, CT brain unremarkable, BFCRS 14

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Increase the aripiprazole dose to 30 mg daily intramuscularly with concurrent prophylactic benzatropine 2 mg IM to reduce extrapyramidal side effects and target the underlying psychotic illness that is presumably driving the catatonic state

Administer lorazepam 1-2 mg IV (or IM) as a challenge test, observe for clinical response over 30 minutes (improvement in mutism, immobility, posturing), commence regular lorazepam 6-8 mg/day if response is positive, and escalate or proceed to ECT if no response

Administer haloperidol 5 mg IM as initial treatment for the underlying psychotic symptoms with planned regular dosing every 6 hours, monitoring for extrapyramidal side effects and dystonia in the first 24 hours of therapy

Commence clozapine 12.5 mg with planned titration over 2 weeks given the failure of aripiprazole to control her psychotic illness, with weekly FBC monitoring per the clozapine protocol and adjunctive lorazepam if needed

Proceed directly to electroconvulsive therapy after Mental Health Tribunal authorisation as the most rapidly effective therapy for catatonia, without trial of lorazepam first, given the severity of her clinical state and the urgency of treatment

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic metabolic monitoring at 12 weeks on olanzapine
stem:
You are the community mental health team registrar reviewing a 28-year-old man who has been on olanzapine 10 mg nocte for 12 weeks for a first episode of schizophrenia. He is settled mentally, has good adherence and minimal residual psychotic symptoms. Since starting treatment he has gained 6 kg in weight and reports daytime sedation, increased appetite and reduced exercise.

His baseline 12 weeks ago showed normal weight, normal fasting glucose, normal lipid panel and a normal ECG. He has no chest pain, no orthostatic symptoms, no galactorrhoea and no gynaecomastia. He has no past medical history and is not on any other regular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/82, HR 78, BMI 27 (baseline 23), waist circumference 96 cm (up 8 cm)
data_table.Examination: Settled affect, no extrapyramidal side effects, no orthostatic hypotension, normal cardiovascular and abdominal examination, no obvious tardive dyskinesia
data_table.Investigations: Baseline 12 weeks ago: fasting glucose 4.9 normal, lipids normal, ECG QTc 410 ms, prolactin not done

lead_in: What is the most appropriate panel of monitoring investigations to request at this 12-week review?

options.text: HbA1c alone as the most sensitive marker for olanzapine-related glucose dysregulation, given that fasting glucose may miss postprandial hyperglycaemia in early metabolic disturbance and is more practical in the community mental health setting

Thyroid function tests including TSH free T4 free T3 and thyroid antibodies given the weight gain, sedation and possible iatrogenic hypothyroidism related to olanzapine treatment, and assessment of any underlying thyroid contribution to ongoing symptoms

Fasting glucose or HbA1c, fasting lipid profile, body weight, BMI and waist circumference, with consideration of metformin and clozapine review if metabolic parameters have deteriorated significantly compared to the baseline values taken before olanzapine commencement

Serum prolactin level alone as the primary monitoring test given that olanzapine carries a class warning for hyperprolactinaemia and patients may not volunteer sexual dysfunction or galactorrhoea symptoms without specific prompting at review consultations

Repeat 12-lead ECG for assessment of QTc prolongation as the highest priority safety check on antipsychotic therapy at this stage, given that 12 weeks corresponds to the typical timeframe for delayed cardiac repolarisation changes to manifest fully

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose sodium bicarbonate for QRS prolongation
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar managing a 19-year-old woman brought in 2 hours after ingesting 50 tablets of her grandmother's amitriptyline 25 mg as a deliberate self-poisoning. She is drowsy but rouses to voice. Her airway is patent and she is breathing spontaneously. A 12-lead ECG taken now shows sinus tachycardia at 122 with a QRS duration of 130 ms, a terminal R wave of 4 mm in aVR, and no other ischaemic features.

There is no significant past medical history, no allergies, and no other co-ingestants identified or admitted. Activated charcoal was not given as ingestion was more than an hour ago. Senior emergency consultant and clinical toxicologist have been called.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 122, BP 92/58, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), bedside glucose 5.6 mmol/L
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, dilated pupils 6 mm bilaterally reacting sluggishly, dry mucous membranes, hypoactive bowel sounds, no clonus, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: 12-lead ECG: sinus tachycardia 122, QRS 130 ms, terminal R wave 4 mm in aVR; VBG pH 7.32 pCO2 38 HCO3 18; potassium 3.4, sodium 138, creatinine 78

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer intravenous physostigmine 2 mg slowly with continuous cardiac monitoring to reverse the central and peripheral anticholinergic features, with atropine immediately available at the bedside to manage any clinically significant bradycardia

Activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube to bind the remaining tricyclic antidepressant in the gastrointestinal tract, with intubation prior to administration if the patient's Glasgow Coma Scale falls further during preparation for the procedure

Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 1 to 2 mmol/kg as a bolus aiming to narrow the QRS and alkalinise serum pH to 7.45 to 7.55, intubate and ventilate to support pH if needed, continuous cardiac monitoring and intensive care admission

Commence intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg titrated to GCS improvement, with continuous cardiac monitoring during administration and observation in resuscitation for 4 hours, alongside intravenous fluids to support blood pressure and reverse the anticholinergic syndrome

Commence haemodialysis urgently with vascular access via right internal jugular vein quad-lumen catheter to clear the tricyclic antidepressant from the systemic circulation, with continuous cardiac monitoring and intensive care admission for the procedure

subtopic_detail: Borderline personality disorder DBT first-line outpatient referral
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 24-year-old woman with five emergency department presentations over the past 8 months for recurrent superficial cutting and overdose threats following relationship conflicts. She describes a pervasive sense of emptiness, marked identity disturbance, intense unstable interpersonal relationships, and impulsive episodes of binge eating, spending and sexual activity. Her affect varies sharply over hours.

She has been on three different antidepressants and a low-dose antipsychotic over the last 2 years with no sustained benefit. She has no current intent or plan to end her life today, and has agreed to engage with outpatient mental health services for a sustainable longer-term plan.

data_table.Examination: Multiple superficial linear scars on the forearms in different stages of healing, no fresh wounds, mildly tearful affect, clear sensorium, no thought disorder, no psychotic symptoms, no current suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TFTs all within normal limits; urine drug screen negative; ECG normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase her current sertraline to 200 mg daily with addition of quetiapine 100 mg nocte for affective instability and impulsivity, with weekly general practice review for the first month and mental health care plan referral for supportive counselling

Admit voluntarily to an acute psychiatric inpatient unit for 4 to 6 weeks to provide containment and intensive day-long therapy with daily group work and individual sessions, with discharge planning back to the community mental health team

Initiate weekly cognitive behavioural therapy alone delivered through a 10-session mental health care plan with the general practitioner, given the high prevalence of cognitive distortions and maladaptive coping strategies underpinning the personality presentation

Refer to a community-based dialectical behaviour therapy program as first-line treatment with planned 12-month duration involving weekly individual therapy, weekly skills group and between-session coaching, with general practice mental health care plan as the funding pathway

Discharge to general practice care only with planned mental health care plan and supportive counselling, given that personality disorders typically do not respond to specialist mental health input and management is primarily through chronic disease care frameworks

subtopic_detail: Cannabis-induced psychosis observation off substance before antipsychotic
stem:
You are the early psychosis team registrar reviewing a 19-year-old man brought to the assessment unit by his family for a 2-week history of persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations and disorganised behaviour. He has been smoking high-potency cannabis daily for the past 2 years and increased to multiple uses per day in the month prior to symptom onset. There is no family history of schizophrenia or other psychotic illness.

He has had no previous psychotic episodes, no suicidal or homicidal intent today, has no acute aggression, and has agreed voluntarily to inpatient assessment with his family supportive. Urine drug screen is positive for THC only. He has had a negative test for methamphetamine and other stimulants.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.0, HR 98, BP 124/78, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, BMI 22
data_table.Examination: Mildly anxious, persecutory delusions, occasional auditory hallucinations, no thought disorder evident on examination, no extrapyramidal signs, no neurology deficit, no signs of intoxication or withdrawal currently
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen THC positive, all other substances negative; FBC, UEC, LFTs and TFTs normal; ECG normal; non-contrast CT head normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Admit to an inpatient psychiatric unit voluntarily, cease all cannabis use with structured withdrawal support, observe for up to 4 weeks off cannabis, commence low-dose olanzapine 5 mg nocte if symptoms persist, and refer to early psychosis intervention service

Commence clozapine 12.5 mg nocte titrating up over 2 weeks under the early psychosis service for treatment-resistant first-episode psychosis given the chronicity of cannabis use, with weekly FBC monitoring and cardiac monitoring per protocol

Commit to involuntary detention under the Mental Health Act and arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy for severe disorganised psychotic features, given the failure of community management to date and the chronic high-potency cannabis use pattern documented

Commence outpatient management with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor for likely underlying mood and anxiety symptoms, with cognitive behavioural therapy referral and harm-minimisation cannabis counselling through the local drug and alcohol service

Refer urgently for schizoaffective disorder workup including mood charting and family interview, commence lithium 750 mg nocte after baseline renal and thyroid testing, and arrange outpatient psychiatric follow-up within the next 2 weeks for definitive diagnostic clarification

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD methylphenidate initiation with driving counselling
stem:
You are the consultant psychiatrist completing the new diagnosis of adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (combined presentation) in a 26-year-old IT engineer who has had longstanding inattention, impulsivity and emotional dysregulation. He drives 1 hour each way for his daily commute. There is no history of cardiac disease, no family history of sudden cardiac death, no current substance misuse, and no current depression or anxiety requiring treatment.

His baseline ECG is normal with QTc 410 ms and his blood pressure is 130/80. He is keen to start medication and understands stimulants are first-line. He has read consumer information and consented to monitoring.

data_table.Examination: Mildly restless, no thought disorder, no psychotic features, no neurology deficit, no signs of intoxication
data_table.Investigations: ECG normal QTc 410 ms, FBC, UEC, LFTs, TFTs all within normal limits; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy plan and accompanying counselling?

options.text: Counsel that stimulants are contraindicated for daily drivers due to the impact on cognition and reaction time, and commence atomoxetine 40 mg daily as a non-stimulant first-line therapy with planned 6-week review of symptom response and tolerability

Commence methylphenidate immediate-release 10 mg twice daily titrating weekly to symptom response and tolerability, counsel that driving while titrating is acceptable once side effects have stabilised, and arrange 4-week review with repeat BP, HR and side-effect assessment

Refer to a private neuropsychologist for cognitive testing and computerised continuous performance task to confirm diagnostic uncertainty before commencing any pharmacotherapy, with planned review after the formal cognitive assessment results are available

Commence sertraline 50 mg daily for likely comorbid anxiety or depression as the most parsimonious treatment for adult ADHD-like presentations, given the substantial overlap of symptoms and the favourable side-effect profile of SSRIs as a first step

Commence clonidine 50 micrograms three times daily for adult ADHD, with planned 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring during titration and dose escalation, and a planned outpatient review at 4 weeks for symptom and side-effect assessment

stem: A 15-year-old girl is reviewed by her general practitioner with her mother. Over the past 4 months she has had persistent low mood, anhedonia, fatigue, mid-afternoon naps, dropping school grades, and irritability. She denies suicidal ideation. She has tried 8 weeks of psychological therapy with no improvement. There is no substance use. Her mother is keen to consider medication.

data_table.Examination: Affect dysphoric, mood subjectively low, reactive, no psychomotor retardation, insight preserved, no psychotic features, MSE otherwise normal
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TFTs, B12, vitamin D, urine drug screen all normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate pharmacological first step?

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg orally daily, titrated upward as clinically tolerated
Mirtazapine 15 mg orally at night to address sleep difficulty and appetite
Fluoxetine 10 mg orally daily with weekly review during the first 4 weeks
Venlafaxine 75 mg orally daily as a sustained-release titration schedule
Amitriptyline 25 mg orally at night for low mood and insomnia management

stem: A 36-year-old paramedic presents 4 months after a critical-incident motor vehicle collision in which a colleague died. He describes intrusive memories, nightmares, hypervigilance, avoidance of the highway, and emotional numbing. Symptoms are present most days. He has had no previous mental illness, no substance use, and is currently on leave from work. There is no suicidal ideation. He prefers a non-pharmacological starting point.

data_table.Examination: Affect anxious, mood subjectively low, sleep poor with nightmares 4 nights/week, no psychotic features, insight preserved
data_table.Investigations: PCL-5 score 52

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first-line therapy?

options.text: Supportive counselling without trauma-focused techniques over 12 weeks
Critical incident stress debriefing delivered as a single-session intervention
Sertraline 50 mg orally daily as first-line pharmacological monotherapy
Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy weekly for 8 to 12 sessions
Prazosin 1 mg orally at night targeting trauma nightmares as sole therapy

stem: A 52-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has been on lithium 750 mg at night for 6 years. Two days ago he started ramipril 5 mg for newly diagnosed hypertension. Today he attends with 24 hours of coarse hand tremor, nausea, vomiting and ataxia. He has been struggling to keep down fluids. His last lithium level 3 weeks ago was 0.7 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.0 degrees Celsius, HR 88, BP 130/82 mmHg, RR 16
data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor of both hands, mild ataxia on standing, normal mental status, mild dehydration, no nystagmus, deep tendon reflexes brisk
data_table.Investigations: Lithium level pending, Na 138, K 4.2, urea 8.4 mmol/L, creatinine 132 micromol/L (baseline 92)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer oral activated charcoal 50 g to bind any further absorbed lithium
Continue lithium and administer ondansetron 4 mg intravenously for nausea
Arrange urgent haemodialysis now without waiting for the lithium level result
Switch the antihypertensive to a thiazide diuretic and continue the lithium
Hold lithium and give intravenous normal saline at 1 L per hour and recheck

stem: A 19-year-old woman with severe anorexia nervosa (BMI 13.5) is admitted to a medical ward for refeeding. Day 2 of structured refeeding at 30 kcal/kg/day, she develops new-onset peripheral oedema, calf cramps and palpitations. She is conscious and oriented. Her electrolytes were normal on admission.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.4 degrees Celsius, HR 110, BP 100/64 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98% in room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral pitting ankle oedema, calf tenderness on stretch, normal heart sounds, no peripheral neuropathy, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Phosphate 0.42 mmol/L (1.05 on admission), magnesium 0.58 mmol/L, potassium 3.1, glucose 4.4, ECG shows QTc 480 ms with no arrhythmia

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Replace phosphate, magnesium and potassium intravenously and reduce calories
Stop nutrition entirely until serum phosphate is above 1.0 mmol/L overnight
Administer intravenous furosemide 40 mg for the new bilateral peripheral oedema
Increase the caloric load to compensate for any ongoing weight loss observed
Commence a beta blocker for the tachycardia with serial QTc monitoring

stem: A 38-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia on clozapine 450 mg at night for 5 years was admitted to a general ward after a road traffic collision. He has been nil by mouth for 65 hours pending surgery and has not received any clozapine. Surgery is now postponed for 24 hours and oral intake can resume. He has had no agitation or psychotic relapse, his ECG is normal and he has a normal white cell count.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius, HR 84, BP 124/76 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Calm, oriented, no psychotic symptoms
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.4, neutrophils 4.1, ECG normal sinus rhythm, troponin normal, no QTc prolongation

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate clozapine prescription tonight?

options.text: Restart clozapine at his usual maintenance dose of 450 mg tonight only
Restart clozapine at 12.5 mg tonight with day-by-day retitration as new
Give clozapine 225 mg tonight as a half-dose then 450 mg from tomorrow
Switch to intramuscular olanzapine pamoate 300 mg as a temporary bridge
Restart clozapine at 200 mg tonight without using a test-dose initial step

subtopic_detail: Capacity and the NSW Mental Health Act 2007
stem: A 28-year-old woman is admitted to a NSW medical ward after a paracetamol overdose. She has severe major depressive disorder and says she wants to die. She refuses intravenous fluids and N-acetylcysteine, understands what is proposed, but says nothing will work. There are no psychotic features. She is calm and engaging.

data_table.Examination: Affect flat, suicidal ideation with intent, no psychotic features, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Paracetamol above the nomogram line, ALT 240 U/L, INR 1.3, lactate 1.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Accept her refusal as competent and move to symptom-focused palliation
Seek a Supreme Court order before starting any treatment at all
Complete a schedule under the NSW Mental Health Act and treat actively
Apply to the NCAT Guardianship Division before starting the antidote infusion
Allow 48 hours of reflection with capacity reviewed at every shift

stem: A 38-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte for 4 years (steady-state level 0.7 mmol/L). She presents to her GP for routine review. She has noticed increasing thirst and polyuria over the last 6 months and is now drinking 4 L of fluid daily. She is otherwise well, sleeping normally with no mood symptoms. Her partner reports no behavioural change. She is concerned about her kidneys.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius, HR 76, RR 14, BP 124/76 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Well, hydrated, no peripheral oedema, no tremor, thyroid not enlarged
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.68 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L (baseline 62), eGFR 84 mL/min, TSH 2.6 mIU/L, calcium 2.42 mmol/L, urine osmolality 220 mosmol/kg after overnight fluid restriction

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to psychiatry for review of lithium dose and consider switching to an alternative mood stabiliser
Ignore the symptoms because the lithium level is within range and continue routine 6-monthly testing
Recommend further fluid restriction to under 1.5 L daily as treatment of polyuria from lithium therapy
Commence desmopressin 100 microgram nocte without specialist review for symptomatic relief at home
Increase lithium dose to 1000 mg nocte to maintain mood stability if level remains under 1.2 mmol/L

stem: A 28-year-old man presents to a psychiatrist with longstanding inattention, disorganisation and restlessness that have impaired his university and work performance since adolescence. Symptoms are present at home and at work. A structured clinical interview and ASRS confirm features of ADHD with onset in childhood. Substance use, mood and anxiety disorders are excluded. He has no personal or family history of cardiac disease, hypertension or seizure. He prefers a once-daily medication. ECG is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius, HR 72, RR 14, BP 122/76 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Mental state - mildly fidgety, mood euthymic, no psychotic features, insight preserved
data_table.Investigations: 12-lead ECG normal sinus rhythm, FBC, UEC and TSH all within normal limits

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg sustained release each morning as off-label first-line therapy for adult ADHD
Atomoxetine 40 mg orally each morning titrated up to 80 mg over 4 weeks for symptom control
Immediate-release methylphenidate 10 mg three times daily as initial therapy for adult ADHD
Clonidine 75 microgram orally twice daily as a non-stimulant alternative to amphetamine-based therapy
Lisdexamfetamine 30 mg orally each morning, titrated up over 4 weeks to symptom response

stem: A 24-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 2 years. She presents to her psychiatrist saying she is considering pregnancy in the next year. She is on no other psychotropic medications. Her last manic episode was 18 months ago; she has had no depressive episodes for 2 years. She is sexually active with one male partner using condoms. She has no other medical conditions.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.6 degrees Celsius, HR 72, RR 14, BP 116/74 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Mental state - euthymic, no psychotic or suicidal features, full insight
data_table.Investigations: Valproate level 480 micromol/L, LFTs normal, FBC normal, beta-hCG negative

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Plan a cross-titration to lithium or lamotrigine with effective contraception until the new agent is established
Continue valproate at the current dose and recommend high-dose folate 5 mg daily for 3 months pre-conception
Reduce valproate to 600 mg daily and continue this dose throughout pregnancy as a minimal teratogenic dose
Stop valproate immediately without cross-titration and review in 4 weeks for clinical mood relapse
Insert a copper IUD and continue valproate indefinitely as long as effective contraception is maintained

stem: A 26-year-old man with first-episode schizophrenia was commenced on olanzapine 10 mg nocte 11 weeks ago. He is being reviewed at the community mental health clinic. His positive symptoms have improved markedly. He has gained 5 kg since starting olanzapine. He reports increased appetite and lethargy but no new physical symptoms. He has no personal or family history of cardiometabolic disease. He smokes 10 cigarettes daily and is not physically active.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius, HR 84, RR 16, BP 128/82 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: BMI 28 kg/m^2 (up from 26.5), no acanthosis, no tremor or rigidity, mental state stable
data_table.Investigations: Baseline pre-treatment - fasting BSL 4.8 mmol/L, total cholesterol 4.2 mmol/L, ECG QTc 410 ms

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate set of monitoring tests at this 12-week review?

options.text: Liver function tests, thyroid function and serum creatinine only as the 12-week metabolic screen
Serum prolactin and bone densitometry as the 12-week metabolic screen for second-generation antipsychotics
Annual ECG with QTc, clozapine level and full blood examination as the 12-week monitoring panel
Fasting glucose, lipid profile, weight, waist circumference and blood pressure as the 12-week metabolic screen
Symptom rating scale (PANSS) and a Simpson-Angus scale with no metabolic blood tests required at 12 weeks

stem: A 24-year-old woman known to the community mental health team for borderline personality disorder presents to ED after superficial cutting of her forearm following an argument with her partner. She has had multiple similar presentations and is engaged in weekly dialectical behaviour therapy with her usual psychologist. She denies suicidal intent and asks to go home. She has no medical injury requiring suturing. She is calm at interview and has a safety plan she co-developed with her DBT therapist.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius, HR 82, RR 16, BP 118/72 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Superficial linear lacerations on left forearm, no deep injury, no signs of intoxication, mental state - distressed but engaged, mood reactive, no psychotic features

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate ED management?

options.text: Commence a low-dose quetiapine 25 mg as required regimen for her presentation today and on discharge
Admit to the inpatient psychiatry ward overnight for crisis stabilisation and review by the on-call team in the morning
Validate her distress, review her safety plan with her, dress the wounds and discharge to her usual DBT clinician with rapid follow-up
Make her an involuntary patient under the Mental Health Act because of her history of repeated self-harm
Discharge without follow-up because she is engaged in ongoing private psychology and has no acute medical injury

stem: A 32-year-old man with a 4-year history of schizoaffective disorder is admitted to a general medical ward from a psychiatric inpatient unit because he has stopped eating, drinking and moving over 48 hours. He has been on risperidone 6 mg daily for 2 years. Physical examination shows mutism, waxy flexibility and persistent staring. He resists passive arm movement but yields once the arm is positioned. CK is 480 U/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, glucose 5.0 mmol/L, urinalysis normal and there is no fever or autonomic instability.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.9 degrees Celsius, HR 86, RR 18, BP 118/74 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, eyes open and tracking, waxy flexibility on arm posturing, no fever, no diaphoresis, no rigidity, no tremor
data_table.Investigations: CK 480 U/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, glucose 5.0 mmol/L, CRP 4 mg/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange MRI brain and CSF examination before any treatment to exclude autoimmune encephalitis as the cause
Cease risperidone and commence dantrolene 1 mg/kg intravenously for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Commence electroconvulsive therapy this morning without further pharmacological challenge first
Increase risperidone to 8 mg daily for inadequate antipsychotic effect causing residual negative symptoms
Administer lorazepam 2 mg intravenously and reassess catatonic features at 10 minutes for a positive response

stem: A 48-year-old man presents to the emergency department 36 hours after his last drink. He had been consuming approximately 200 g of alcohol daily for 25 years. He has tremor, sweating, anxiety, nausea, and feels his heart racing. He has had no hallucinations, seizures or recent head injury. His LFTs are mildly deranged but there are no clinical features of decompensated cirrhosis.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 165/95, HR 110 sinus, RR 18, SpO2 99% in room air, temp 37.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor of outstretched hands, diaphoretic, anxious; no asterixis, no jaundice, abdomen soft with no ascites; orientated to time, person and place
data_table.Investigations: CIWA-Ar score 18 of 67; ALT 80, AST 110, GGT 240, bilirubin 16, albumin 36, INR 1.1; glucose 5.4, Mg 0.7

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?

options.text: IV haloperidol 5 mg for agitation control as the primary withdrawal treatment
Atenolol 50 mg daily as monotherapy targeting autonomic withdrawal symptoms only
Chlordiazepoxide 100 mg single dose then PRN regimen without further scheduled dosing
IV chlormethiazole infusion titrated to sedation as the inpatient withdrawal regimen
Oral diazepam 20 mg loading dose with repeat dosing per CIWA-Ar and IV thiamine 300 mg daily

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome from SSRI plus tramadol
stem: A 35-year-old woman with major depressive disorder has been on sertraline 100 mg daily for 6 months. Her GP prescribed tramadol 50 mg four-times daily for back pain 36 hours ago. She now presents to the emergency department with fever, agitation, tremor, sweating and intermittent involuntary lower limb jerking. She has not started any other new medication and denies illicit substance use.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 39.5 degrees Celsius, HR 130 sinus, BP 160/95, RR 24, SpO2 98% in room air
data_table.Examination: Agitated, mydriasis, hyperreflexia, sustained ankle clonus, tremor of outstretched hands, diaphoretic; no muscular rigidity
data_table.Investigations: CK 800, creatinine 95, sodium 138, potassium 4.0, glucose 6.2; ECG sinus tachycardia

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Stop both serotonergic agents, IV fluids and benzodiazepines, active cooling, and consider cyproheptadine if persistent
IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg as first-line treatment for hyperthermia and muscle rigidity in this setting
IV bromocriptine 2.5 mg three times daily to reverse dopaminergic blockade and stabilise the syndrome
Continue sertraline and add propranolol 40 mg three times daily for ongoing autonomic instability
Empiric IV ceftriaxone and vancomycin for presumed sepsis with confirmatory blood cultures pending

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to her GP with 8 months of excessive worry about work, family, finances and her own health. She describes restlessness, fatigue, irritability, muscle tension and insomnia most nights. She has had 2 episodes of panic in the last month. Her mood is anxious but she denies persistent low mood, anhedonia or thoughts of self-harm. She uses no substances. GAD-7 score is 16.

data_table.Examination: Vital signs within normal limits; mental state: anxious affect, normal speech, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation; cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.8, full blood count and electrolytes normal; urine drug screen negative; ECG normal

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Benzodiazepine diazepam 5 mg three times daily for 6 weeks as first-line monotherapy
Sertraline 50 mg daily titrating to 100-200 mg with referral for cognitive behavioural therapy
Olanzapine 5 mg daily as augmentation for severe anxiety symptoms ongoing despite GP review
Beta-blocker propranolol 40 mg three times daily as first-line monotherapy for somatic symptoms
Refer for inpatient psychiatric admission given the severity score on GAD-7 questionnaire

stem: A 24-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia is on day 18 of clozapine titration, currently at 175 mg daily. He has been responding well to treatment but today presents to the emergency department with fever, malaise, persistent tachycardia and mild dyspnoea on exertion. He denies cough, sputum or urinary symptoms. He has no source of infection on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.7 degrees Celsius, HR 120 sinus, BP 110/68, RR 22, SpO2 96% in room air
data_table.Examination: No focus of infection on ENT or chest examination; chest clear; heart sounds soft with no murmur; abdomen soft; no rash
data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 250 ng/L (less than 14), ECG: sinus tachycardia with non-specific T wave flattening, CXR: clear, WCC 9.5 with no left shift, CRP 60, BNP 200, blood cultures sent

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Continue clozapine and treat symptomatically with paracetamol given non-specific viral picture
Reduce clozapine dose by 50 percent and recheck the troponin level in 48 hours review
Cease clozapine immediately, admit for cardiac assessment with echocardiogram, and never rechallenge
Add propranolol 40 mg three times daily for tachycardia and continue clozapine titration as planned
Switch directly to olanzapine 20 mg daily and discharge with outpatient cardiology follow-up review

stem: A 26-year-old woman on risperidone 4 mg daily for 6 months for schizophrenia has had a good symptomatic response. She presents to the early psychosis clinic with 4 months of amenorrhoea, milk discharge from both breasts and reduced libido. She wishes to retain antipsychotic efficacy. She is sexually active and uses condoms; pregnancy test is negative.

data_table.Examination: Breast examination: bilateral expressible non-bloody galactorrhoea, no palpable mass; visual fields full to confrontation; mental state stable with no psychotic relapse features
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 1800 mIU/L (less than 500), TSH 1.6, beta-hCG negative, FSH and LH suppressed; MRI pituitary normal; LFTs and renal function normal

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Add cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly to reduce prolactin while continuing risperidone unchanged
Stop risperidone and commence oral oestradiol-progestogen combined contraceptive only
Reduce risperidone to 2 mg and add bromocriptine 2.5 mg daily as combination management
Switch from risperidone to aripiprazole and titrate to symptom control over 4-6 weeks
Continue risperidone and reassure as hyperprolactinaemia is asymptomatic and benign here

subtopic_detail: Severe anorexia nervosa medical admission criteria
stem: A 19-year-old female university student presents to her GP with 8 months of progressive restrictive eating and 30 percent weight loss from baseline. She has weakness, dizziness on standing and feels cold. She denies binging or purging. Mental state shows intense fear of weight gain and distorted body image. She does not feel suicidal.

data_table.Vital signs: BMI 12.8 kg/m2; HR 38 sinus, BP 85/55 supine and 70/40 standing, temp 35.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, lanugo hair, cold peripheries, slow capillary refill 3 seconds, proximal weakness on squat test; abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: K 2.8, PO4 0.6, Mg 0.6, Na 134, glucose 3.2, urea 4.2, creatinine 50, LFTs ALT 90 AST 110, albumin 28; ECG sinus bradycardia QTc 470 ms

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate disposition and initial management?

options.text: Refer to specialist outpatient eating disorder team with weekly weights and dietitian reviews scheduled
Discharge with family-based therapy referral and weekly GP review for weight monitoring at home
Admit to a general adult ward with a standard three-meal regimen at full calories from day one
Cognitive behavioural therapy for eating disorders intensive outpatient program with weekly therapy
Admit to medical ward with cardiac monitoring, electrolyte correction and slow refeeding with daily monitoring

subtopic_detail: Long-term lithium monitoring frequency in stable bipolar I disorder
stem: A 38-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium 1000 mg nightly for 5 years with no acute mood episodes. Her most recent 12-hour trough lithium level is 0.7 mmol/L. She is otherwise well and on no other regular medications. She has no symptoms of polyuria or polydipsia. Her primary care GP is reviewing her chronic disease management plan and asks about monitoring intervals. She has had no surgery or significant illness in the past year.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no fine tremor, no weight gain over 12 months
data_table.Investigations: Most recent (3 months ago): lithium 0.7 mmol/L, TSH 2.4 mIU/L, eGFR 92, calcium corrected 2.34 mmol/L; ECG normal

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate monitoring plan?

options.text: Six-monthly lithium level, TSH, eGFR and calcium, with a 12-hourly trough lithium level taken 5 to 7 days after any dose change or new interacting medication
Annual TSH and lithium level only, with no renal or calcium monitoring required and no additional monitoring around dose or interacting-medication changes
Five-yearly lithium level only with no other monitoring intervals, on the basis that her current ranges have been stable for 5 consecutive years at therapeutic targets without symptoms
Replace lithium with sodium valproate empirically without further monitoring of any chemistry, levels or organ function and discontinue all bipolar-specific reviews going forward
Monthly lithium level and ECG indefinitely as the default monitoring schedule for any patient on lithium, regardless of stability or duration of therapy

subtopic_detail: First-line pharmacotherapy for tobacco use disorder in an adult smoker
stem: A 47-year-old man smokes 20 cigarettes a day, has done so for 25 years, and wants to quit. He has tried nicotine patches without behavioural support twice in the past with relapse within weeks. He has no history of seizures, no eating disorder, no recent myocardial infarction in the last month and no severe renal impairment. He has a remote episode of mild depression 8 years ago, fully resolved without treatment. He is on no regular medications.

data_table.Examination: No respiratory distress, breath sounds normal; mild dental staining
data_table.Investigations: FEV1/FVC 0.74; eGFR 88; HbA1c 5.5%; PHQ-9 score 3 (minimal symptoms)

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Encourage transition to electronic cigarettes (vapes) without any other pharmacological cessation aid as the recommended first-line strategy in this patient with prior NRT failures
Varenicline 0.5 mg daily for 3 days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks, with a quit date set for day 8, alongside behavioural support
Brief nicotine replacement therapy for 3 days only at low dose to minimise systemic exposure, with no concurrent behavioural support, no extended duration, and no longer-acting agent considered
Bupropion sustained-release 150 mg daily as monotherapy in a patient with an active eating disorder requiring close psychiatric follow-up and concurrent low-dose benzodiazepine support
Oral naltrexone 50 mg daily indefinitely as monotherapy specifically targeting nicotine craving, with no other cessation aid or behavioural support added at this initial visit

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD assessment and stimulant initiation pathway
stem: A 27-year-old graphic designer reports lifelong inattention, frequent task-switching and procrastination that now impair his work. He recalls academic difficulties from primary school. He drinks alcohol moderately and uses no other substances. He has no cardiac history, no significant mood symptoms today and no anxiety disorder requiring treatment. He has no first-degree relative with sudden cardiac death. His GP is the first doctor to assess these concerns formally.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: euthymic, no thought disorder, concentration intermittently poor on serial 7s; PHQ-9 score 4, GAD-7 score 5
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm, normal QTc; AUDIT score 5; collateral history from mother confirms childhood inattention at school

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Commence a trial of oral methylphenidate immediate-release 10 mg twice daily empirically at this initial visit without further diagnostic workup, collateral history or specialist referral
Commence an SSRI as first-line pharmacotherapy for adult ADHD symptoms with no further specialist assessment, no further investigation and no plan to consider stimulants for this presentation

Complete a structured DSM-5 ADHD interview, gather corroborating childhood history, screen for comorbid mood, anxiety and substance use, then refer to a psychiatrist for stimulant initiation under AU prescribing restrictions
Refer for CBT alone without any consideration of stimulant or non-stimulant pharmacotherapy, regardless of severity, functional impairment or response to non-pharmacological interventions over time

Trial of lithium for impulse control as the first pharmacological intervention with no specialist referral, no structured ADHD diagnostic interview, and no consideration of stimulant or non-stimulant agents

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose with QRS prolongation and hypotension
stem: A 24-year-old woman is brought to ED 2 hours after ingestion of an estimated 4 grams of amitriptyline. She is now drowsy, hypotensive and tachycardic. She had a single seizure in the ambulance. The ECG demonstrates sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 140 ms and a right axis. She has no significant past medical history, no allergies and is not pregnant. There is no concurrent alcohol or other drug ingestion documented.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 86/52, HR 124, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air, Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius, GCS 11
data_table.Examination: Dilated pupils 6 mm, dry mucous membranes, urinary retention; ECG QRS 140 ms, right axis
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.30, lactate 3.6 mmol/L, K 3.6 mmol/L, Na 138 mmol/L; salicylate and paracetamol levels negative; serum amitriptyline pending

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous lipid emulsion 20 percent at 1.5 mL/kg as a sole agent with no concurrent bicarbonate, no airway support and no antiarrhythmic therapy in this presentation
Single dose activated charcoal 50 g orally 4 hours after the ingestion as the sole and primary intervention, with no other haemodynamic or cardiac stabilising therapy commenced at this time
Intravenous diazepam 10 mg as a single dose for the seizure with no further cardiovascular intervention beyond observation in a monitored bay over the next 4 hours
Intravenous 8.4 percent sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg as a bolus to narrow the QRS and target arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55, with airway support and crystalloid resuscitation as adjuncts
Initiation of urgent haemodialysis as the sole and primary management strategy for TCA cardiotoxicity, with no concurrent bicarbonate therapy and no specific airway or cardiac monitoring

subtopic_detail: Catatonia in major depression with positive lorazepam challenge
stem: A 58-year-old woman with a history of recurrent major depressive disorder is admitted after 6 days of becoming progressively mute, immobile and refusing food. She maintains odd postures and exhibits waxy flexibility. There is no fever. Investigations exclude infection, hypoglycaemia, electrolyte disturbance and intoxication. CT brain is unremarkable. She has been off her usual sertraline for 3 weeks before admission. There is no history of antipsychotic exposure.

data_table.Examination: Mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility; no rigidity, no tremor, no autonomic instability; Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale 14
data_table.Investigations: Na 139 mmol/L, K 4.0, glucose 5.4 mmol/L, CK 220 U/L, CRP 4 mg/L, ammonia 28 micromol/L, TSH 1.8 mIU/L; CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial step?

options.text: Commence electroconvulsive therapy this afternoon without any pharmacological trial first, with no informed consent or capacity assessment process performed before treatment in this patient
Initiate sertraline 50 mg daily as the sole intervention with the expectation of full response within 72 hours and no other pharmacological or psychiatric measures arranged at this admission
Commence haloperidol 5 mg intramuscular every 6 hours as monotherapy for catatonia, with no benzodiazepine challenge and no other pharmacological measure considered at this point in admission
Commence a single dose of biperiden 5 mg intramuscularly as the sole pharmacological intervention for catatonia and reassess in 24 hours with no other immediate measures
Intravenous lorazepam 1 to 2 mg challenge with reassessment of catatonia score at 5 to 10 minutes; if responsive, scheduled lorazepam and plan for ECT if symptoms persist or recur

subtopic_detail: Discriminating schizoaffective disorder from bipolar I with mood-congruent psychosis
stem: A 32-year-old man has had three discrete depressive episodes over 4 years, each with mood-congruent paranoid delusions and auditory hallucinations. Between episodes, his depressive symptoms have remitted but the paranoid delusions and auditory hallucinations have persisted continuously for at least 3 weeks at a time, in the absence of an acute mood episode. He has no history of manic or hypomanic episodes. He uses no substances. There is no first-degree family history of bipolar disorder.

data_table.Examination: Today: persecutory delusions present; mood euthymic; speech normal; no manic features
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative; TSH 1.6 mIU/L; CT brain normal; PANSS positive 28

lead_in: Which is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, given the persistence of psychotic symptoms for 2 weeks or longer in the absence of an acute major depressive episode in this patient
Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features, given his recurrent psychotic mood symptoms with full remission of psychotic symptoms between acute mood episodes in his presentation
Brief psychotic disorder, given the episodic nature of his psychotic symptoms over 4 years of intermittent illness, with mood symptoms considered incidental in this patient

Major depressive disorder with psychotic features, given the depressive episodes and concurrent psychotic features, with psychosis considered episode-bound in this patient's longitudinal course of illness
Schizophreniform disorder, given the under-6-month duration of any individual psychotic episode in this patient with intermittent mood symptoms and recurring discrete intervals of psychosis

subtopic_detail: Acute behavioural disturbance in the ED requiring rapid tranquillisation
stem: A 36-year-old man brought in by police is highly agitated, shouting and pacing in the ED short-stay unit. He has paranoid delusions and a history of treatment-resistant schizophrenia, with intermittent methamphetamine use. He is intermittently approaching staff aggressively but has not yet assaulted anyone. He is refusing oral medication and verbal de-escalation has failed. There is no documented allergy, no current QT prolongation on ECG, and no concurrent CNS depressant ingestion suspected.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/86, HR 108, SpO2 98% on room air, Temp 37.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, dilated pupils 5 mm, ECG sinus tachycardia QTc 412 ms, blood alcohol 0
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen pending; previous ECG 3 weeks ago QTc 408 ms; weight 80 kg

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Single oral diazepam 2 mg only without any antipsychotic, with no further escalation pathway and no re-evaluation interval planned for this patient with acute behavioural disturbance
De-escalation first, then offer oral olanzapine 10 mg or oral lorazepam 1 to 2 mg; if refused or unsafe, intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg or droperidol 10 mg with cardiac and respiratory monitoring
Single intramuscular haloperidol 20 mg as a one-off dose without ECG, without monitoring and without re-evaluation, regardless of comorbid stimulant intoxication or QTc status
Rapid IV midazolam infusion at 5 mg/hour without monitoring, escalation plan or airway support, in a general ward bed with no immediate access to flumazenil or other airway adjuncts
Physical restraint indefinitely without medication, with no clear monitoring plan, no medical review interval and no de-escalation attempt offered to the patient before restraint is applied

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective disorder vs bipolar I with psychotic features
stem: A 24-year-old woman is admitted with a third episode of acute psychosis with prominent persecutory delusions, third-person auditory hallucinations, and disorganised behaviour. Collateral from her sister indicates these psychotic symptoms have been present for the past 6 weeks. During the first 3 weeks of this episode she was sleeping 3 hours nightly, spending compulsively, and grandiose. Over the past 3 weeks her mood has stabilised but the psychotic symptoms persist unchanged.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: thought disorder, persecutory delusions held with full conviction, third-person auditory hallucinations; mood euthymic for the past 3 weeks; no current suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative; CT brain normal; TSH, B12, FBC, calcium, electrolytes normal; structured interview confirms two prior episodes of mania each lasting at least 7 days

lead_in: What is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type because the psychosis has persisted at least 2 weeks in the absence of prominent mood symptoms during a longitudinal course with mood episodes
Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features because mania was clearly present in the first 3 weeks of this index episode of illness
Schizophreniform disorder because the psychotic symptoms have been present for over 1 month but less than 6 months in total since the prodromal onset
Substance-induced psychotic disorder because methamphetamine remains detectable for up to 3 months in clinical practice despite a current negative screen
Major depressive disorder with psychotic features and mood incongruent persecutory delusions despite the absence of depressive symptoms over recent weeks

stem: A 47-year-old smokes 25 cigarettes daily for 28 years and presents for cessation support after a hospital admission for a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction 4 weeks ago. He has previously tried nicotine patches and tried cold turkey twice without success. He is on aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol, perindopril. His mood is euthymic with no previous depression or suicidal thoughts. He has no renal impairment.

data_table.Examination: BMI 28, BP 132/82, no signs of withdrawal, no respiratory disease on examination
data_table.Investigations: eGFR 78 mL/min/1.73 m2, normal liver function, recent echocardiogram with preserved ejection fraction

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate plan for varenicline?

options.text: Start varenicline 1 mg twice daily today and stop smoking immediately on the same day as the first dose to maximise medication coverage at the receptor
Substitute varenicline 1 mg twice daily for his metoprolol because beta-blockers interfere with the action of varenicline at nicotinic receptors
Avoid varenicline entirely after recent acute coronary syndrome and recommend nicotine inhalator plus oral nortriptyline combination instead
Begin varenicline 2 mg daily with a planned cessation date 6 weeks after starting to allow gradual tapering of cigarettes during titration
Start varenicline 0.5 mg daily for 3 days then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days then 1 mg twice daily, with a quit date 8 to 14 days from first dose, for 12 weeks

subtopic_detail: Cannabis-induced psychosis vs first episode schizophrenia
stem: A 19-year-old male is admitted with 5 days of persecutory delusions about being followed by police and second-person command auditory hallucinations. He uses high-potency cannabis daily and his last use was 12 hours ago. He has had previous brief paranoid episodes after heavy cannabis sessions that resolved within 48 hours of cessation. His older brother was diagnosed with schizophrenia at age 22.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: marked paranoia, third-person auditory hallucinations, blunted affect, formal thought disorder; appears internally preoccupied
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for cannabis only; CT brain normal; TSH and electrolytes normal; collateral confirms no premorbid functional decline before recent cannabis escalation 9 months ago

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate diagnostic and management approach now?

options.text: Diagnose first episode schizophrenia and commence long-acting paliperidone palmitate intramuscular depot before discharge home with community mental health follow-up
Diagnose cannabis intoxication and discharge home today with cessation counselling alone and review at the local community mental health team within 1 month
Admit to a specialist youth early psychosis service for low-dose oral antipsychotic, cannabis cessation support, and longitudinal review for emerging psychosis
Diagnose substance-induced psychotic disorder definitively and avoid antipsychotic medication entirely while encouraging abstinence over the next 4 weeks
Commence high-dose intramuscular zuclopenthixol acuphase 100 mg with physical restraint maintained for the duration of all acute behavioural symptoms

subtopic_detail: Augmentation strategy in treatment-resistant unipolar depression
stem: A 52-year-old has had inadequate response to two adequate trials of antidepressant: sertraline 200 mg daily for 10 weeks then venlafaxine extended release 225 mg daily for 12 weeks. She has a current Hamilton Depression Rating Scale of 22. She remains in partial remission with persistent low mood, anhedonia, and middle insomnia. She has no psychotic features, no bipolarity in personal or family history, and no suicidal ideation. Her thyroid function, vitamin B12, and full blood count are normal.

data_table.Examination: BMI 27, BP 124/78, no parkinsonism, no acute distress
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.9 mIU/L, B12 320 pmol/L, fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, lithium not previously tried, cardiac echo normal, ECG QTc 410 ms

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Cross-titrate to oral fluoxetine 60 mg daily over 2 weeks before reassessing for a further antidepressant switch
Augment with aripiprazole 2.5 mg daily, titrating to 10 mg as tolerated, with metabolic and akathisia monitoring at 4 and 8 weeks
Combine venlafaxine with a tricyclic antidepressant such as amitriptyline 75 mg nightly to maximise noradrenergic effect over the next 6 weeks
Augment with the dopamine agonist pramipexole 0.125 mg three times daily as a first-line augmentation strategy
Recommend immediate electroconvulsive therapy as initial next step without further pharmacological augmentation trials

stem: A 32-year-old has been stable on clozapine 350 mg nightly for 8 months for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. His routine weekly bloods today show an absolute neutrophil count of 1.4 x10^9/L, down from 2.1 x10^9/L a week ago. White cell count is 3.0. He is afebrile, asymptomatic, and has had no recent infections. He uses no other myelosuppressive medications. He continues to attend his weekly clozapine clinic.

data_table.Examination: No oral ulceration, no lymphadenopathy, no infective focus, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Today: WCC 3.0, neutrophils 1.4 x10^9/L, lymphocytes 1.3, platelets 220, Hb 142; previous week: WCC 4.1, neutrophils 2.1 x10^9/L; clozapine level 540 microgram/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next action?

options.text: Continue clozapine unchanged and resume routine 4-weekly bloods after a single repeat full blood count tomorrow morning
Stop clozapine permanently and switch to oral aripiprazole 10 mg daily, starting cross-titration today before discharge home
Hospitalise and commence intravenous filgrastim 300 microgram daily until neutrophil recovery without changing the clozapine dose
Continue clozapine at the current dose, repeat full blood count twice weekly, and notify the clozapine program as the patient is now in the amber zone
Halve the clozapine dose to 175 mg nightly and continue routine 4-weekly bloods, with general practitioner review only if febrile illness emerges

stem:
You are a GP registrar reviewing a 47-year-old woman who has been on lithium carbonate 1000 mg daily for bipolar I disorder for 4 years. Her mood has been stable on this dose with no relapses. She presents for an annual review and reports fatigue, mild constipation, modest weight gain, and dry skin over the past 6 months. She has no tremor, no polyuria, and no neurological symptoms.

Her psychiatrist last reviewed her 6 months ago and was happy with her mood state. Her most recent lithium level 3 months ago was 0.7 mmol/L. The annual monitoring bloods have just been performed.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/76 mmHg, HR 64 bpm, BMI 28 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: No goitre, no tremor, no peripheral oedema, slow ankle jerk relaxation
data_table.Investigations: TSH 18.2 mIU/L, free T4 9 pmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, eGFR 78 mL/min/1.73m2, calcium corrected 2.42 mmol/L, lithium level 0.7 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease lithium immediately and substitute sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily as mood stabiliser
Commence levothyroxine 50 micrograms orally daily and continue lithium at current dose
Reduce lithium to 500 mg daily to allow thyroid recovery and continue close monitoring of mood
Recheck thyroid function in 6 weeks before considering replacement therapy in this asymptomatic phase
Refer to endocrinology for thyroid autoantibodies and ultrasound before starting any treatment

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar called to review a 24-year-old man with a first episode of psychosis admitted 5 days ago. He was started on olanzapine 10 mg daily 3 days ago. Today he is mute, staring, and immobile. The nurse reports he has not eaten or drunk since this morning and has held his arm in an awkward position for over an hour without complaint.

There is no fever and no rigidity. He has no past medical history and takes no other medications. His vital signs are stable. The medical registrar saw him this morning and excluded delirium with a normal collateral history of acute onset and stable medical workup.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88 bpm, BP 122/78 mmHg, Temp 37.0 degrees C, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, posturing, waxy flexibility, no tremor, no rigidity, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 180 U/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, glucose 5.2 mmol/L, urinalysis clear, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer haloperidol 5 mg intramuscularly for behavioural disturbance and continue olanzapine
Increase olanzapine to 20 mg daily for presumed exacerbation of underlying psychotic illness
Cease olanzapine and commence intravenous dantrolene 2 mg/kg as muscle relaxant for rigidity
Administer lorazepam 2 mg intramuscularly and reassess catatonic features at 30 to 60 minutes
Defer pharmacological intervention and arrange brain MRI to exclude structural neurological cause

stem: A 29-year-old man ingested amitriptyline two hours ago. He has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure in the resuscitation bay that is still going at two minutes. He is intubated and ventilated and sodium bicarbonate is running.

data_table.Investigations: Arterial pH 7.48, glucose 6.1 mmol/L, sodium 142 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous midazolam 5 mg, repeated if needed
Intravenous phenytoin 1000 mg by slow infusion
Intravenous levetiracetam 1000 mg over 15 minutes
Intravenous propofol 100 mg then an infusion
Intravenous physostigmine 2 mg over 5 minutes

stem:
You are a psychiatry registrar reviewing a 32-year-old IT consultant referred by his GP for assessment of possible adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. He reports lifelong difficulty completing tasks, frequent careless mistakes, and being easily distracted. He has held his current job 8 years but says he relies on tight deadlines and a self-built reminder system. He achieved high school graduation with average results despite his difficulties.

He drinks 2 standard drinks per week and uses no other substances. His mood is euthymic. He has no anxiety or sleep disturbance. His mother reports he was always restless in primary school but managed academically.

data_table.Examination: Mental state normal, no thought disorder, no psychomotor abnormality
data_table.Investigations: Standardised adult ADHD rating scale: 18 of 18 inattentive items endorsed at threshold severity, 6 of 9 hyperactive-impulsive items, symptoms present since age 7, impairment present in occupational and home domains

lead_in: Which feature is essential to support an adult ADHD diagnosis under the Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline?

options.text: Documented IQ below 90 to establish baseline cognitive impairment before stimulant therapy
At least 6 of 9 symptoms in BOTH inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive domains for adult diagnosis
Persistent functional impairment in two or more settings attributable to symptoms present before 12 years old
Normal brain MRI and electroencephalogram excluding structural and epileptiform causes
Failed trial of nonpharmacological strategies including cognitive behavioural therapy and coaching

subtopic_detail: ECT consent in severe depression under NSW law
stem: You are the consultation-liaison registrar. A 68-year-old woman detained in a NSW mental health facility has psychotic depression with nihilistic delusions, has lost 11 kg in 3 months and refuses food and fluids. Three antidepressant trials have failed over 6 months. She is drowsy from dehydration and declines ECT, saying it will erase her memories. Her family supports treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/58 mmHg, HR 102 bpm, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 132 mmol/L, urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 102 micromol/L

lead_in: Under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start ECT today under emergency provisions without any Tribunal involvement
Respect her refusal and continue antidepressant escalation with intravenous fluids
Obtain her next of kin's written consent and proceed with ECT now
Apply to the Mental Health Review Tribunal for an ECT administration inquiry
Transfer for nasogastric feeding and defer ECT until her capacity returns

stem: You are the community mental health team registrar reviewing a 28-year-old man four months after commencing olanzapine 15 mg nightly for a first episode of schizophrenia. He reports improved sleep and reduced positive symptoms. He has gained 8 kg, with new central adiposity and increased thirst. He smokes 20 cigarettes daily and has a family history of premature ischaemic heart disease.

data_table.Examination: Central adiposity, no acanthosis nigricans, no peripheral neuropathy
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.4 mmol/L, HbA1c 6.0%, triglycerides 2.6, HDL 0.9, LDL 3.4, ALT 64, prolactin 320 mIU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch to an antipsychotic with a lower metabolic risk profile such as aripiprazole and continue lifestyle intervention with monitoring
Continue olanzapine and add metformin titrated to 1500 mg daily for weight management without any change to the antipsychotic regimen at this stage
Reduce olanzapine to 5 mg nightly to minimise side effects and reassess weight and metabolic parameters at the next six-monthly clinic review
Add clozapine at low dose as an augmentation strategy with weekly haematological monitoring and continue olanzapine at the current daily dose
Refer for bariatric surgery assessment and continue current antipsychotic regimen unchanged given the response to therapy for the primary psychiatric illness

stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 48-year-old woman who smokes 25 cigarettes daily and wants to quit. Her past medical history includes major depressive disorder in remission on sertraline, well-controlled hypertension on perindopril, and stable angina with an ETT performed last year that was reassuring. She has tried nicotine patches alone twice without success.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable, no signs of depression on current review
data_table.Investigations: Recent FBC, UEC, LFTs all within normal range; ECG normal
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 100 mg, perindopril 5 mg, GTN PRN, aspirin 100 mg

lead_in: Which smoking cessation pharmacotherapy has the strongest evidence and is most appropriate here?

options.text: Recommend electronic cigarettes as primary smoking cessation aid given previous nicotine replacement therapy has failed in this patient with stable cardiac disease
Repeat nicotine patches alone at higher 21 mg dose and provide written information about quitting and a follow-up appointment in four weeks for review
Commence bupropion 150 mg daily titrated to twice daily after one week with weekly review to monitor for mood deterioration and seizure threshold change
Commence varenicline with structured dose titration over twelve weeks alongside behavioural support and counsel about possible neuropsychiatric monitoring
Refer to a residential drug and alcohol service for inpatient withdrawal management with intensive nursing and counselling provided over a four-week admission
