Advise against completing this document as it may compromise her future clinical care

subtopic_detail: SSRI use in pregnancy risk counselling
stem: A 30-year-old woman with recurrent major depression stable on sertraline 100 mg daily presents for preconception counselling. She had two previous severe episodes requiring hospitalisation, both occurring after stopping antidepressants. She is planning her first pregnancy. Her current PHQ-9 score is 3 (remission).

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, normal mental state examination

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding sertraline?

options.text: Cease sertraline immediately as all SSRIs are teratogenic in the first trimester
Continue sertraline through pregnancy after discussing low absolute neonatal risk
Switch to paroxetine as it is considered the safest SSRI option in pregnancy
Taper sertraline over 4 weeks and substitute with St John's wort as a natural alternative
Reduce sertraline to the minimum effective dose and plan to cease by 36 weeks gestation

subtopic_detail: Lithium management in pregnancy - peripartum dosing
stem: A 33-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has continued lithium throughout pregnancy after shared decision making. She is now 36 weeks gestation and stable. Her most recent lithium level is 0.7 mmol/L. Her renal and thyroid function are normal. She is planning a vaginal delivery. Her previous manic episodes were severe, requiring ICU admission during one episode.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72, HR 82, normal fetal heart rate
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L, TSH 2.8 mIU/L, creatinine 58 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate lithium management strategy around delivery?

options.text: Continue current lithium dose through delivery and postpartum without changes
Cease lithium at 36 weeks to avoid neonatal toxicity and restart 48 hours postpartum
Reduce lithium to the pre-pregnancy dose at onset of labour and monitor levels closely postpartum
Switch from lithium to sodium valproate at 36 weeks for safer peripartum management
Increase lithium dose by 25% from 36 weeks to ensure therapeutic levels during delivery stress

stem: A 35-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been charged with serious assault. During psychiatric assessment, he can name his solicitor and understands the charge. However, he holds a fixed delusional belief that his solicitor is conspiring with the prosecution against him and refuses to communicate with his lawyer. He cannot challenge prosecution witnesses because he believes they are government agents. He is on clozapine 400 mg daily with a level of 0.42 mg/L.

data_table.Examination: Persecutory delusions involving legal representatives, mild thought disorder, suspicious and guarded affect, orientated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate opinion regarding fitness to stand trial?

options.text: Fit to stand trial because he understands the charge and can identify his solicitor
Unfit on permanent basis with recommendation for indefinite forensic order
Fitness assessment is premature; defer until clozapine level is above 0.60 mg/L
Currently unfit due to inability to instruct counsel; recommend treatment and reassessment
Fit to stand trial with a recommendation for a support person during proceedings

subtopic_detail: Structured professional judgement in violence risk assessment
stem: A 40-year-old man with schizophrenia is being assessed by the forensic psychiatry team prior to a tribunal review. He was found not guilty by reason of mental impairment for a serious violent offence 5 years ago. He has been in a forensic facility since. His psychosis is well controlled on long-acting injectable aripiprazole. He has completed a violence prevention program. The tribunal has asked for a violence risk assessment.

data_table.Examination: No active psychotic symptoms, good insight, cooperative, expresses remorse

lead_in: Which risk assessment approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Unstructured clinical judgement based on interview and clinical experience
Static-99R actuarial tool to quantify recidivism probability
PCL-R (Psychopathy Checklist - Revised) as the primary assessment framework
GAF (Global Assessment of Functioning) scale to quantify current functioning
HCR-20 structured professional judgement framework with scenario planning

stem: An 82-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer disease in residential aged care has been increasingly agitated in the late afternoon for 3 weeks, pacing and calling out. There is no acute illness, pain, urinary retention, constipation, or medication changes. A urine dipstick and blood tests are unremarkable.

data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, UEC normal, CRP 4 mg/L, urinalysis negative, BSL 6.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Implement structured afternoon activities, environmental changes, and carer education
Commence risperidone 0.25 mg twice daily for behavioural symptom management
Add memantine 5 mg daily titrating to 20 mg for behavioural symptoms
Increase donepezil to 23 mg daily to target behavioural symptoms more effectively
Commence regular lorazepam 0.5 mg three times daily for anxiety-driven agitation

subtopic_detail: Pseudodementia vs early Alzheimer disease differentiation
stem:
A 72-year-old retired teacher presents with her husband who reports 8 months of progressive memory difficulties. She has stopped reading novels because she cannot follow the plot. She is withdrawn and has lost interest in her garden. She has had two previous depressive episodes (ages 48 and 61), both fully remitting with sertraline. On testing, she scores 22/30 on the MoCA.

When she cannot recall a word she becomes frustrated and says 'I don't know - I can't remember anything anymore.' She gives multiple 'don't know' responses. Her verbal fluency for animals is 8 in 60 seconds. Her FDG-PET shows bilateral temporoparietal hypometabolism.

data_table.Investigations: TSH 2.4 mIU/L, B12 380 pmol/L, folate 18 nmol/L, MoCA 22/30, GDS-15 score 11/15
data_table.FDG-PET: Bilateral temporoparietal hypometabolism with relative frontal sparing

lead_in: Which feature most strongly suggests the cognitive impairment is not solely attributable to depression?

options.text: The presence of 'don't know' responses on cognitive testing
The bilateral temporoparietal hypometabolism on FDG-PET
The GDS-15 score of 11/15 confirming significant depression
The verbal fluency score of 8 animals in 60 seconds
The history of two previous fully remitting depressive episodes

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to a psychiatric outpatient clinic for diagnostic clarification. Over the past 4 years she has had three manic episodes lasting 4-8 weeks each, with grandiosity and reduced need for sleep. During these episodes she also experiences auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions. Between mood episodes, she has periods of euthymia lasting several months. However, her treating team has documented persistent auditory hallucinations and referential delusions for at least 3 weeks during two of these euthymic intervals when no mood symptoms were present.

data_table.Medications: Lithium 900 mg daily (level 0.7 mmol/L), quetiapine 400 mg nocte
data_table.Investigations: TSH 2.1 mU/L; urine drug screen negative; MRI brain normal

lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits this clinical picture?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features
Schizophrenia with co-occurring bipolar spectrum disorder
Schizoaffective disorder with a bipolar-type presentation
Brief psychotic disorder with recurrent mood-triggered episodes
Delusional disorder with superimposed bipolar mood episodes

stem: A 24-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder stabilised on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 2 years presents for a routine psychiatry review. She mentions she has recently entered a new relationship and is not currently using contraception. She has had no manic or depressive episodes since starting valproate. She asks about the risks if she were to become pregnant.

data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 1000 mg daily, quetiapine 50 mg nocte PRN
data_table.Investigations: Valproate level 72 mg/L (therapeutic 50-100); LFTs normal; FBC normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management regarding her valproate?

options.text: Continue valproate and add high-dose folic acid 5 mg daily now
Reduce valproate to 500 mg daily to minimise the fetal risk
Cease valproate immediately and commence lamotrigine at 200 mg
Maintain valproate only if she agrees to use depot contraception
Plan a gradual cross-taper to lamotrigine with effective contraception

stem: A 35-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance after being found unresponsive at home with empty amitriptyline blister packs nearby. His partner estimates he may have taken up to 3 g. He arrived 90 minutes after the estimated time of ingestion. He is obtunded with a GCS of 8 and has had one witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure in the ambulance.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128/min, BP 88/54 mmHg, RR 14/min, T 37.4 C, pupils 6 mm bilaterally and sluggishly reactive
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia, QRS duration 142 ms, right axis deviation, prominent R wave in aVR greater than 3 mm; VBG: pH 7.28, pCO2 48 mmHg, HCO3 18 mmol/L, lactate 3.6 mmol/L; BSL 6.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most important immediate pharmacological intervention?

options.text: IV diazepam 10 mg to prevent further tonic-clonic seizures
IV flumazenil 0.2 mg to reverse any co-ingested benzodiazepine
IV amiodarone 300 mg for management of the wide-complex rhythm
Activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube for decontamination
IV sodium bicarbonate 8.4% bolus of 1-2 mmol/kg body weight

stem: A 48-year-old man with a 30-pack-year smoking history presents to his GP requesting help to quit. He has tried nicotine patches twice before but relapsed within 4 weeks both times. He has a stable past history of well-controlled schizophrenia on olanzapine 15 mg daily with no psychotic symptoms for 2 years. He has no history of seizures. He is motivated and has a planned quit date in 2 weeks.

data_table.Investigations: Fagerstrom Test for Nicotine Dependence: score 7/10 (high dependence)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy strategy?

options.text: Nicotine patches 21 mg daily alone starting on the quit date
Bupropion 150 mg twice daily commenced 1-2 weeks before quit
Nortriptyline 75 mg daily as a non-nicotine cessation agent
Varenicline titrated to 1 mg twice daily combined with NRT patch
Combination NRT with patches 21 mg and nicotine gum 4 mg PRN

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation with clozapine - CYP1A2 interaction management
stem: A 42-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia stabilised on clozapine 400 mg daily wants to quit smoking. He smokes 25 cigarettes per day. His most recent clozapine trough level is 0.42 mg/L (therapeutic range 0.35-0.60 mg/L). He has no cardiac risk factors, no seizure history, and his metabolic monitoring is stable.

data_table.Investigations: Clozapine trough level 0.42 mg/L (0.35-0.60). FBC: WCC 6.8 x10^9/L, neutrophils 3.4 x10^9/L. Fasting glucose 5.8 mmol/L. HbA1c 5.6%. Fasting lipids within normal limits. ECG: QTc 418 ms.

lead_in: What is the most important pharmacological consideration when supporting his smoking cessation?

options.text: Varenicline is contraindicated due to psychiatric illness
Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold with clozapine
Smoking cessation raises clozapine levels via CYP1A2 changes
NRT patches are contraindicated with antipsychotic therapy
Clozapine dose should be increased to prevent relapse

subtopic_detail: GHB withdrawal - recognition and benzodiazepine management
stem: A 29-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe agitation, tremor, diaphoresis, and tachycardia. His housemate reports he uses GHB (gamma-hydroxybutyrate) daily - approximately 5-10 mL every 2-3 hours including overnight - and his last dose was 8 hours ago when he ran out. He has no history of alcohol use disorder. He has had one previous episode of GHB withdrawal requiring ICU admission 6 months ago.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128 bpm, BP 168/98 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO2 98% on room air, Temp 38.4 degrees C.
data_table.Examination: Agitated, diaphoretic, coarse tremor in all limbs. Dilated pupils. No focal neurological deficit. No signs of head injury.
data_table.Investigations: BSL 6.2 mmol/L. UEC normal. LFTs normal. Blood alcohol 0. Urine drug screen: negative for amphetamines and opioids.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Diazepam 20 mg IV with repeated doses titrated to effect
Chlordiazepoxide loading protocol as per alcohol withdrawal
Baclofen 10 mg three times daily for GABA-B agonism
Haloperidol 5 mg IM for acute agitation management
Phenobarbital 130 mg IV as adjunctive sedative agent

subtopic_detail: Cannabis-induced psychosis vs primary psychotic disorder - discrimination
stem: A 21-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police after threatening passersby, believing they were conspiring against him. He has been using cannabis daily for 4 years, with escalating use to multiple cones per day over the past 6 months. His urine drug screen is positive for THC only. He reports auditory hallucinations commanding him to protect himself. There is no family history of psychotic disorders. He was functioning well at university until 3 months ago when his cannabis use increased significantly.

data_table.Examination: Agitated, suspicious, poor eye contact. Persecutory delusions - believes strangers are government agents. Third-person auditory hallucinations. Thought form is linear. Oriented to time, place, and person. No evidence of formal thought disorder.
data_table.Investigations: UDS: THC positive, all others negative. BSL 5.4 mmol/L. FBC, UEC, LFTs, TFTs - all normal.

lead_in: Which clinical feature most strongly favours substance-induced psychotic disorder over a primary psychotic disorder in this presentation?

options.text: The presence of persecutory delusions and auditory command hallucinations
Symptom resolution within one month of confirmed cannabis abstinence
The absence of formal thought disorder in this presentation
The negative family history for any psychotic disorders
The good premorbid functioning until cannabis use escalated

subtopic_detail: Brief psychotic disorder vs schizophreniform timeline
stem:
A 22-year-old university student is brought to the emergency department by her flatmate after 2 weeks of increasingly bizarre behaviour. She has been talking to people who are not there, expressing beliefs that her lecturers are monitoring her through her laptop camera, and has not slept for 3 days. She has no significant medical or psychiatric history. Urine drug screen is negative.

There is no family history of psychotic illness. Her flatmate reports a significant stressor 3 weeks ago when the patient discovered her partner was having an affair.

data_table.Investigations: UDS negative, FBC/UEC/TFTs/CRP normal, BSL 5.2 mmol/L

lead_in: Based on the duration of symptoms, what is the most appropriate provisional diagnosis?

options.text: Schizophrenia with acute onset presentation
Delusional disorder with persecutory type
Schizophreniform disorder with good prognostic features
Brief psychotic disorder with marked stressor
Acute stress disorder with psychotic features

stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department with tremor, agitation, diaphoresis, and visual hallucinations. He reports using gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB) daily for the past 8 months, taking approximately 3-5 mL every 2-3 hours including overnight doses. His last dose was 14 hours ago. He is oriented to person only. He has tachycardia and hypertension. He reports two seizures witnessed by his partner in the preceding 4 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/98 mmHg, HR 126 bpm, Temp 38.2, RR 24
data_table.Investigations: BSL 6.8 mmol/L, UDS positive for GHB only, CK 480 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological management of his withdrawal?

options.text: Commence symptom-triggered diazepam per alcohol withdrawal protocol
Administer naloxone 400 mcg IV as GHB is an opioid-like drug
High-dose benzodiazepines with consideration of adjunctive baclofen
Commence phenytoin loading dose for seizure management
Commence chlordiazepoxide tapering dose as outpatient

stem: A 21-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department from a music festival. She is agitated, confused, and diaphoretic. Friends report she took two MDMA capsules approximately 4 hours ago. On examination, she has clonus (greater in lower than upper limbs), hyperreflexia, dilated pupils, and jaw clenching. Her temperature is 39.4 degrees Celsius. She has not had any seizures. She is not on any regular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 152/94 mmHg, HR 134 bpm, Temp 39.4, RR 22
data_table.Investigations: Na 128 mmol/L, K 4.8 mmol/L, CK 1840 U/L, BSL 7.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most critical immediate intervention?

options.text: Active cooling measures to reduce core temperature below 38.5
Administer cyproheptadine 12 mg orally as serotonin antagonist
Administer IV hypertonic saline 100 mL for hyponatraemia
Administer IV dantrolene 1 mg/kg to reduce muscle rigidity
Sedate with IV midazolam 5 mg for agitation control

stem: A 35-year-old man from Afghanistan, who arrived in Australia 6 months ago on a humanitarian visa, is referred to your psychiatric clinic by his GP. He reports poor sleep, nightmares about his journey, hypervigilance, and avoidance of crowds. He becomes visibly distressed when discussing his past but insists he does not want to talk about specific traumatic events. He has difficulty trusting authority figures. An accredited interpreter is present.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to the initial psychiatric assessment?

options.text: Conduct a detailed trauma history to establish PTSD diagnosis
Establish safety and rapport; assess symptoms without trauma detail
Administer the PCL-5 questionnaire for PTSD screening first
Commence an SSRI immediately before establishing a diagnosis
Refer directly for trauma-focused CBT without any assessment

stem: A 30-year-old man with a diagnosis of schizophrenia has been stable on paliperidone palmitate monthly injections for 2 years. He is working part-time, living independently, and has good social supports. At his review, he asks about reducing or ceasing his antipsychotic medication. He acknowledges his past psychotic episodes were severe and required hospitalisation, but he finds the weight gain and sedation distressing. His treating team is concerned about relapse risk.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate response consistent with recovery-oriented practice?

options.text: Inform him that lifelong antipsychotic treatment is mandatory
Cease medication as patient autonomy overrides clinical advice
Refuse to discuss dose reduction given that relapse risk is high
Switch to a different antipsychotic without addressing request
Discuss risks collaboratively and explore dose reduction options

subtopic_detail: BPD therapy selection DBT vs MBT
stem: A 26-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder is referred for specialist psychotherapy. She has a history of recurrent self-harm (cutting), emotional dysregulation, unstable relationships, and chronic feelings of emptiness. She has had multiple ED presentations for self-harm, most recently 2 weeks ago. She is not currently on psychotropic medication. She has previously tried 'general supportive counselling' for 6 months without significant improvement. She is motivated to engage in structured therapy.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate evidence-based psychotherapy to recommend?

options.text: Psychodynamic psychotherapy with twice-weekly sessions
Dialectical behaviour therapy with skills group and individual therapy
Cognitive behavioural therapy for depression protocol
Schema-focused therapy with limited reparenting approach
EMDR therapy targeting traumatic memories from childhood

subtopic_detail: ECT cognitive side effects and electrode placement
stem: A 62-year-old man with severe treatment-resistant depression is being considered for electroconvulsive therapy. He has failed adequate trials of sertraline, venlafaxine, and lithium augmentation. He is currently experiencing psychomotor retardation, anhedonia, and passive suicidal ideation. He is a retired accountant who is concerned about cognitive side effects, particularly memory impairment, as he is writing his memoirs. He has no contraindications to anaesthesia.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate counselling regarding electrode placement and cognitive effects?

options.text: Bilateral ECT is the only effective placement with no memory loss
RUL brief-pulse ECT has equivalent efficacy with less cognitive impact
All cognitive effects are permanent and he should weigh this carefully
TMS would be equally effective and should be tried first before ECT
Ultra-brief pulse RUL ECT offers good efficacy with less cognitive impact

stem: An 18-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa is admitted to a medical ward. Her BMI is 13.8 kg/m2. She has been restricting intake to less than 500 kcal/day for the past 3 months. On examination, she is bradycardic, hypotensive, and hypothermic. Her sit-to-stand test shows a heart rate rise from 52 to 96 bpm. Blood tests reveal phosphate 0.62 mmol/L, potassium 3.0 mmol/L, and magnesium 0.58 mmol/L.

data_table.Investigations: BMI 13.8, Phosphate 0.62 mmol/L, K 3.0 mmol/L, Mg 0.58 mmol/L, Na 137, glucose 3.4 mmol/L, sit-stand HR rise 52 to 96

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial nutritional management strategy?

options.text: Commence nasogastric feeding at 2000 kcal/day to restore weight
Correct electrolytes only and defer feeding until she is stable
Total parenteral nutrition to bypass the gastrointestinal tract
Start 10-15 kcal/kg/day with electrolyte supplementation and monitoring
Start refeeding at 20 kcal/kg/day with daily electrolyte monitoring

stem: A 48-year-old man is referred by his GP for management of delusional disorder, persecutory type, diagnosed 2 years ago. He has the fixed belief that his neighbours are surveilling him through hidden cameras and contaminating his water supply. He has no hallucinations, thought disorder, or negative symptoms. His functioning is preserved in all domains except his relationship with neighbours, which has deteriorated. He has been trialled on risperidone 4 mg daily for 8 weeks with no improvement in his delusions, though he has been adherent.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase risperidone to 8 mg daily as higher dose may be needed
Add an SSRI to the antipsychotic as combination therapy trial
Switch antipsychotic and combine with CBT for psychosis treatment
Commence clozapine for treatment-resistant psychotic presentation
Cease antipsychotic as delusional disorder is medication-resistant

stem: A 32-year-old man is newly diagnosed with ADHD, combined presentation, after comprehensive neuropsychological assessment. He works as a delivery driver and holds a commercial vehicle licence. He is commenced on methylphenidate modified-release 18 mg daily. At his 4-week review, he reports improved concentration and reduced impulsivity. He asks about the implications for his driving licence and whether he needs to notify the road transport authority.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding his driving licence?

options.text: Notification to the road transport authority required for commercial licence
No notification required as ADHD does not affect driving ability
He must cease driving immediately and permanently lose his licence
Stimulant medication is incompatible with any driving licence at all
Only notify if he has had a motor vehicle accident in the past year

subtopic_detail: ADHD adult diagnosis and stimulant initiation
stem:
A 28-year-old graphic designer is referred to a community psychiatrist with 12 years of inattention, procrastination and disorganisation. She has just been retrenched after losing her third role for missed deadlines. She meets DSM-5 criteria for adult ADHD with childhood symptoms documented in school reports. She has no cardiovascular history, BP 124/76, ECG sinus rhythm with QTc 410 ms. She is not pregnant and uses condoms reliably.

She drives daily for work and to a child-care centre. She has a remote history of cocaine use in her early 20s, with no substance use for 5 years. Her younger brother takes methylphenidate.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 124/76, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7 degrees C, BMI 23
data_table.Examination: Engaged, eye contact good, no extrapyramidal features, no thyroid enlargement
data_table.Investigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs, TFTs normal; urine drug screen negative; ECG sinus rhythm QTc 410 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological choice?

options.text: Commence bupropion 150 mg daily as a stimulant-sparing strategy
Commence atomoxetine 40 mg daily and titrate to 80 mg over 2 weeks
Commence immediate-release dexamfetamine 5 mg three times daily
Commence cognitive behavioural therapy only and review in 8 weeks
Commence lisdexamfetamine 30 mg mornings, advise driving disclosure obligations

stem: A 32-year-old female teacher presents to a community psychiatry clinic at her partner's suggestion after 8 weeks of escalating exhaustion, social withdrawal and meltdowns at home after work. She has been treated by a GP for generalised anxiety disorder and recurrent depression since age 19 with multiple SSRI trials of partial benefit. She describes feeling 'always overwhelmed by sensory input' (lights, noise, clothing tags), having intense interests in classical opera and tortoises, and rehearses social scripts before meetings. She has had two long-term partners and one close friend since childhood. Her younger brother has a confirmed autism diagnosis.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Engaged eye contact (described as effortful), no thought disorder, mood mildly low, no psychotic features, no acute risk
data_table.Investigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs, TFTs normal; PHQ-9 score 14, GAD-7 score 16

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for borderline personality disorder evaluation given mood lability
Increase SSRI to high-dose sertraline 200 mg and continue management
Refer for structured ADOS-2 and ADI-R adult assessment with autism specialist
Recommend 6 months of cognitive behavioural therapy before further assessment
Discuss antipsychotic augmentation with low-dose aripiprazole therapy

subtopic_detail: GHB intoxication: airway and avoiding flumazenil
stem:
A 24-year-old man is brought to a metropolitan ED by ambulance at 0330 from a nightclub. He was found unresponsive in the bathroom. His friends report he had been drinking heavily and had taken something they called 'G'. On arrival he is deeply sedated, with shallow breathing, snoring respirations and no response to voice. He has a strong gag reflex when suctioned.

There is no evidence of opioid use on examination (pupils 3 mm). Naloxone 0.4 mg IV produced no response 5 minutes ago. IV access is patent.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 62, BP 108/64, RR 8, SpO2 91% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C, GCS 6 (E1 V1 M4)
data_table.Examination: Snoring respirations, gag reflex present, pupils 3 mm equal reactive, no needle marks, no head injury signs
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.31, pCO2 56 mmHg, lactate 1.6 mmol/L, glucose 5.8 mmol/L, ethanol 0.18 g/dL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed directly to rapid sequence intubation and ventilation now
Administer IV flumazenil 0.2 mg as a benzodiazepine reversal agent
Administer repeat IV naloxone 2 mg and admit for opioid withdrawal
Recovery position and supportive airway care with continuous capnography
Activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube to bind ingested toxin

stem: A 56-year-old man is reviewed in cardiac rehabilitation 4 weeks after an uncomplicated anterior NSTEMI managed with primary PCI. He has smoked 25 cigarettes a day for 35 years. He has tried unassisted cessation twice in his 40s but relapsed within 2 months. He has no history of depression, suicidal ideation, or psychiatric disease. He is taking aspirin, ticagrelor, atorvastatin, perindopril and bisoprolol. He says he is highly motivated to quit and asks for the most effective pharmacotherapy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 64, BP 122/78, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, BMI 28
data_table.Examination: Recovering well, no chest pain, ECG sinus rhythm
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 score 3, no suicidal ideation, FBC, U&E, LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Brief intervention with motivational interviewing and review in 3 months
Nicotine replacement patch 21 mg daily with oral lozenges as required
Bupropion 150 mg daily for 6 days then twice daily for 12 weeks
Varenicline with 7-day titration, then 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks
Electronic cigarettes (nicotine vaping) as primary cessation therapy

stem: A 31-year-old man is brought to a metropolitan ED at 2200 by police after threatening a stranger in the street. He is shouting incoherently, threatening staff, has assaulted two security officers and is at high risk of self-harm. De-escalation by experienced senior staff has failed. There is no available collateral. He has not responded to offered oral medication. The team has him in a safe assessment room with adequate staffing. He has no known cardiac history and no documented allergies; his weight is estimated at 80 kg. The senior nurse is preparing IM medication.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, BP 152/94, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: Highly aroused, pacing, no overt psychotic features identifiable, no medic-alert, no injection sites noted
data_table.Investigations: Not yet obtained

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological choice?

options.text: IM droperidol 10 mg as a single dose with continuous monitoring
IM olanzapine 10 mg with concurrent IM lorazepam 2 mg simultaneously
IM ketamine 4 mg/kg as sole sedative without an antipsychotic
Oral haloperidol 5 mg in liquid form offered again with verbal encouragement
IM midazolam 10 mg as sole agent without an antipsychotic

subtopic_detail: Aboriginal social and emotional wellbeing engagement
stem:
A 19-year-old Aboriginal man from a remote NSW community is brought to a regional ED by his auntie after a third presentation in 4 weeks with self-harm by superficial cutting. His parents died in a motor vehicle crash 18 months ago. He has not engaged with the community psychologist after a single appointment, declined antidepressant prescription, and was discharged each time within 4 hours.

He says he does not want to talk to 'another whitefella in a clinic'. He is calm at presentation and denies suicidal intent currently. He has no formal psychiatric diagnosis. He worked in mine maintenance until 6 months ago.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Engaged with auntie but minimal eye contact with clinician, superficial linear cuts on forearm, no active bleeding, no acute medical issue
data_table.Investigations: K10 score declined, alcohol audit pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.text: Involuntary admission under the Mental Health Act for involuntary treatment
Provide a written safety plan and discharge with GP follow-up only
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily and review again in 4 weeks
Refer to the local ACCHO and offer engagement with an Aboriginal Health Worker
Refer for inpatient psychotherapy with a metropolitan trauma team

stem: A 24-year-old man was diagnosed with ADHD combined type three months ago and started on dexamfetamine 10 mg twice daily. He reports significant improvement in concentration at work and asks about his driver licence obligations. He holds a private (Class C) licence in New South Wales. He has had no accidents or traffic infringements. His prescriber confirms stable dosing with no adverse effects.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding his driving licence?

options.text: He must notify the RMS and obtain a conditional licence with annual medical review with ongoing clinical monitoring
No notification is required provided his prescriber documents fitness to drive in the medical record
He must cease driving for six months after commencing the stimulant before reapplying for a conditional licence
He must downgrade to a non-stimulant medication such as atomoxetine before he can retain his unrestricted licence
No action is needed because ADHD treated with a stable stimulant dose does not meet the threshold for a reportable medical condition

stem: A 32-year-old woman with newly diagnosed ADHD predominantly inattentive type also has comorbid generalised anxiety disorder managed with escitalopram 20 mg daily. She is a registered nurse and expresses concern about Schedule 8 prescribing implications for her AHPRA registration. She prefers to avoid stimulant medication. Her resting heart rate is 84 bpm and blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line non-stimulant pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Guanfacine extended-release 1 mg daily at bedtime at this stage
Clonidine 100 mcg twice daily with dose adjustment to sedation
Bupropion sustained-release 150 mg daily for dual ADHD and anxiety benefit
Atomoxetine 40 mg daily, titrated over four weeks to target dose
Venlafaxine extended-release 75 mg daily for combined ADHD and anxiety coverage

stem: A 41-year-old man with ADHD has been on methylphenidate extended-release 54 mg daily for eight months with good symptom control. He presents for routine review. He is otherwise healthy with no cardiac history and no family history of sudden death. He denies chest pain, palpitations, or exercise intolerance.

data_table.Observations: HR 92, BP 142/88 mmHg (previous visit: HR 76, BP 126/78 mmHg)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat blood pressure on two further occasions over the next two weeks before making changes
Arrange a 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram before any medication changes at this stage
Switch to atomoxetine 40 mg daily given the cardiovascular concerns at this stage
Add amlodipine 5 mg daily to manage the hypertension while maintaining the current stimulant dose
Reduce methylphenidate to 36 mg daily and review blood pressure in two weeks

stem: A 29-year-old woman with ADHD combined type controlled on dexamfetamine 15 mg twice daily presents at 6 weeks gestation in an unplanned but desired pregnancy. She works as a paramedic and reports that without medication she cannot safely perform clinical tasks. She has no other psychiatric comorbidities. Her obstetrician has referred her for psychiatric review regarding medication continuation.

data_table.Medications: Dexamfetamine 15 mg BD, folate 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Cease dexamfetamine immediately given first-trimester teratogenicity and implement workplace adjustments
Discuss shared decision-making with lowest effective dose, occupational risk assessment, and trimester-by-trimester review
Continue dexamfetamine at current dose without modification as the evidence shows no teratogenic risk
Switch to atomoxetine which has a safer pregnancy profile than amphetamines and review clinical response accordingly
Cease dexamfetamine and commence cognitive behavioural therapy for ADHD as sole management at this stage

stem: A 26-year-old man is referred by his GP for assessment of possible ADHD. He reports lifelong difficulties with concentration, organisation, and impulsivity. However, his partner describes distinct episodes lasting 5-7 days every few months where he sleeps 3 hours per night, starts multiple business ventures simultaneously, spends excessively, and speaks rapidly. Between episodes his concentration difficulties persist. He has no substance use. His mother has bipolar I disorder.

data_table.History: Childhood school reports describe persistent inattention since age 7. Three hospitalisations in the past two years for agitation and grandiosity with spontaneous resolution after one week each.

lead_in: What is the most likely primary diagnosis?

options.text: Adult ADHD combined type with episodic hyperfocus misidentified as mania
Bipolar I disorder with comorbid ADHD given childhood-onset inattention predating mood episodes
Adult ADHD with episodic anxiety misinterpreted as mood cycling at this stage
Cyclothymic disorder with ADHD as the primary attentional diagnosis at this stage
Bipolar I disorder with inter-episode cognitive dysfunction mimicking ADHD symptoms

stem: A 35-year-old woman has been commenced on methylphenidate immediate-release 5 mg twice daily for newly diagnosed ADHD. At two-week review she reports mild improvement in focus during the morning dose but symptoms return by midday. She tolerates the medication well with no appetite suppression, insomnia, or cardiovascular concerns. She works full-time requiring sustained concentration across an 8-hour day.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Convert to methylphenidate extended-release 18 mg each morning with review in two weeks
Add a third dose of methylphenidate IR 5 mg at 4pm to extend afternoon coverage
Switch to methylphenidate extended-release 20 mg each morning at this stage
Increase to methylphenidate IR 10 mg twice daily and review in two weeks
Switch to lisdexamfetamine 30 mg daily as it provides longer duration of action

stem: A 22-year-old university student presents requesting assessment for ADHD. He reports difficulty concentrating during lectures and failing two subjects. He mentions his flatmate gave him dexamfetamine tablets before exams which he found helpful. He drinks 10-15 standard drinks each weekend. He denies other substance use. His childhood school reports do not mention attentional or behavioural concerns.

data_table.History: No childhood symptoms documented. AUDIT score 14. PHQ-9 score 8. No prior psychiatric contact. No family history of ADHD.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.text: Decline ADHD assessment as the absence of childhood symptoms excludes the diagnosis at this stage
Complete full ADHD assessment with collateral history, and address hazardous alcohol use and academic stress concurrently
Commence a dexamfetamine 5 mg trial as his positive response supports the ADHD diagnosis at this stage
Refer directly for neuropsychological testing as the definitive diagnostic tool for ADHD at this stage
Prescribe atomoxetine as it has lower misuse potential while the ADHD assessment proceeds at this stage

stem: A 38-year-old man with ADHD combined type has trialled methylphenidate ER titrated to 72 mg daily over 12 weeks with only partial response. He then trialled dexamfetamine titrated to 40 mg daily over 8 weeks with modest improvement but developed significant appetite suppression and 6 kg weight loss. His psychiatrist now wishes to trial lisdexamfetamine.

data_table.Medications: Currently dexamfetamine 40 mg daily (to be ceased)
data_table.History: Two adequate stimulant trials failed. No substance use. No cardiac history.

lead_in: What PBS criterion must be met for lisdexamfetamine authority prescription?

options.text: Failure of at least one adequate trial of methylphenidate at maximum tolerated dose for a minimum of four weeks at this stage
A neuropsychological assessment confirming ADHD diagnosis within the preceding 12 months with regular monitoring of clinical parameters
Failure of methylphenidate plus documented cardiovascular contraindication to dexamfetamine as the sole alternative pathway
Prior authority approval for atomoxetine with documented failure before stimulant class escalation and review clinical response accordingly
Documented inadequate response to both methylphenidate and dexamfetamine at adequate doses with specialist confirmation of ongoing functional impairment

stem: A 62-year-old woman with severe melancholic depression has not responded to two adequate antidepressant trials and lithium augmentation over 16 weeks. She is severely psychomotor retarded and has lost 12 kg. Her psychiatrist recommends ECT. She has capacity and understands the recommendation but refuses, stating she does not want general anaesthesia. She is an involuntary patient under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007.

data_table.History: Failed escitalopram 20 mg 8 weeks, venlafaxine 225 mg 8 weeks, lithium augmentation 8 weeks. BMI 17.2.

lead_in: What is the correct legal position regarding ECT administration?

options.text: ECT can proceed under the treating psychiatrist's authority alone as she is involuntary at this stage
ECT cannot be given as she has capacity and has refused regardless of involuntary status at this stage
Her designated person responsible can provide substitute consent for ECT with multidisciplinary team involvement
ECT can proceed under emergency provisions given her malnutrition poses immediate risk to life
Application must be made to the Mental Health Review Tribunal which can authorise ECT despite her refusal if criteria are met

stem: A 55-year-old man with treatment-resistant major depression with psychotic features has consented to ECT. He works as a barrister and expresses strong concern about cognitive side effects, particularly retrograde amnesia affecting case recall. He has no contraindications to anaesthesia. His psychiatrist is planning treatment parameters.

data_table.History: Treatment-resistant MDD with persecutory delusions. No prior ECT. MMSE 28/30 at baseline.

lead_in: What electrode placement offers the best balance of efficacy and cognitive preservation?

options.text: Right unilateral at six times seizure threshold with standard brief pulse width of 1.0 ms
Right unilateral at six times seizure threshold with ultra-brief pulse width of 0.3 ms
Bifrontal at 1.5 times seizure threshold as the lowest cognitive impact option
Bilateral bitemporal at 1.5 times seizure threshold with ultra-brief pulse width
Left unilateral to preserve non-dominant hemisphere verbal memory function

stem: A 48-year-old woman on lithium carbonate 900 mg daily (level 0.7 mmol/L) for bipolar depression is scheduled to commence ECT. Her anaesthetist raises concerns about continuing lithium. She has previously relapsed within weeks of lithium cessation. Her renal and thyroid function are normal.

data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L, eGFR 92, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, Na 139 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to lithium management during ECT?

options.text: Continue lithium at current dose throughout the ECT course without modification
Withhold lithium on the evening before and morning of each ECT treatment, resuming after recovery
Cease lithium entirely two weeks before commencing ECT and restart after the course
Reduce lithium by 50% throughout the ECT course to maintain a level below 0.4 mmol/L
Switch from lithium to valproate for mood stabilisation before commencing ECT

stem: A 70-year-old woman with recurrent severe melancholic depression has responded excellently to an acute course of 10 bilateral ECT sessions. She has had three prior episodes in 8 years, each requiring ECT as she is intolerant of SSRIs (hyponatraemia) and TCAs (urinary retention). After each previous course she relapsed within 3 months despite lithium. Her MADRS is now 4.

data_table.History: Three previous ECT courses with excellent response. Relapse within 12 weeks each time on lithium alone.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate relapse prevention strategy?

options.text: Continue lithium monotherapy with close monitoring and re-referral if symptoms recur
Commence maintenance ECT with gradually increasing intervals combined with ongoing lithium
Switch lithium to nortriptyline for post-ECT relapse prevention as evidence supports this
Trial venlafaxine as a post-ECT antidepressant given SSRIs caused hyponatraemia but SNRIs may not
Recommend rTMS as a less invasive maintenance strategy with comparable efficacy

stem: A 58-year-old man undergoing his sixth bilateral ECT session for catatonic depression receives the stimulus at the same parameters as previously (which produced a 35-second seizure), but EEG shows no seizure activity. A second stimulus at 10% higher charge also fails. His concurrent medications include sodium valproate 1000 mg twice daily.

data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 1000 mg BD, mirtazapine 30 mg nocte
data_table.Pre-ECT: Propofol, suxamethonium, glycopyrronium bromide as per previous sessions

lead_in: What is the most likely cause of the failed seizure induction?

options.text: Progressive rise in seizure threshold from repeated ECT sessions as normal physiological adaptation
Excessive propofol dose raising seizure threshold above stimulation parameters
Anticonvulsant effect of sodium valproate raising seizure threshold above the maximum deliverable charge
Electrode-scalp impedance artefact causing current shunting without cerebral stimulation
Mirtazapine-induced sedation compounding propofol anticonvulsant effects synergistically

stem: A 34-year-old man with schizophrenia was started on haloperidol 10 mg daily for acute psychosis. Five days later he developed rigidity, mutism, posturing, and negativism with temperature 38.9 degrees C and CK 4200 U/L. Haloperidol was ceased. After two doses of lorazepam 2 mg IV over 6 hours he showed no improvement. His temperature is now 39.2 degrees C and CK has risen to 6800 U/L with creatinine rising from 78 to 142 micromol/L.

data_table.Investigations: CK 6800 U/L, WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, Na 141 mmol/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 78)
data_table.Examination: Generalised rigidity, waxy flexibility, mute, no eye tracking

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step given lorazepam non-response?

options.text: Increase lorazepam to 4 mg IV every 6 hours and reassess in 24 hours at this stage
Commence dantrolene 1 mg/kg IV as this represents neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Commence bromocriptine 2.5 mg TDS and dantrolene as combination NMS-specific therapy
Arrange emergency ECT given lorazepam non-response in deteriorating malignant catatonia
Transfer to ICU for supportive management while avoiding all psychotropic medications for 14 days

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with acute-onset right leg weakness after an argument with her partner. She cannot bear weight. Examination reveals give-way weakness of right hip flexion, but when asked to flex her left hip against resistance, strong involuntary right hip flexion is observed. Sensation is reduced in a non-dermatomal distribution below the right knee. CT brain and CTA are normal. She has a history of childhood sexual abuse.

data_table.Examination: Right leg 2/5 hip flexion (give-way), positive Hoover sign, non-dermatomal sensory loss right leg, normal reflexes, plantars downgoing
data_table.Investigations: CT brain normal, CT angiogram normal

lead_in: What clinical sign provides the strongest positive diagnostic evidence for functional neurological disorder?

options.text: Non-dermatomal sensory loss below the right knee and review clinical response at follow-up
Give-way weakness pattern with brief full power before sudden release at this stage
Acute onset temporally related to a psychosocial stressor with trauma history
Normal CT brain and CTA excluding structural neurological pathology at this stage
Positive Hoover sign demonstrating involuntary right hip extension during contralateral hip flexion

stem: A 31-year-old nurse presents to the emergency department for the fourth time in six months with recurrent hypoglycaemia. Each episode occurs early morning with confusion and diaphoresis resolving with glucose. Her BSL is 2.1 mmol/L. Insulin is markedly elevated at 840 pmol/L with suppressed C-peptide of 0.08 nmol/L. She has no diabetes. CT pancreas is normal. She becomes evasive when questioned about insulin access at work.

data_table.Investigations: BSL 2.1 mmol/L, insulin 840 pmol/L (RR 20-150), C-peptide 0.08 nmol/L (RR 0.4-1.5), sulfonylurea screen negative, CT pancreas normal

lead_in: What biochemical pattern confirms the mechanism of hypoglycaemia?

options.text: Recurrent early-morning pattern suggesting fasting-related autonomous insulin secretion
High insulin with high C-peptide indicating endogenous hyperinsulinism from insulinoma
Negative sulfonylurea screen excluding surreptitious oral hypoglycaemic ingestion
High insulin with low C-peptide indicating exogenous insulin administration
Normal CT pancreas excluding insulinoma and confirming a functional cause

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with bilateral leg weakness four weeks after a workplace injury for which he has a compensation claim. He uses a wheelchair. Examination shows give-way weakness and positive bilateral Hoover sign. MRI spine is normal. Nursing staff document him walking to the bathroom independently when unobserved. When confronted he becomes distressed saying he does not understand why his legs sometimes work and sometimes do not.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral give-way weakness, positive Hoover sign bilaterally, normal reflexes, normal sensation
data_table.Investigations: MRI lumbar and thoracic spine normal, NCS normal

lead_in: What feature most strongly argues against malingering in favour of FND?

options.text: His genuine distress and confusion when confronted with the inconsistency between observed and reported function
The positive Hoover sign which cannot be voluntarily produced by a malingerer at this stage
The absence of secondary gain as his compensation claim predates symptom onset at this stage
Normal investigations excluding organic pathology and supporting a non-organic process
Bilateral symptoms which are more characteristic of FND than strategic malingering at this stage

stem: A 3-year-old boy has been admitted 8 times in 14 months with unexplained apnoeic episodes occurring only when his mother is alone with him. Extensive workup is normal. His mother has a nursing background. Covert video during the latest admission shows the mother placing a pillow over the child's face before pressing the call button.

data_table.History: 8 admissions, all normal workup. Apnoea only witnessed by mother.
data_table.Investigations: Normal: PSG, EEG, Holter, metabolic screen, CXR

lead_in: What is the immediate priority action?

options.text: Confront the mother with the video evidence and offer psychiatric assessment at this stage
Request hospital legal counsel review the video before taking action to ensure procedural validity
Arrange a multidisciplinary team meeting within 48 hours to discuss findings at this stage
Discharge the child to the father's care while arranging outpatient psychiatric referral for the mother
Ensure continuous supervised contact between mother and child and notify child protection services immediately
